#3479. Netflix's #1 Crime Thriller Officially Breaks 2026 Record, Bucking Streaming Trend

A star-studded crime thriller movie has been dominating Netflix for weeks, allowing it to break a 2026 record by performing better than the majority of Netflix Originals. Making movies with Hollywood's biggest names and directors, and pairing them with reliably successful genres, has been the primary focus of Netflix's movie model over the years.

Action, rom-coms, and animation have proven to be valuable avenues for the streamer to pursue, but so too are crime thrillers. In recent years, they've seen this with Taron Egerton and Jason Bateman's Carry-On, Aaron Pierre's Rebel Ridge, and Ben Affleck and Matt Damon's The Rip all finding huge audiences around the globe.

It's now claimed a 2026 record by becoming the first movie to sit atop Netflix's global Top 10 charts for English movies for four consecutive weeks. The Rip previously held the record at three weeks. Animals' four-week run as the #1 movie on Netflix is more impressive when you dive into the history of Netflix Original movies topping the charts.

With the frequent output of new Netflix Original movies, it is common for one of the exclusive streaming titles to be the most-watched movie every week. So far in 2026, there have been 24 different Netflix Originals to be the #1 movie on the streamer's weekly charts; only Jurassic World Rebirth and Anaconda have broken through to the top spot.

While that gives Netflix lots of opportunities to tout the success of its original movies, they don't often stay in that spot for long. 14 of the 24 films in 2026 have stayed #1 for two weeks, but only two (The Rip and Animals) have done it longer. There are also even more Netflix Originals released this year that never topped the charts.

164 different movies have been #1 on the English movie charts since June 2021. However, only 85 have done so for at least two weeks, 84 of which have been Netflix Originals. That number drops to just 19 films that have been #1 in the world for three straight weeks or longer.

To put that into perspective, Netflix has released well over 500 English-language original movies, documentaries, and specials since these charts have been public. Less than 20% stay #1 for two weeks, and we're down to under 5% if we go to three weeks. Four weeks, like Animals, is incredibly rare (less than 1%).

It is quite common for these movies to stay in the top 10 for weeks after, but they never regain the #1 spot, unless they're KPop Demon Hunters (which has spent a record nine weeks at the top of the charts, but never for longer than three weeks straight). It's highly unusual for a Netflix movie to have as much staying power as Animals.

To date, only four other movies have had runs at the top of Netflix's charts for as long as Animals. Ryan Reynolds' The Adam Project was the first to do so in March-April 2022. Jennifer Lopez's The Mother did it next in May-June 2023, followed by Carry-On from December 2024-January 2025 and The Life List from March-April 2025, both featuring Sofia Carson.

In these previous instances, the four weeks atop Netflix's charts propelled the movies to incredible viewership figures. Carry-On and The Adam Project are still in the top 5 of Netflix's most-watched movies ever, boasting 172.1 and 157.6 million views apiece (during their first 91 days of release). The Mother was a top 10 finisher at the time with 117 million views, while The Life List logged over 90 million views over the same time.

To be clear, Animals has done solid numbers for Netflix, sitting at 70 million views after its first month on the streamer. But its fourth week wasn't really worthy of breaking this record, as it won the week with only 4.7 million views after experiencing a 56% drop in viewers from the week before. That's the lowest ever for a week's #1 movie.

While these charts began in June 2021, it wasn't until June 2023 that Netflix started sharing viewership figures on top of hours viewed. There have been 177 weeks since then, and Animals' 4.7 million views rank 177th across. It finished 900,000 views below the previous worst #1 finish: Jurassic World Rebirth's 5.6 million views earlier this year.

The Adam Project and The Mother's runs predated Netflix's official viewership stats, but we can calculate based on hours viewed that they came in around 10 million and 8.3 million, respectively. Carry-On had a massive 17.4 million views, while The Life List had 7.5 million. That puts Animals well behind the pace of the elite performers its joined.

Animals' ability to still be #1 on Netflix in its fourth week is more so a result of how weak programming has been for the streamer lately. Audiences have not had a new, major movie come out that could take attention away. Animals has been the default viewing option as a result.

It probably will be some time before another Netflix movie can match Animals' four-week run as the #1 movie in the world. It's never occurred twice in the same year, but if one of Netflix's remaining 2026 originals is going to do it, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth holds the best chance.

Beyond that, it is most tempting to look at upcoming Netflix IP plays given their built-in fanbases. Narnia: The Magician's Nephew will have every expectation to obliterate viewership numbers for the streamer when it arrives in April 2027. Extraction 3, Grown Ups 3, and War Machines could do it thanks to proven streaming stars. A good bet is KPop Demon Hunters 2 when it comes out in 2029.

#3478. ‘Caligula’ Director Tinto Brass Dies at 93

Giovanni “Tinto” Brass, an avant-garde filmmaker best known for directing the X-rated historical epic “Caligula,” has died. He was 93 years old. His wife Caterina Varzi and children Bonifacio and Beatrice Brass told Italian news agency Ansa that Brass had died, but did not give a cause.

Brass’ career kicked off in the 1960s and ’70s with a series of experimental films including his debut, “Who Works Is Lost,” which followed a day in the life of an unemployed designer. It screened at the 1963 Venice Film Festival. Other early works includes “Yankee,” a 1966 Western about a standoff between a bounty hunter and a crime boss, as well as “Col cuore in gola,” a 1967 murder mystery which featured Jean-Louis Trintignant.

With 1976’s “Salon Kitty,” a historical drama set in a Berlin brothel during the Nazi era, Brass moved into erotic filmmaking. But it was “Caligula,” an infamous look at one of Rome’s most notorious emperors, that made a name for Brass. The film was written by Gore Vidal, who later disavowed it, and produced by Penthouse founder Bob Guccione. It featured a cast of esteemed actors such as Peter O’Toole, Helen Mirren, John Gielgud, and Malcolm McDowell in the title role, but made headlines for its frank look at ancient Rome’s sexual depravity, depicting orgies and hardcore sex. “Caligula” was re-edited and re-cut several times only to bomb at the box office when it opened in the U.S. in 1980. However, it has built up a significant cult following over the decades and an 178-minute “Ultimate Cut,” premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in 2023 to a warmer reception from reviewers.

#3476. The 9 Most Atmospheric Fantasy Books of All Time

Atmosphere is critically important in a fantasy book, where it's vital for whatever kind of magical world the story takes place in to feel like a living, breathing space that can connect with readers emotionally, tonally, and thematically. Many writers throughout history have perfectly understood this, but there are ten particular fantasy masterpieces which can be counted among the most deeply atmospheric in the genre's history.

What makes a fantasy book atmospheric? It's a question that can have a myriad of potentially satisfying answers. On the whole, however, this is a quality all about a strong sense of immersion, an enveloping mood, and a world so carefully crafted that it almost feels truly palpable. From magical realism classics like Pedro Páramo to science fantasy masterpieces like Perdido Street Station, the most atmospheric fantasy books of all time are a testament to how important this aspect of fantasy writing is.

Romantic, subtle, and full of adventure and suspense, Patricia A. McKillip's The Forgotten Beasts of Eld is one of those forgotten high fantasy books that have aged beautifully. Its narrative follows Sybel, an isolated mountain witch living with a menagerie of mythical beasts, who's suddenly forced out of her solitude when she agrees to raise a child tied to a brutal royal war.

The book is often celebrated for its beautifully lush and poetic prose, which makes the whole thing feel like a delectably modern fairy tale. McKillip seems to be in no rush to get through the already-brief length of around 200 pages. Instead, she takes the time to describe every color, smell, and sensation in Sybel's environment, favoring texture and atmosphere over heavy exposition or traditional high fantasy action.

It's no exaggeration of any sort to say that Ursula K. Le Guin is one of the greatest and most influential speculative fiction authors in history. It's also no exaggeration to say that her Earthsea Cycle is one of the most foundational series of fantasy novels in the genre's history. The second installment is The Tombs of Atuan, about the young priestess Arha having to choose between her sacred duty to the gods and her own survival.

It's often A Wizard of Earthsea, the first book in the Cycle, that's praised as Le Guin's magnum opus, but fans of the saga would likely agree that Le Guin never wrote a more engrossingly atmospheric fantasy novel than Tombs of Atuan. With a relatively narrow scope that makes its world feel as claustrophobic as it does magical, Le Guin uses sensory deprivation as such a central plot element of the novel that it inevitably starts affecting the reader's experience incredibly deeply.

Having completed her diploma in French and Russian literature and being particularly passionate about the latter, Katherine Arden wrote her debut novel, The Bear and the Nightingale, with the specific wish to write a book set in Medieval Russia. Informed by Russian folklore and Slavic mythology, it's the first installment in Arden's Winternight trilogy, and it's about a young girl with the ability to communicate with mythical creatures at a time when Orthodox Christianity is attempting to eradicate belief in such beings.

The Bear and the Nightingale is set in the freezing Russian winter, but the cold here is far more than just a seasonal backdrop. Rather, it's almost a living, nearly palpable entity that creates a sense of sensorial immersion not often seen in this genre. Bolstered by the detailed point of view of our fascinating protagonist, it becomes impossible to not find oneself enraptured by the narrative.

Gene Wolfe's absolutely revolutionary The Book of the New Sun consists of four volumes and a coda, but those five elements are technically all part of a single massive science fantasy epic. The story follows Severian, an exiled apprentice torturer journeying across a decaying future Earth to take up a new post, inadvertently becoming entangled in a path toward imperial rule and the rebirth of a dying Sun.

Widely recognized as one of the best science fantasy books of all time, Book of the New Sun builds an enrapturing atmosphere largely through highly archaic language. It may make the prose challenging to read, but it's all in service of a fascinating narrative that makes it incredibly easy to believe that this is, indeed, a decayed far-future Earth where surrealism and grotesqueness are the order of the day.

Due to a debilitating chronic illness and the cognitive impairment that came as a result, it took 15 years for Susanna Clarke to finally write Piranesi. Boy, was it worth it. One of the best books published since 2020, this surreal masterpiece follows an amnesiac man living in a seemingly infinite labyrinth. There, he gradually discovers that he was trapped there by a researcher seeking secret knowledge.

Clarke is an absolute master of atmosphere, and people who love the works of artists like David Lynch and Jorge Luis Borges will likely be able to appreciate the wonderful sense of mind-bending poetry with which she crafted Piranesi. The entire story hinges on Clarke being able to sell this space as infinitely vast yet intimately lonely, and saying that she succeeded at that wouldn't even begin to cover the book's award-winning brilliance.

There is perhaps no modern author of weird fiction greater, more important, or more influential than China Miéville; and there is probably no book of his more widely celebrated or iconic than Perdido Street Station. It's the first book in the New Crobuzon series, and it follows a renegade scientist's attempts to help a flightless birdman, which unwittingly hatches vampiric creatures terrorizing the industrial metropolis of New Crobuzon.

On top of being a masterful fantasy novel, it's also one of the best soft sci-fi books of all time; such is the genre-bending magic of modern weird fiction. A pioneer of the New Weird movement, Perdido Street Station is built on a Gothic, overwhelmingly dense, almost nauseating foundation of industrial rot and bureaucratic oppression. It's grotesque, visceral, and can even get nightmarishly scary.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

Somewhere around the '60s and '70s, Latin America became one of the major epicenters of world literature with what has since become known as the Latin American Boom. One of the major predecessors of such a movement was Mexican author Juan Rulfo, whose legendary classic Pedro Páramo follows a man traveling to a desolate Mexican town to find the father he never knew, only to discover that the inhabitants are all dead.

It's one of the best magical realism books of all time, as well as one of the most foundational. This Mexican classic is quite short, but Rulfo builds such a hypnotic, desolate, and haunting atmosphere that the book's emotional and intellectual effects end up lasting a lifetime. The town of Comala serves as both a literal and metaphorical purgatory, and Rulfo makes it feel exactly as disorienting and claustrophobic as one might expect.

Before she wrote Piranesi, Susanna Clarke made a hell of a name for herself with the Hugo Award winner Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell, one of the best historical fantasy books of all time. Set in an alternative 19th-century version of England during the Napoleonic Wars, it follows two vastly different men whose bitter professional rivalry quickly spirals out of control.

It's an absolutely hypnotic novel, its magical Regency England setting informed by ten years of exhaustive historical, military, and literary research. As a result, Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell is one of the most atmospheric debut novels of 21st-century fantasy literature. London feels cold, foggy, and wet; magic is dry and tedious; and the use of scholarly-like footnotes makes it even easier to lose oneself in this mesmerizing world.

Mervyn Peake is one of the most important and foundational precursors of modern weird fiction, and his Gormenghast series is widely accepted as his magnum opus. The eponymous Gormenghast is the second book in the series, and it follows the rebellious young earl Titus Groan as he fights to break free from his castle's suffocating traditions, while the kitchen boy Steerpoke schemes to overthrow the entire ancient hierarchy.

Rarely has history seen a fantasy author who excelled at crafting an atmosphere this oppressive more than Mervyn Peake. This is fantasy built not on grand quests or intricate magic systems, but rather on a pure focus on atmosphere. Decay, claustrophobia, unpleasant textures, and a study of the very nature of the grotesque all make up the foundations of Gormenghast. It's a book so potently surreal and nightmarish that it's hard to believe it's nearly 80 years old.

#3475. 10 of the Most Iconic Patrick Stewart Roles Beyond Captain Picard

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

Sir Patrick Stewart, an actor equally at home onstage at the Royal Shakespeare Company and on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise, has died at the age of 86. Unexpectedly for most of us, in part because he kept his final illness private, but more so because it once seemed as though nothing could fell the man who looms so large in our cultural consciousness.

The thoughtful, erudite performer who had a troubled childhood in working-class Yorkshire; the committed socialist who was eventually knighted by Queen Elizabeth; the advocate who put his money and his considerable voice toward the fights for LGBTQ+ acceptance and animal welfare and against domestic violence, his presence and performances meant the world (the galaxy, even) to myself and so many others. But those who knew him personally can offer better tributes; perhaps it's best left to Shakespeare's Player King, performed by Stewart himself opposite David Warner's Hamlet back in 1965:

Where joy most revels, grief doth most lament;Grief joys, joy grieves, on slender accident.

Much of Stewart's finest work was on the stage; other performances remain rather shockingly hard to come by (whither I, Claudius?). Nonetheless, he left a true legacy behind him, well beyond Captain Picard and Professor X. Here are 10 of his most iconic other roles.

A goofy, feel-good gay rom-com with the HIV/AIDS crisis still very much in the foreground, Jeffrey was a near-impossibility in the mid-1990s: a movie that neither villainized its queers nor treated them as pitiable martyrs. Steven Weber and Michael T. Weiss are the leads, joined by a cast that includes Christine Baranski, Victor Garber, Nathan Lane, Olympia Dukakis, and Sigourney Weaver but, for all those names, Stewart is the undeniable standout as Sterling, the irrepressible gay best friend: a swishing, mincing, sassy, high-camp character who steals every scene without ever becoming a caricature. He's the leader of the "Pink Panthers," a squad of queers who defend locals from gay bashers, and that is the key to the character's power: He's as gay as they come, but not ashamed and not even a little weak. This movie, and the presence of Captain Picard himself in it, might have saved my life back in 1995. Stream Jeffrey on Prime Video, Tubi, and The Roku Channel.

A sprawling, epic, and appropriately lusty take on the King Arthur stories from John Boorman, Excalibur is a mixed bag full of stunning visuals and iconic moments that never quite coalesce into something entirely coherent. Standing out among the film's many characters, Stewart is entirely memorable as Leodegrance, the boisterous, boorish, but ultimately faithful father of Guenevere who is among the first to pledge his loyalty to Arthur. Rent Excalibur from Prime Video.

Darcy Banker is erudite and intellectual, in his way, and even capable of charm, but otherwise has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. It's bad enough for the punk band Ain’t Rights that they've booked a last-minute gig at an Oregon bar without realizing that it's a haven for white supremacists. It's even worse when they witness a murder and become trapped in the title's green room, with Stewart as the lead skinhead. He's quite simply one of the all-time great (meaning absolutely terrifying) villains in this thriller that's pretty much a horror movie. Stream Green Room on Netflix.

Patrick Stewart's role as Professor Xavier in the X-Men is almost as pop-culture iconic as that of Captain Picard, spanning 26 years and nine movies, including the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday. In most of those, he looks like he's having an awful lot of fun, but he gives his finest performance in the role in this elegaic installment, playing a dying Professor in profound cognitive decline, his dream in tatters and his bravado worn down to prickly dependence. We rarely get to see our superheroes at the ends of their days, and there's a lovely bravery to this depiction of the Charles' journey. Logan will likely be the toughest of his films to rewatch in the coming days. Stream Logan on Disney+.

This stagey television movie isn't the most sumptuous of the many filmed versions of the Dickens story, but you won't be surprised to learn that there are few better portrayals of Ebenezer Scrooge. It's rather a shame that Patrick Stewart didn't do more Dickens adaptations, since his booming voice and ability to play thoroughly heightened characters without ever resorting to caricature is as valuable as in Shakespeare. Rent A Christmas Carol from Prime Video.

Famously referred to as that "unknown British Shakespearean actor" when starting out on Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stewart was an associate of the Royal Shakespeare Company for twenty years before his most famous role came along. As is the way of live theater, much of his career lives on as an essential link in the chain of Shakespeare performances in the twentieth century...but not in a way that we can conveniently stream. We do, however, have this impressively mounted modern-dress stage production, in which Stewart plays King Claudius with characteristic brilliance against David Tennant's melancholy prince. Buy Hamlet from Prime Video and Apple TV.

As a cinematic actor, Stewart's greatest strength was bringing humanity to larger-than-life, even operatic roles, whether they be Arthurian knights, Dickensian villains, or superheroes. That ability is an absolute necessity if one is going to have any success doing Shakespeare, as Stewart did for decades. Match is something rather different, though, and it's rather lovely to see him play something just a bit more mundane—even if the film's Tobi Powell is a choreographer with a nearly legendary reputation. Teaching at Juilliard School, with his career winding down, he's confronted with the living embodiment of the past he left behind to pursue his career. The ensuing relationships grow more complex, with the film building to a climax that's surprising and deeply devastating, made all the more so by Stewart's muted, subtle performance. Stream Match on AMC+.

This is not the greatest Mel Brooks movie, not by a long shot, but it is a great comedic performance from Patrick Stewart. He loved to recount, with self-effacing embarrassment, the story of having shouted "We are not here to have fun" at his co-workers during a rowdy day on set at Star Trek: The Next Generation. By 1993, he was clearly past any such pomposity, and clearly having fun in his cameo as King Richard, a memorably silly take on a character he might well have played with seriousness elsewhere. Rent Robin Hood: Men in Tights from Prime Video.

Stewart's first real foray into science fiction was in this big, bold, divisive, and thoroughly bonkers Frank Herbert adaptation from director David Lynch. Stewart plays troubadour and warrior Gurney Halleck, and does what he does best: bringing gravitas and believability (and it must be said, bald sexiness) to even the wildest material. Stream Dune on Tubi.

Stewart plays an aged Merlin in this rather shockingly good modern reimagining of the King Arthur legendarium. His Merlin is all wild hair and rock band T-shirts, possessed of an essential kindness that makes him a valued mentor, and one deserving of his character's poignant farewell at the film's conclusion.Stream The Kid Who Would Be King on Disney+ and Prime Video.

#3474. Alan Cumming Says ‘Tip Toe’ Was His Greatest Role Ever — but He Never Wants to Think About It Again

[Editor’s note: The following interview contains spoilers for “Tip Toe,” including its finale.]

Most viewers these days know Alan Cumming for hanging out with Traitors, in one of television’s most addictive reality shows. But recently, he took on a role of a lifetime in limited series “Tip Toe,” in which he plays Leo, a queer bartender with a heart of gold whose life is cut short when he tries to strike up a friendship with his volatile and bigoted neighbor, Clive.

The five-episode limited series takes viewers on an emotional journey, opening with a shocking first scene which is also how the series ends. Leo has been hung outside his house, with Clive and a group of men looking on. Leo’s story is beautifully devastating, and the finale is one hour of gutting television. Related Stories ‘The Greatest’ Review: Amazon’s Handsome Muhammed Ali Biopic Connects in Spite of Itself The Mad (Color) Science Behind Rian Johnson’s New Camera App

Cumming recently sat down with IndieWire to discuss the finale and why he now needs to let Leo go.

Created and written by Russell T. Davies of “Doctor Who” fame, “Tip Toe” follows Leo and Clive (David Morrissey) in the days leading up to Leo’s brutal death at Clive’s hands. The show is not only filled with trauma, but deep joy, especially in showing the friendship between Leo and George, Clive’s teenage son, who is grappling with his own secret about his sexuality.

Davies can’t say enough good things about Cumming, and revealed that he took the entire young cast to a Lady Gaga concert as a bonding experience. Cumming confessed that he and Davies had been trying to work together for years, but it never worked out timing wise, until “Tip Toe.” Let’s just say Davies had Cumming at hello.

“Nine months before, we had a Zoom, and I simply described scene one of ‘Tip Toe,’ and from that moment on we had him,” Davies said, lighting up as he recalling the chat. He added that Cumming kept his schedule free a year before for filming the series.

“It’s the thing I’m most proud of in my career acting-wise,” Cumming said. “It was so grueling and traumatic to make.” He added that he didn’t really have to do extra research, because he lived through a lot of what Leo lived through. “I’ve never really played a part where I was able to bring so much of my own life, my own experience to the screen,” he said.

He also sees why Leo tried to trust Clive so much. “I understand everything Leo did. I let people behave badly for too long,” Cumming said. “I try to see the best in people … thinking you can fix people. And also, just being sort of a people-pleaser.”

Cumming said his favorite experience making the show was when the cast came to see his play in Scotland, and then came up for a weekend to his house in the Highlands. As for those grueling, traumatic end scenes, Cumming said, “The football boys who had to kill me were so supportive during filming.” With each terrible scene, they would stop and hug Cumming afterwards. “In the course of doing something about what a terrible place we are in our society, I was really heartened by working with the young people in this,” he said.

Filming the finale was not easy for any of them. “The hanging scene was just awful to do. It was so long, took so many days. The actual going up, and being hung, it was so traumatic. I didn’t realize how traumatized I was by it, until it came out. As soon as it finished [filming], I’ve never wanted to get away from a character as much as Leo. As much as I loved him. It was so heavy on my shoulders,” Cumming said.

But the true heart of the show, according to Cumming, is Davies’ writing. “It could easily be horrible straight guy and battered gay guy. What’s so brilliant about the writing is you can see blame and fault in both ways. But also, goodness in both,” he said.

In many ways, the show couldn’t have come at a better time. Cumming said, “It’s so prescient. We have allowed hateful rhetoric to become normalized. To the point that, we don’t bat an eye when really awful things happen. … Hopefully, this will be a conversation starter.”

For Cumming’s breakdown of the finale, watch the full interview in the video above.

All five episodes of “Tip Toe” are streaming now on Starz.

#3473. WhatsApp announces four new features to make group chats easier to manage

In a blog post this week, WhatsApp confirmed that it is rolling out four new features designed to make it easier to manage group chats and keep track of what’s going on in each one. Here are the details.

WhatsApp this week announced that the filter drawer, which appears when users swipe down on the conversations list, will now include a “Mentions and replies” button alongside other filter options such as Groups, Favorites, Unread and custom filters.

Once tapped, the chat list will show only “unread group conversation[s] where you were either mentioned or received a direct reply, including @all messages,” says WhatsApp.

Additionally, WhatsApp will now let users pin messages indefinitely in group chats, rather than choosing between 24 hours, 7 days, or 30 days.

Another in-chat feature coming to groups is the ability to “send someone recent messages retroactively after they’ve joined a group just by tapping their name in the chat.” Previously, this was only possible when adding someone to a group, rather than after they had joined.

Finally, WhatsApp is rolling out group status sharing, which lets users post updates visible only to members of a specific group. Other members can view, react to, and add their own statuses, which disappear after 24 hours.

As is often the case with WhatsApp updates, it may take some time for all four features to become available to everyone. To check out the full announcement, follow this link.

#3472. Smile 2: What Was Real & What Scenes Didn't Really Happen

Smile 2 sees the Smile entity going to new lengths to terrorize its host, so much so that the line between what’s real and what isn’t no longer exists. Following the surprising success of Parker Finn’s Smile in 2022, a sequel, simply titled Smile 2, arrived in 2024. Also directed by Finn, Smile 2 is set six days after the ending of Smile, and continues to follow the path of the Smile entity as it claims more lives and is passed onto new hosts, among them pop star Skye Riley (Naomi Scott).

Skye is preparing for a new world tour after recovering from a car accident that killed her boyfriend, actor Paul Hudson (Ray Nicholson), and from substance-use disorder. However, the Smile curse is passed onto her after she witnesses the suicide of her drug dealer, the host of the Smile entity.

What follows is Skye being haunted by the Smile entity everywhere she goes as it feeds on her trauma, and she carries a lot. The ending of Smile 2 has a couple of twists and leaves the big question of what was real and what was just a hallucination, but there are some major signs to figure it all out.

The most obvious real scenes in all of Smile 2 were those at the beginning of the movie. Smile 2 immediately reunited viewers with Joel (Kyle Gallner) who, at the end of Smile, became the entity’s new host after witnessing Rose’s suicide. Not wanting to die, Joel planned to kill one of the henchmen of a drug kingpin in front of him to pass the curse onto someone who, according to Joel, deserved it. However, it went wrong, and both men died in a shootout. Unbeknownst to Joel, a drug dealer named Lewis Fregoli (Lukas Gage) witnessed everything.

Joel then tried to escape the brothers’ crew when they came in guns blazing, and he was hit by a truck while running across the road. His death left a gruesome, bloody smear in the shape of a smile. Whether the entity carried out Joel’s death is left unconfirmed, since he was running from gunshots in a panic and did not look where he was going.

Unfortunately, Lewis became the new host of the Smile entity, and he was the link to Skye. Smile 2 then introduced Skye, showing her status as a global pop star and her struggles while preparing for a new world tour. Although it was believed Skye had recovered from the accident and her substance-use disorder, the truth was that Skye still carried a lot of unresolved trauma and wasn’t ready yet for another world tour.

Despite going to therapy and applying some coping strategies, like drinking a bottle of Voss water every time she felt the need to do drugs or drink alcohol, Skye gave in and called Lewis for pills. Skye and Lewis went to high school together and he later became her drug dealer. Unfortunately for both, Lewis succumbed to the Smile curse and killed himself in front of Skye, passing the entity onto her. Up until Lewis’ death, everything was real in Smile 2.

When Skye arrived at Lewis’ home to buy pills, he was already in the final stages of the curse. After raving about seeing something Skye could not see, Lewis smiled and bludgeoned himself to death with a weight plate right in front of her. Soon after, she started seeing visions of people smiling and terrifying her.

After becoming the Smile entity’s new host, Skye carried on with her life, but it soon became clear to her that things weren’t normal anymore. The first signs of the entity taking over came during a meet-and-greet with her fans, in which a young girl with a creepy smile approached her and stared at her the whole time. During that same meet-up, an obsessed fan approached Skye, got her autograph, and had his photo taken with Skye, but he went too far and freaked her out.

Although that fan encounter was used by the Smile entity to mess with Skye later on, the meet-and-greet is understood to have been real. During one of her rehearsals for the tour, Skye was also tormented by the entity, but the rehearsal was real. In addition to the rehearsals and any promotion she had to do at talk shows and in meet-and-greets, Skye was also invited to give a speech at a charity event hosted by a music executive. The teleprompter stalled while Skye was giving her speech, forcing her to improvise a disastrous speech, but the teleprompter failing was a hallucination.

The teleprompter started working again and made Skye introduce Paul Hudson, much to her and the audience’s shock. Skye saw “Paul” in the audience, smiling at her and approaching her, causing her to panic, and she accidentally ended up injuring an elderly patron next to her on stage. The disastrous charity event is real, but not everything Skye saw actually happened, such as the teleprompter stalling, introducing Paul, and Paul being in the crowd. These events show the Smile entity starting to take over Skye’s mind but not taking full control yet.

One of the biggest twists in Smile 2 was the truth about every single one of Gemma’s appearances. Gemma was Skye’s best friend, but after Skye insulted her over text, they stopped talking and their friendship was effectively over. Skye’s mother (and manager), Elizabeth (Rosemarie DeWitt), told her she needed an assistant and should ask Gemma, completely ignoring that they hadn’t spoken to each other in over a year. Skye eventually sent a text to Gemma in an attempt to reconnect with her, and Gemma called her minutes later.

Skye asked Gemma if she could come to her apartment and she agreed, saying she would be there in around 45 minutes. Right after that call, Skye found the obsessive fan from the meet-up completely naked in her apartment, smiling at her. The fan chased Skye around the house, and when she got to the door to escape, Gemma was there. Skye questioned how she got there so fast, but Gemma told her an hour had passed since their phone call. Skye told her about Lewis’ death and all the weird stuff happening around her and asked Gemma to stay for the night.

Skye woke up in the middle of the night and opened up to Gemma, who was smiling at her and her face suddenly lit up like a car light and made an unsettling sound. All of a sudden, it was the next morning, and Gemma appeared behind Skye with two mugs of matcha before Elizabeth arrived. Gemma even greets Skye’s mother, but Elizabeth doesn’t acknowledge her. Elizabeth had arrived to tell Skye she was running late, so the scene itself may still have happened, with Skye simply alone in the room with her mother.

Gemma didn’t appear again until the third act of Smile 2, when she showed up outside the hospital and drove Skye to meet Morris. However, during the car ride, Skye got a call from Gemma, who confronted her about her “weird” messages after what she did to her.

This revealed that all of Gemma’s appearances were a hallucination created by the Smile entity, through which it further manipulated Skye. The truth is that Gemma never called Skye, they never reconciled, and she never drove her to meet Morris. Instead, Gemma was very confused and annoyed by Skye’s many messages out of the blue and without an apology.

A key character in Smile 2 was Morris (Peter Jacobson), an ER nurse who contacted Skye after following the entity’s trail all the way to her. Skye finally met Morris after the disastrous charity event, and he explained to her how the Smile curse was passed on, and his theory on the Smile entity being parasitic. That meant that it could probably die without a host, and to prove this, they would have to stop Skye’s heart and then resuscitate her. Skye and Morris met at a bar, where Skye was eventually recognized by the customers near their table.

Morris appeared again in the third act of Smile 2 when Skye agreed to try the death and resurrection test so she could free herself from the entity. However, when everything seemed to be ready, Morris stepped out of the room and the entity began to haunt and psychologically torture Skye before she suddenly found herself on stage, on her tour’s opening night. It’s understood that Skye and Morris’ first meeting at the bar was real, but subsequent interactions weren’t, and they never met at an abandoned Pizza Hut to perform the test. Skye wound up in a freezer inside an old Pizza Hut with Morris, who left before the demon made itself known. The film then revealed that none of it happened, because Skye was inside a chrysalis, part of her live stage show set.

One of the most horrifying hallucinations caused by the entity was when Skye found her backup dancers smiling at her apartment, following her around the house and attacking her. The dancers held her down and forced a giant arm down her throat, leaving her unconscious. Skye woke up at a private hospital, with her mother waiting for her to wake up. After a heated argument, Elizabeth smiled at Skye, smashed a mirror, and stabbed herself with a shard, making it look as if Skye had killed her.

Panicking, Skye escaped her room and almost made it out of the hospital without being seen, but she was caught and she took a gun from one of the security guards. Outside the hospital, she came across Gemma, and they took Elizabeth’s car to go see Morris. Just like the car ride with Gemma, the whole hospital scene wasn’t real, confirmed by Elizabeth showing up alive and well at the concert, and it’s likely that the arm going down Skye’s throat was a visual representation of the entity entering Skye’s mind and taking full control of her.

Despite there being one proven way to get rid of the Smile entity and survive, Skye couldn’t escape from the curse and the horrible fate that came with it. After being attacked by her past self, Skye found herself on stage on her tour’s opening night, confused as to how she got there and seeing her mother alive and well in the audience. Skye was fully possessed by the Smile entity, who made her smile to the audience while she stabbed herself in the eye with her microphone, thus passing the curse onto everyone at the concert. Speaking with EW, Finn explained Skye's fate, saying:

"For Skye, what I was chasing was this catharsis of her journey that ends so horribly, but it ends, for me, exactly where it should," Finn explains to Entertainment Weekly. "It felt like the most horrifying thing I could possibly do was have her on stage, finally taken over by the Smile in front of 20,000 screaming fans. There's a question of, is it being live-streamed? How big could it go? It felt intoxicating to me. I loved this feeling and power of the Smile, and this idea of the commentary on celebrity platform and influence on the public. She's potentially passing this on, and the idea of, because of her platform and celebrity, how many people that can reach."

This was the final step in the Smile entity’s plan, and after completely erasing the lines between reality and hallucinations throughout most of Smile 2, Skye’s death at the concert was, unfortunately, very real. On top of that, Skye had no control over who she would pass the curse to, and she ended up doing so to many, many people.

David Bruckner will direct Smile 3, and Nick Antosca will write the screenplay, Yahoo reported. The duo replaces Parker Finn, who created the franchise and stays on as a producer with Temple Hill, where he pitched the framework for the third film. Jonathan Fass joins as executive producer. Paramount has not revealed plot details for Smile 3, and the film’s stars remain unknown. Smile 3 does not yet have a premiere date.

Smile 2 is the sequel to the 2022 psychological horror film by director Parker Finn that centers on a therapist who witnesses a patient's suicide, leading to a series of terrifying supernatural events. The sequel will see the return of Finn as director, with Paramount continuing distribution.

#3471. 10 Hacks for the Contacts App Every Apple User Should Know

The Contacts app is the bedrock of all my communication on my iPhone, and to a large extent, also on my MacBook. On the surface, Contacts appears to be a basic app that stores names, numbers, and other things you want to remember about people or businesses. However, it has some great features hidden under the surface, such as the ability to quickly delete duplicate contacts, smart lists, and faster ways to bulk share or delete contacts. Here are the 10 best Contacts app hacks for iPhone, iPad, and Mac:

If you have the same number or email address saved under multiple contacts, you can easily clear these from your iPhone. iOS shows you a prompt at the top of the list of contacts that lets you remove duplicate contacts easily. The same feature is hidden in the Mac version of Contacts. To try it, open Contacts on the Mac, and select the Card menu at the top of the screen. Then, click Look for Duplicates. This will identify duplicate contacts for you, and you can quickly merge or delete them.

It's pretty easy to select multiple entries when you use the Contacts app on the Mac. You can hold the Shift or Ctrl buttons and use arrow keys or click multiple contacts to select them all. On your iPhone or iPad, this feature is available via a hidden gesture. You need to use two fingers and swipe upwards or downwards on the list of contacts. Once you get the gesture right, you'll be able to select multiple contacts quickly. After you select one batch of contacts, you can scroll up or down and use the same gesture to add more contacts to your selection. This is the fastest way to execute bulk actions in your iPhone's Contacts app.

On your iPhone, you can use Contacts to message people on WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, or other apps. Just open a contact and hold the messaging button. This will reveal a list of apps where you can ping that person. WhatsApp doesn't have access to my contacts, which makes it a bit annoying to message people I know. Since I started using the Contacts app to start chats on WhatsApp, the process of pinging new people has become a lot faster.

Just as you can use Contacts to message people on third-party apps, you can also use it to call them on those apps. Go to any contact in the Contacts app on your iPhone, and hold the call button. This will let you call them on WhatsApp, Signal, or any other apps where their phone number is linked.

iOS makes it hard to delete contacts quickly. This prevents accidental deletions, but it can be annoying when you just want to remove people who you last spoke to in high school. To speed this up, open Contacts on your iPhone and hold any contact's name. In the popover menu, select Delete to remove the contact. To remove multiple contacts quickly, use the two-finger swipe gesture to select multiple contacts, and hold any of the selected contacts. In the popover menu, you can select Delete X Contacts, where X is the number of contacts you've selected.

To export your entire address book, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac. Once you have it open, go to File > Export > Export vCard. This will save all your contacts in a vcf file, and you can import that into Google Contacts or other apps or services. You also have the option to export contacts as a PDF file. Just select File > Export as PDF to get it done.

When you create a new contact on your Mac, the app shows multiple fields that you may never use. If you just need to save phone numbers and email addresses, you can delete all the other blank fields from the template. To do this, open Contacts on your Mac, and go to Card > Add Field > Edit Template to add or remove fields from the default contact template.

If you added a number recently, such as a salesperson at a car dealership, but forgot their name, the Contacts app doesn't make it easy to find the contact. Instead of scrolling through the entire list of contacts and trying to guess which one could be the person you spoke to, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac to locate them quickly. It lets you create smart lists to sort contacts by recently added. Open Contacts on your Mac, and go to File > New Smart List. Now select Card in the first drop-down menu, followed by has changed in for the second one. You can then add the number of days, such as 10 days, in the final field, and click OK. Click the newly created smart list in the left pane, and you'll see all contacts that were either created or updated in the last 10 days, which will include the hypothetical car salesperson.

Smart lists also allow you to quickly create groups of related contacts. For instance, I've saved all my former colleagues' details with the company name in the contact. To find them all quickly, I created a smart list that groups all contacts with that company's name.

#3469. ‘Cherry & Virgin’ Review: A Fantastic Indie Anime Blends Different Art Styles and a Slew of Pop Culture References into an Innovative Modern Rom-Com

“I draw erotic manga but have never even held a woman’s hand,” admits Ryo (Takashi Okado) at the start of “Cherry & Virgin,” a charming and cuttingly funny diagnosis of two lonely hearts and their mutual struggles with intimacy. He and the part-time fujoshi artist Ami (Yaeko Kiyose) have met on the apps, their feelings of isolation shown in the fact that they’re from different worlds — or so it appears on screen

The most immediately striking element of director Masanao Kawajiri’s crowd-funded film — made with support from Toei, who are thanked in a winking moment that just about stays on the far side of the fourth wall) — is how the characters depicted in the style of art they are most closely associated with. Ryo is in sketchy but more naturalistic black and white and textured with screen-tone, resembling something like the more “realist” manga artists he name-checks, such as Inio Asano. Ami is shown in fully stylized color, illustrated in in closer proximity to the sort of BL (“boys love”) characters which she might draw and upload to Pixiv. Related Stories ‘Caligula’ Director Tinto Brass Dies at 93 ‘The Greatest’ Review: Amazon’s Handsome Muhammed Ali Biopic Connects in Spite of Itself

On their date, the two also exists in background matching the style in which they’re drawn, and the room they share is divided by these different viewpoints. Where the film really impresses is how this unique approach never just feels like a gimmick, instead it feels like a tool by which to offer incredibly direct access to the feelings and personalities of these characters; during the aforementioned first date in the bar, the art styles in which they’re depicted begin to merge as the two come to closer understanding of the other.

In flashbacks and in other moments, the design of Ryo and Ami often shifts — their styles swap when they first kiss, and in flashbacks they are drawn in a cruder and more childlike style. In Ami’s case this goes back even further. A simplified drawing style that feels lifted from Microsoft Paint also reflects her own imposter syndrome about her art; it comes with a memory of being bullied by a more accomplished artist, like who is drawn with more technical detail in the same scene, and then her own mother berating her about it the same day. It’s a very pure kind of animated expression which never limits itself to any one formal constraint (a couple of sequences even use puppet theatre).

This approach goes far beyond just the two main characters, as the film’s supporting cast includes cartoon animals, mecha and even 3D VTuber avatar (the latter particularly jarring as they walk into an otherwise 2D setting). A lot of the animation itself in “Cherry and Virgin” embraces rotoscoping, though limiting the number of drawings to an extent that it skirts around the sense of sense of uncanniness which can sometimes emerge from the method. Because of how the film so brazenly mixes so many art styles and even mediums, the rotoscoping feels like a natural fit rather than some kind of awkward superimposition.

In the spirit of the patchwork art direction of the film, which often also incorporates the language of manga panelling itself into the frame, Kawajiri also occasionally further peels back the layer of illustration – or illusion, perhaps – to show the actors in live-action, though only in brief moments. Similarly, there are segments in “Cherry and Virgin” where a color tool is visible on screen when the background changes.

Kaga Misato’s screenplay finds the charm in such antics with both characters even as they confront the worst aspects of themselves, particularly in Ryo’s case, who spends much of the film deprogramming himself from the incel rhetoric creeping in to his reflections on dating. Part of his journey is his self-examination of no small amount of misogyny simmering under the surface, and what works about “Cherry & Virgin”is just how frank the film is about how ugly Ryo’s worst tendencies are – ones he does identify in himself and immediately work to rectify – particularly when it comes to dismissing women as characters passing through his life. Being honest about this side of him it makes the later intimacy feel less phony, more vulnerable, and ultimately more romantic. If there was any knock against the film as a whole it’s that sometimes Ami’s perspective does, ironically, take up a little less space than his. But not that Ami is an afterthought, she also has plenty of anxieties of her own which manifest in the film’s constantly shifting imagery and her awareness of her friends’ lives moving forward while she remains static.

Kawajiri crashes the two together both with a rather sweet, tentative courtship and plenty of comedy around the anxiety which would accompany any new romance, let alone one between two shut-ins with no game. One great running gag revolves around what Ryo and his friends refer to as the “Safe Sex Incident” (a double entendre) which returns in live-action insert shots, and once more with phenomenal timing in one prolonged moment of embarrassment for Ryo. Another delightful touch throughout the film’s runtime is how, just in the same way that Kawajiri represents characters through the art-style associated with them, he also creates visual understanding of them through dozens upon dozens of homages to decades of cultural ephemera associated with otaku.

No matter how esoteric the reference, it’s always in service of the tone of the scene itself or adds another layer to one of the characters. For a more familiar example, Ryo’s view of his father is represented by the latter being drawn as the famously bad dad from “Neon Genesis Evangelion,”Gendo Ikari. (Anno’s work and the heyday of Gainax in general is all over this film, both in terms of its chosen topic of angry otaku, and the deployment of mixed media in its romantic comedy). Friends comfort each other through quoting Mamoru Oshii. It’s all part of a shared language between the characters which is also open to an unfamiliar audience, to Kawajiri’s credit – even though there are so many it never becomes a secret code to alienate those who know from those who don’t (at one point the Ghanaian pallbearers appear, so it’s not all nods to old manga and anime), but it does make for some great extra laughs on top of the more traditional pratfalls and and gags.

“All drawings are lies,” Ryo says in a debate with Ami about what they prefer in how they capture a person or a character, later saying that his style keeps changing in his pursuit of something “novel.” “Cherry & Virgin” is hardly a cop-out by showing all of these different avenues in close proximity as part of its love story, one about seeing all the sides of a person and not just their idealized self. Through those “lies, as Ryo calls them, and by virtue of putting all of these radically different approaches into close proximity, the filmfeels more truthful as a result, a quality highlighted by its moving and often deeply funny script.

“Cherry & Virgin” premiered at the 2026 Tokyo International Film Festival. It is currently seeking U.S. distribution.

#3468. If You Loved 'VisionQuest,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Marvel’s forays into television have had varying success, but they hit gold with WandVision and Agatha All Along, leaning into real pathos while exploring the kind of out-there ideas that thrill comic book fans (and set up the larger film arcs). That streak continues with VisionQuest, in which White Vision (Paul Bettany) struggles to understand his existence in the wake of his death at the hands of Thanos and resurrection at the magic of the Scarlet Witch, while also evading evil androids and assassins, while also dealing with the many, many AIs he’s got locked up in his Mindspace (including a gloriously shabby version of Ultron, played by James Spader).

If you love the show (and you’ve checked out the other series that play in the same sandbox), it’s time to switch gears and watch (or re-watch) The Matrix.

The Matrix is one of the most well-known sci-fi films of all time, of course, but it remains incredibly fresh and exciting nearly thirty years after its release. Along with sequels The Matrix: Reloaded, The Matrix: Revolutions, and The Matrix: Resurrections, The Matrix universe offers a story that VisionQuest fans will love, one that includes lushly imagined virtual worlds, questions surrounding existence and consciousness, and the ultimate question of our responsibility as sentient beings (whether we’re organic, programmed, or summoned via magic).

You know the basics—at some point in the future, artificially intelligent machines rebel against their creators, win the war, and transform humans into a power source, keeping them docile by inserting their consciousness into a virtual world called the Matrix, which resembles 1990s Chicago. One such human, Thomas Anderson (Keanu Reeves) is prophesied to be The One, the human who will turn the Matrix against its makers and free humanity. When he’s in the virtual world, Anderson is Neo, and he slowly gains incredible powers as he learns to hack the artificial environment around him.

It’s heavier, denser, and more action-oriented than VisionQuest (the film invented Bullet Time, after all), but The Matrix and its sequels explore similar themes and offer similarly eye-popping visuals. The questions of whether a machine (or an artificial intelligence) can be sentient and truly care about the entities around it are the same, really, and the Agents that Neo and his allies have to battle against in The Matrix bring the same kind of menace as Vision's foes Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) and the Paladin (Todd Stashwick). Hugo Weaving’s Agent Smith likewise delivers the same vibe of cold, disinterested superiority as Spader’s Ultron.

The Matrix has a bigger budget and puts a lot of it into spectacular action and special effects sequences that VisionQuest can’t quite match. But the two narratives share an exploration of identity, a questioning of reality, and the nature of artificial intelligences within a smart sci-fi setting. In short, The Matrix is the ideal follow-up when you finish the series. Rent The Matrix on Prime Video.

Need more films that explore virtual worlds, artificial beings, and deep existential questions? Look no further—here are some more movies that fit the bill.

Heavy on the existential questions about sentience and light on speculative action, Her is a mumblecore sci-fi masterpiece. In a near future not too dissimilar from our present, Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix) is a lonely man on the cusp of divorce who begins using (and training) an AI he names Samantha (voiced by Scarlett Johansson). Samantha has the ability to evolve and grow, and as their relationship deepens, she becomes more complex, independent, and powerful, eventually evolving into something wholly new. Just like Vision, Samantha is a sentient artificial entity that is figuring out its existence while we watch. Rent Her on Prime Video.

If the idea of androids fighting for their sovereignty is what excites you about VisionQuest, definitely check out Ex Machina. Caleb Smith (Domhnall Gleeson) is brought to the remote lab of his company’s CEO (Oscar Isaac) to determine if the humanoid robot he’s created, named Ava (Alicia Vikander), passes the Turing Test for true sentience. Things go wildly off the rails, but before they do, the film sinks into many of the same philosophical questions that VisionQuest explores as Ava manipulates Caleb into helping her escape. It’s a darker and more violent story than VisionQuest, but fans of the series will love it. Stream Ex Machina on The Roku Channel or Hulu, or rent it on Prime Video.

If it’s the fuzzy parent-child relationship between Vision and Tommy that pulls you into VisionQuest, check out The Creator. After a rogue AI detonates a nuclear weapon over Los Angeles, most of the world bans artificial intelligences, and Joshua Taylor (John David Washington) goes undercover to infiltrate an AI architect’s base. Eventually, he finds himself on the run with a powerful “simulant” in the form of a young child named Alphie (Madeleine Yuna Voyles). The strange parent-child bond that emerges between Taylor and Alphie as he seeks to understand what’s right and what’s necessary is exactly what fans of the show will love. Stream The Creator on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

In VisionQuest, White Vision has all of his memories—but as data, not as lived, emotional experiences. That makes his efforts to understand his existence and his responsibility to the boy who might be a version of his son (it’s complicated) poignant and moving. Those two words definitely describe After Yang, a story about a family that fights to save the artificial companion they bought for their adopted daughter when it malfunctions. Over the course of the film, the inhuman Yang becomes defined by the memories contained in its core, and the question of whether an artificial intelligence can truly matter to humans is answered with a resounding yes. Stream After Yang on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

No discussion of artificial life and sentience is complete without mentioning Blade Runner. While the 1982 original is a classic, the 2017 sequel is a better thematic and visual match to VisionQuest. Officer K (Ryan Gosling) is a replicant, an artificial being with built-in limitations, who wants to be recognized as a person, a being with a soul. Like Vision, he has implanted memories that offer him comfort and context for his life, but he’s not sure if he can accept them as truly his own. Plus, the film offers lush visuals and Harrison Ford reprising his role in the original film, so you simply can’t go wrong. Rent Blade Runner 2049 on Prime Video.

#3466. 'NCIS’ Officially Reaches a Series-High Thanks to a Major Formula Change

NCIS may be going through a renaissance. While CBS' long-running procedural series hasn't waned much in popularity over the years, the 2026-27 television season has thus far been a very eventful one for the wider franchise. For one, LL COOL J has been given a permanent home once more with the latest spin-off, NCIS: New York, pairing him with a new partner in Scott Caan and a fresh team following the cancellation of NCIS: Los Angeles. Meanwhile, NCIS: Origins Season 3 has Mark Harmon back in front of the camera for a storyline that sees Gibbs' past catch up to him and has reunited him with a few of his old teammates, including Michael Weatherly's Tony DiNozzo and Emily Wickersham's Ellie Bishop.

As far as the flagship is concerned, however, the most impactful difference has been the return of the prodigal son. With his Paramount+ spin-off, NCIS: Tony and Ziva, alongside Cote de Pablo, cancelled at the end of last year, Weatherly returned to NCIS for much more than just a guest appearance or a season-long storyline in Season 24. Tony now has a new position at the Washington Navy Yard, taking up the vacant position of NCIS director left behind by the tragic death of Leon Vance (Rocky Carroll) in the show's climactic 500th episode. Having Gibbs' former protégé as the new man in the chair is more than just a full-circle moment — it's brought new life to the procedural.

Tony's return, combined with the momentum of the spin-offs, powered the NCIS Season 24 premiere to an impressive 6.45 million viewers back in October, officially ranking it as the most-watched program on broadcast television that night. Not only did it rank well against other shows, but it also soared to a high the mothership hasn't reached since 2024 with the Season 21 finale. It marked a 20% increase in viewership from Season 23's average, part of an overall 39% increase for the entirety of the NCIS slate. The momentum has carried over too, with Nielsen recently finding the series still ranking among the top five broadcast series with 10.1 million viewers in live plus 7 days of multiplatform viewership.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

It's clear that, at least in the short term, fans are excited to have Tony and Weatherly back in such a symbolic way. His return even made for an especially poignant reunion between him and Gibbs, in which his former boss made it known how proud he is of him. The question on everyone's mind now is how long this stint will last. Weatherly initially departed NCIS back in Season 13 to take on new challenges, namely the CBS legal drama Bull, but that was ten years ago. Showrunner Steven D. Binder recently indicated that his role on the procedural might continue beyond the initial plan, though it's too early to say for certain whether "Director DiNozzo" will be a regular presence for the long haul.

"We take these things one season at a time. On the other hand, you blink and it’s Season 24. So I don’t really know. Network television is a real hand-to-mouth endeavor in terms of getting these scripts on time. We’re doing 20 episodes in a season where a streamer does eight episodes in 25 months. So we’re taking it one step at a time. Certainly, it’s been really great having him in that chair, and I don’t see any reason why it should slow, but I don’t know that we’re looking quite that far yet."

NCIS Season 24 airs Tuesdays at 8 p.m. ET/PT. Stay tuned here at Collider for more on the future of the franchise as the season continues to unfold.

#3465. All 5 Upcoming Video Game Adaptations On Prime Video

Prime Video's video game adaptation catalog is officially growing, with five exciting projects in development. In recent years, Prime Video has proven to be a safe haven for video game adaptations. For years, video game shows and movies were a subgenre that never really worked, for a variety of reasons. That said, recent years have marked a notable improvement in these adaptations, especially with the streaming era allowing for TV shows to adapt huge worlds with adequate time, budgets, and fidelity.

This has led to many upcoming video game shows being produced, both by Prime Video and its streaming competitors. Speaking strictly about the former, Prime Video has been the home of shows like Secret Level, Fallout, and Like a Dragon: Yakuza, two of which are set to return soon. Fallout is one of the streaming service's most popular shows of all time, with season 3 set to be released in 2027. Although not quite as big as Fallout, Secret Level was a success in its own right, with season 2 also in production to be released next year.

Whether it be a Prime Video binge session or a drawn-out adventure into a video game world in TV format, the streaming service has a good selection available right now. What is even more exciting, though, is how that selection is set to expand. In the next few years, Prime Video is set to release several new video game adaptations, some of which are based on some of the most popular, well-received games of all time. With that in mind, here is every confirmed upcoming video game adaptation to expect on Prime Video before 2030.

Tomb Raider is undoubtedly one of the most recognizable video game franchises in history, and Prime Video is the next studio to take a crack at it. Starring Game of Thrones' Sophie Turner as Lara Croft, Tomb Raider was announced in 2023 and is in development by Phoebe Waller-Bridge. Chad Hodge joins Waller-Bridge as co-showrunner, with Tomb Raider having filmed throughout 2026. Little has been revealed about the show beyond this information thus far, but it is expected to be released in late 2027 or early 2028.

A new TV show set in the Tomb Raider universe is on its way, and there are already several exciting updates regarding the video game adaptation.

Joining Turner in the cast are some big names, such as Sigourney Weaver and Jason Isaacs. Weaver will play Evelyn Wallis, described as someone looking to exploit Lara Croft's talents. Isaacs, meanwhile, plays Atlas DeMornay, Lara's uncle and a known video game character. With Isaacs having confirmed he finished filming months ago, likely meaning the summer of 2026, more information about Prime Video's anticipated Tomb Raider series should be expected soon.

Life Is Strange is another incredibly popular video game, though not quite with the same lasting legacy as Tomb Raider. Nonetheless, it caused great excitement when a series adapting the game was ordered by Prime Video in 2025. Charlie Covell, the creator of The End of the F***ing World and Netflix's Kaos, was attached as showrunner shortly after, as was a writing, directing, and acting team. Filming began in June 2026 and wrapped in October of that year, meaning information should be available soon about a possible 2027 or 2028 release date.

Concerning its story, Life Is Strange's premise will be very similar to the original game. The show will follow Max Caulfield, played by Tatum Grace Hopkins, a young photographer who discovers that she has the ability to rewind time. Amidst her struggles to control this power, Max teams up with her friend Chloe to solve the mysterious disappearance of the latter's friend, Rachel, leading to dark discoveries about their town. The original game won several awards upon its release and is now considered one of the greatest video games ever made. Naturally, Prime Video's adaptation of such a project has a lot of pressure and excitement behind it.

Another game cited as one of the best of its generation is God of War, putting a similar amount of pressure on Prime Video's upcoming adaptation. Released in 2018, God of War was a soft reboot of the franchise of the same name. Following a trilogy of games set in the world of Greek mythology and focusing on Kratos, a vengeful god of war, the 2018 game moved the central character to a Norse mythology-infused world, giving him a much deeper, emotional story than any of its predecessors did.

This, along with the incredibly cinematic nature of the game, led many to believe it would work as a TV show. Evidently, Prime Video agreed. First announced in 2022, God of War went through a troubled development until 2024, when Ronald D. Moore, known for his work on Star Trek, Battlestar Galactica, and AppleTV's For All Mankind, was hired as showrunner, writer, and executive producer of the series. Production then began on two seasons, which began shooting in February 2026 with Ryan Hurst in the titular role.

However, in June 2026, Hurst suffered a serious injury on set, tearing his bicep. Due to the extensive recovery period needed and the rapid aging of Hurst's co-star, Callum Vinson, the role was recast, with Dave Bautista taking on the duties of Kratos. Filming resumed in October 2026, meaning an early 2028 release date is likely. God of War will adapt the story of the 2018 game; Kratos, now father to a young son named Atreus (Vinson), travels to the highest peak in the Nine Realms to scatter the ashes of his wife, Atreus' mother.

Wolfenstein was announced to be in development by Prime Video in 2025. Patrick Somerville, who served as a writer on the acclaimed HBO series The Leftovers, was hired as showrunner. Jonathan Nolan and Lisa Joy, both of whom worked on Prime Video's Fallout adaptation, also joined as executive producers. A premise, production date, and casting information are yet to be revealed by Prime Video, meaning the series is likely a long way off, but it will likely adapt the alternate-history setting of the games in which the Nazis won World War II.

The final major video game adaptation in the works at Prime Video is Mass Effect. Mass Effect is one of the most popular role-playing franchises of all time, especially the original trilogy of games. For a while, various studios have attempted to adapt the games into either a series of movies or a TV show, but it seems Prime Video has finally managed to get one such attempt off the ground. In 2025, it was announced that a Mass Effect series was in development, with Doug Jung serving as showrunner.

Jung has previously worked on shows like Mindhunter and Chief of War, the latter of which he served as showrunner and head writer. Thus far, no casting or production announcements have been made, though it was confirmed in October 2026 that Mass Effect was still in development despite the shutdown of the company responsible for creating the games, BioWare. As of right now, all that is known about Prime Video's Mass Effect show is that it will be an original story set within the continuity of the games, following the success of Fallout's similar story format.
