#3464. Will Brill Won a Tony and Got His First Leading Film Role, but That’s Not How He Measures Success

It’s all glamorous — chatting Tony wins and snagging leading roles in movies and sterling New York Times reviews — until your cat needs something. Fortunately, actor Will Brill knows a thing or two about balance, and managed to both a) charmingly answer our many varied queries about his wide-ranging career and b) attend to his yowling tabby’s needs while doing so.

Brill is one of those actors you know, even if you don’t know him by name. One of the “oh, I love that guy!” kind of performers. The kind of performer who shows up and instantly makes things better, or brighter, or somehow richer. His credits are wide and deep — movies like “Caught Stealing” and “Test Pattern,” shows like “The OA” and “The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel,” theater like “Oklahoma” and “Stereophonic” — and things are only picking up for him. Related Stories ‘Cherry & Virgin’ Review: A Fantastic Indie Anime Blends Different Art Styles and a Slew of Pop Culture References into an Innovative Modern Rom-Com Alan Cumming Says ‘Tip Toe’ Was His Greatest Role Ever — but He Never Wants to Think About It Again

In 2024, Brill won his first Tony for the beloved rock musical “Stereophonic,” snagging Best Featured Actor in a Play in a field that included two of his own co-stars. In 2025, he got his first leading role in the film, care of Giselle Bonilla’s darkly hilarious “The Musical.” Not too shabby, right? It gets better.

When Brill spoke with IndieWire, reviews were just hitting for the limited run of “Kramer/Fauci” at St. Ann’s Warehouse. Daniel Fish’s lauded play previously ran at the Skirball earlier this year and, this fall, Brill reprised his role as, yes, that Dr. Anthony Fauci. The creative, thrilling play dramatizes a 1993 C-SPAN call-in show, during which Fauci (then the director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases) and Larry Kramer (the famously outspoken playwright and activist) went at each other over the plans for a new government task force on H.I.V. and AIDS.

“I’m one of those weirdos who will read [reviews],” Brill said with a laugh when asked if he’d been keeping up with the glowing criticism for the show. “I read every single review. I’ve read every review of ‘The Musical’ on Letterboxd. Some would say I’m a glutton for punishment.”

Helen Shaw’s review in the New York Times, he agreed, was not punishment. “I felt auspicious because I knew that Helen Shaw had seen it at Skirball and really enjoyed it,” he said. “But, even so, to say, ‘The most beautiful play I’ve seen all year and I would happily see it 10 more times’ is crazy. I mean, it’s so cool.”

Brill has been doing live theater as long as he’s been acting, getting his start in children’s theater when he was still just a kid in the Bay Area. Process is compelling to him, and he lights up when asked about something as workaday as what he does during the hours between demanding shows.

“It depends on the show a lot, the difference between this show and ‘Stereophonic,’ for instance, is that Stereophonic was a three-hour, 15-minute show where I was screaming and crying most of the times that I was on stage, and this show is an hour long and I never have to raise my voice,” Brill said. “I get to lie down for part of it! Also, for ‘Stereophonic,’ we were in Midtown Manhattan, and for this, I’m in Dumbo, so I get to go outside and sit by the river and read my book, which is dreamy. And then during ‘Stereophonic,’—”

That’s when Curtis the tabby really gets going. “Sorry, my cat is really going through it. Can you hear him?,” Brill said, before darting off-screen to retrieve and present a gorgeous and giant striped feline. “This is Curtis. What is it, baby? He’s screaming. He’s been walking around screaming his head off. Oh, I wonder … I have a robot litter box now and it looks like it is… Sorry, this is such a chaotic morning for me. I think it just needs a reset. Maybe that’s what’s going on with him.”

Yowling cats will keep anyone grounded. In a weird way, so will Tony wins. I asked Brill what changed — or didn’t — after he won his first.

“I think less changed than I sort of expected it would,” he said. “There’s all kinds of legends about what people go through, what changes for people. Oh, my gosh, people love to say, ‘Oh, I thought my entire career was going to change and then I didn’t work for three years.’ And that was certainly not the case for me, but I did have to make a pretty difficult choice about whether or not I was going to go do the show again in London, which I ultimately decided not to do. I had a year where I made less money than I would have, but I did some really rewarding and very challenging things. I starred in a movie for the first time. I had never done that before, so that was really exciting and new and different.”

Bonilla’s feature debut “The Musical” debuted at this year’s Sundance Film Festival and was recently released in theaters and on VOD. It’s a tricky film to explain — it has a twist, sort of, but really just a devilish sense of humor — and Brill loved that. He stars as middle school drama teacher Doug Leibowitz, recently dumped his girlfriend, consumed by his failures as a playwright, and perhaps in the exact right mental headspace to put on an, ahem, shocking new musical.

“I wish I could remember when exactly it dawned on me in the script, because definitely it took me by surprise and it was at that moment where I thought, ‘Oh, I have to do this. There’s no question about this. This is my role,’” he said when asked about the moment he realized what the film was doing with its central musical conceit. “Because it was so exciting and so unlike anything else that I had read. Giselle and I would sneak in to screenings to hear the audience realize what’s happening and listen to them respond to it, and it’s always terribly gratifying.”

We won’t spoil the film here, but suffice to say, Doug and his merry band of middle schoolers put on a show that is based on perhaps the last event you’d ever expect to inspire a musical. The first time Brill saw the film with an audience who had no idea what they were in for, he realized going in cold might be the move.

“I realized that really the best way to experience the movie is with other people not knowing what is coming, because the shock is so crazy,” he said. “And something about the way that it has been finagled is that you are pulled in so many directions, between wanting Doug to fail, but also wanting the children to succeed. It’s such a torrent of things happening that it’s really sort of best to experience with a bunch of other people at the same time.”

The role might have been Brill’s first leading one on the big screen, but he’s no stranger to tough material — or the weight of it. In 2019, he starred alongside Brittany S. Hall in Shatara Michelle Ford’s staggering debut feature, “Test Pattern.” The film follows couple Renesha (Hall) and Evan (Brill) as they navigate a horrific sexual assault and a system not at all equipped to handling survivors with grace.

“They share more DNA than you would think,” he said of Bonilla’s film and Ford’s. “‘Test Pattern’ was the biggest emotional undertaking that I’d ever taken on film before. I was being trusted with a lot by Shatara. They were also a first-time filmmaker, so there was a lot of trust that we were giving to each other, and that was very palpable from the first time we met each other, that we were embarking on something that was pretty untrod territory for both of us and maybe in the landscape of cinema. We both felt tremendous responsibility. We both took it very, very seriously and were asking a lot of ourselves and each other.”

Ford’s film was made “on a shoestring budget” with “absolutely no amenities of any kind,” the actor added. “But that said, it was really rewarding, and everybody showed up really desperate to do well every day,” he said. “Similarly, on ‘The Musical,’ I’m on camera in almost every scene of the movie, so I felt a lot of pressure at the time. I knew that a lot of the success of the thing relied on me, and usually, at least in my career, that’s not been the case. I’ve played a lot of supporting roles, and I know that I can show up for a scene and deliver something special and ultimately get to walk away and say, ‘This thing does not live or die on my performance alone.’ I couldn’t write that off with either of the two movies.”

Brill has also dipped into studio features, including a small but memorable role in Darren Aronofsky’s 2025 crime dramedy “Caught Stealing,” in which he plays a homeless man who offers a surprising key to a complicated story.

“Those experiences are wild, because you walk onyo the set and it’s you and Austin Butler and Zoe Kravitz and Darren Aronofsky,” he said. “And you’re just sort of like, ‘OK…’ It’s a lot of pressure, and it’s a lot of excitement. ‘Test Pattern’ had a crew of 20 people on any given day, and then there were 100 or more people on the set of ‘Caught Stealing’ every time I was there. We were shutting down blocks of New York City traffic for hours in the middle of the night. It was really wild.”

The role might have been firmly supporting, but the experience really stuck with him. “I had two very big votes of confidence while I was working on that movie that I felt really cool about,” the actor said. “One was that when pedestrians got hustled by. on more than one occasion, people were like, ‘Why aren’t they moving this homeless man who’s on the street?’ People had to be like ‘He’s an actor.’ So that felt really good. I got sort of nervous that I was going to be there in the presence of this auteur who was going to be self-serious and formidable and difficult, and Darren was everything you want a director to be. He was so game, he was so fun. He was appreciating the magic of every moment, and he was so supportive of his actors. Every time I did a take, he was like, ‘Oh my God, this is so much fun. I wish we had you for longer.’ It’s very cool to show up to the big game and have it be as cool as you want it to be.”

Brill will round out this year with another supporting turn in a big film. In Sian Heder’s crowd-pleasing biopic “Being Heumann,” he plays Gene Eidenberg, a real-life political adviser who kind of takes the heat when Mark Ruffalo’s Joseph A. Califano Jr. (the U.S. Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare) won’t give much leeway to disability rights activist Judy Heumann and her compatriots during a historic sit-in.

“Sian’s take on the world is so cool, because she has such a good heart and is so funny and fun. The way she sees the world is so filled with light and joy, even when she’s taking on pretty heavy topics,” he said. “I don’t know that I have laughed that much on a set. I can’t remember the last time I did. Sian is so funny and fun, and so is Mark, and so is Dylan [O’Brien]. It was such a joy.”

Heder’s film is remarkable for the way it built actual access into its story about the need for more equitable access for all. Even as an able-bodied actor playing an able-bodied role, Brill felt the power of that.

“I think when the culture is about ‘let’s take care of people and meet needs,’ the work can thrive more,” he said. “I think the camaraderie amongst actors becomes very different. It becomes a lot tighter. There were these group green rooms and dressing rooms that you sort of never get. We had these lounges where we were hanging out and we were able to dissect the day, and that was really lovely. I mean, as with any movie, I think it was still really difficult at times and there are these monumental learning curves, but that’s part of the joy of filmmaking too, is that every single project is a new project. You never stop learning how to make a movie.”

And Brill knows about all kinds of projects. This is the kind of actor who pops up everywhere. A quick glance at his IMDb page is filled with delights — like the year 2017, when he appeared in not only an episode of “Law & Order: SVU,” but also “NCIS: New Orleans.” He laughed when I mentioned that double whammy.

“What was really cool was that I couldn’t have played more different characters,” he said. “I was like a coke dealer who lived in Soho in ‘SVU,’ and in ‘NCIS,’ I was a spirit medium who thought that he was a con artist, but then started actually communing with spirits. ‘NCIS: New Orleans,’ I filmed four days and was in New Orleans for three weeks, so I just had all this free time to explore New Orleans for the first time. It was incredible.”

Brill, it seems, finds value — of all kinds — in every project and part. So, is there some sort of magic balance he wants to strike with his choices? Is there a way to plot this kind of trajectory?

“It’s really tough to say, because there’s no continuity, it always changes,” Brill said. “But I have been lucky enough to really find a family in theater in New York, and so I do feel like it is there for me on some level. There are definitely things that I really want to do. There are challenges that I want to give myself, and I would say that the most open plane for that right now is television. I really want to find out what it’s like to play a character who lives and changes over a decade. I’m desperate for that experience.”

He’d like to be able to do that and still do theater. He added, “I see my friends who are on television shows and are navigating doing theater in their off time. Michael Urie is a huge inspiration in that because he’s such a theater creature, but he’s always been on TV too. So that’s a thing that I think about a lot, is the balance.”

But what he ultimately wants is something a bit harder to pin down, a balance that goes beyond designations like “film” or “TV show” or “theater,” the kind of spot that values experience in all its shapes. And, yes, probably the kind of space in which spending time with his cat is just as rewarding as a varied resume and making stuff with friends.

“I feel like life is long and I’m here for the challenge, and I’m going to get to do all of it. I’m just biding my time,” Brill said. “I feel like nowhere more than in this industry does the aphorism apply of ‘if you want to make God laugh, make plans.’ I’m down to ride the wave and let things come as they come. The most rewarded and fulfilled I’ve ever felt in this industry are the projects that are born out of tight-knit groups of friends or where tight-knit friendships are made, because what we do is storytelling, and storytelling is about creating and solidifying community. I think the thing that I will always keep wanting to do is telling stories with close friends, whatever the medium is. That’s the thing I want to do most.”

Apple will release “Being Heumann” in select theaters on Friday, November 6 and on Apple TV on Friday, November 13. A Blue Harbor Entertainment and Variance Films release, “The Musical” is currently available to rent or buy digitally on major streaming and VOD storefronts.

Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Apple hardware costs more than it did a year ago, and if you have purchased a fleet recently, you are feeling it. Now, one thing I should mention: Macs have not risen in price with inflation or performance. If you think about what a Mac mini or MacBook Air cost when they launched vs. today, I would still say they are extremely affordable. With that being said, there’s a scenario taking shape in the enterprise where the price of a Mac matters a lot less than it used to. If open-weight AI models become a real part of how companies work, Apple Silicon might end up looking basically free compared to the token bill it supplements.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

Cloud AI in the enterprise is priced by the token, and that’s a fine model when usage is moderate. The problem is that usage isn’t staying light. Agentic tools that write code, analyze documents, and run multistep tasks consume tokens at a pace a chatbot never did, and the bill scales right along with them. Earlier this year, Fleet’s IT leadership research cited a company that burned through its entire 2026 AI budget in four months after rolling an AI coding tool out to roughly 5,000 engineers. That’s the risk with a variable cost by token usage. Finance is somewhat in the dark on what the number is until the invoice shows up.

Local hardware works the opposite way, where you pay once, and the cost is capped. Every hour that machine spends running a model after that costs you very little, aside from power usage.

Someone I’ve long respected, Horace Dediu, showed some interesting numbers in a recent Asymco piece that really shows the opportunity ahead for Apple. In one example, a 26-billion-parameter model used for analysis four hours a day, around 150 million tokens a month, runs $450 to $850 per user per month through a cloud provider. A 16″ MacBook Pro with an M5 Max and 128GB of unified memory costs about $6,500 and can run a model locally. That’s a payback period of 7 to 14 months. He gives a lot more examples, and it’s worth a read to see Apple’s opportunity here.

The reason Apple Silicon is so well suited to this is unified memory. On most PCs, the GPU has its own small memory pool, and the model has to fit within it. On Apple Silicon, the GPU shares the entire memory pool, so a laptop with 128GB can hold a model that would need a far more expensive setup elsewhere.

Viewed through this lens, a price increase on a Mac Studio is a rounding error. If the machine pays for itself in under a year, and Apple Silicon Macs can stay in service for four to five years, it’s practically free over a normal refresh cycle. Now, if agentic coding keeps improving at such a rapid pace, you might end up upgrading sooner than that.

All of this hinges on one assumption: the math only works if an open-weight model running locally is good enough for your task day-to-day. For a lot of everyday work, like summarizing docs, drafting, content analysis on internal data, and basic routine coding, the gap between open-weight models and the frontier has narrowed significantly recently. For the hardest reasoning and coding tasks, frontier models still lead, and that isn’t changing anytime soon.

There are other caveats, too: his usage figures in those examples are high, and a typical employee isn’t burning through 150 million tokens a month. Token prices have also been falling, narrowing the gap over time. I am really interested in a hybrid model as well. Cribl recently launched StreamAI, an AI gateway for telemetry that routes each prompt to the right model and includes built-in budget control. At JNUC 2026, Jamf showed on-device AI support that deploys models through blueprints, routes prompts through an on-device AI gateway, and governs all of it with AI policies. Apple is clearly thinking about this too. At JNUC, Apple’s Jeremy Butcher had this to say regarding cloud and on-device AI:

“We think our platform makes for the best way to do both,” said Butcher. “We continue to have these conversations, and we look forward to working with all of you to bring it to life.”

A hybrid model might be the best of both worlds, with routine work running locally and the hardest tasks routed to frontier models in the cloud. Either way, Apple is well positioned. Even with RAM and GPU shortages driving up hardware prices, the ROI on Apple Silicon looks promising if open-weight models end up handling a decent share of enterprise AI workloads. Mac prices are going up, but token bills are going up faster (even if token prices continue to fall).

#3461. Apple Maps begins blurring NASA, Space Force, and Air Force bases

You’re not a real space or aviation nerd unless you’ve taken to a map service and zoomed on the historic NASA launch pads or your local Air Force Bases, just for fun, you know? However, a recent change to Apple Maps now has some of those locations blurred from view, blocking anyone from seeing fighters on tarmacs or rockets on launch pads.

It probably makes sense as a reasonable security measure, why should some of the most sensitive locations to the United States be easily seen from commercial services on anyone’s phone?

Not every base we’ve checked has been blurred. Some rather large US Navy installations like Pearl Harbor, Norfolk, and Naval Station Great Lakes are left unburied. As a Wisconsin resident, I checked my local Air National Guard bases, those two have been left clear to see.

What we have discovered are now blurred are a lot of NASA and US Space Force locations, including Wallops Flight Facility, Virginia, Stennis Space Center, Mississippi, Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, and Vandenberg Space Force Base, California.

This change looks to have been rather recent, with no announcement by Apple for the change. On the contrary, Google Maps, has not blurred any of these military locations. It is presumed that Apple will continue to role out blurred map changes to more bases in the future.

Apple’s choice for which locations to blur first is interesting. Whiteman Air Force Base, the location of the bulk of the Air Force’s B2 stealth bombers, capable of carrying nuclear weapons, is logically blurred from view. Ellsworth Air Force Base, one of two state-side homes of the B-1B stealth bomber, both nuclear capable and can carry the most payload than any other US bomber, is also blurred. However, Dyess Air Force Base, the second home of the B-1B and Barksdale, home of the vast majority of the 74 year old and still kicking B-52s, are not blurred.

It’s no surprise that Cape Canaveral Space Force Station (featured image), is parent base Patricks Space Force Base, and Vandenberg Space Force Base are all blurred. These locations are home to the bulk of military owned launch pads and house some of the world’s most advanced and secretive satellites ever built.

But no need to worry too much, for now it seems that Kennedy Space Center and its historic launch pads, LC-39A and LC-39B, is not blurred. That doesn’t mean NASA isn’t on the list, Wallops Flight Facility, a primarily civil research focused air field owned by NASA is blurred, but it’s launch pads, also owned by NASA, are not.

Finally, two other locations that may be top on the list of online map explorers, Groom Lake (Area 51) and the Los Alamos National Laboratory and also now blurred.

Without a formal announcement from Apple, we aren’t sure how quickly the company plans to blur over future bases; and if it’s just highly sensitive facilities or if all government locations are on the list to be blurred.

Some questions that I now have are how navigation works on these blurred bases. Does Apple CarPlay work still? Or if military personnel and civilians working at these bases need to find a new service for on base navigation needs.

#3460. ‘Being Heumann’ Review: Siân Heder’s ‘CODA’ Follow-Up Is an Essential Biopic That’s Not Afraid to Have Some Fun

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 10, 2026 during the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Apple will release the film in select theaters on Friday, November 6 and on Apple TV on Friday, November 13.]

When Siân Heder’s “CODA” premiered at Sundance in 2021 (during the festival’s online-only “pandemic year” and months and months before the film would go on to win Best Picture), it became an early favorite of mine. Mostly, I wrote in my review, though the “drama is marked by familiar beats, its characters bring new dimension to a staid genre.” The same can be said about Heder’s follow-up feature, “Being Heumann,” which brings real life back to the biopic, not only through innumerable compelling characters, but the smart choice to tightly focus this story on one essential moment in the life of the activist Judy Heumann. Related Stories Will Brill Won a Tony and Got His First Leading Film Role, but That’s Not How He Measures Success ‘Cherry & Virgin’ Review: A Fantastic Indie Anime Blends Different Art Styles and a Slew of Pop Culture References into an Innovative Modern Rom-Com

When we first meet Judy (Ruth Madeley in a true star turn), she’s zipping along a busy New York City street in 1972. That might sound fun, but for Judy, it’s just the way things are; a wheelchair user since she was just a toddler (thanks to an early bout with polio), the world is not made for people like Judy, and she makes her way through it however she can. Often, that means doing things like, oh, zipping down city streets, because there are no curb cuts to assist her in smoothly moving from sidewalk to sidewalk. As Judy goes barreling down the street, people stare, drivers yell, and the brassy Brooklynite throws up a finger.

That Judy has natural presence is a given, but the central question of Heder’s film — which she adapted from Heumann’s autobiography alongside co-writer Rebekah Taussig — is how she will use all that verve to truly enact change. It’s the sort of concern that has always impacted great leaders, and suffice it to say, Heumann was indeed a great leader. But while Heumann’s long, storied life had many incredible chapters (she passed away in 2023, two years after she started working with Heder on the film), the filmmakers smartly zero in one on seminal slice of life to craft “Being Heumann.” Cradle to the grave this is not, but the film still succeeds mightily when contextualizing Heumann’s role in the disability rights movement and her singularity as a true American original.

That’s not to say that the period of time covered by the film — which soon jumps ahead five years — isn’t complicated and dense. The film opens in 1972, because that’s when Judy and eighty other activists staged a sit-in on Madison Avenue to protest the vetoing of Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, which we’re told was one of the very first pieces of federal legislation meant to guarantee certain rights to people with disabilities (from accessibility to education). The act was eventually signed in 1973, but when the film picks back up in 1978, it has not been implemented. It needed one last step: a signature from newly-installed Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare Joseph Califano (Mark Ruffalo). And he wasn’t signing.

Heder and Taussig’s script distills the legal wrangling down well: this piece of legislation will help bring about massive positive change for the disabled community, but it will cost a lot of money, and Califano has already been asked to slash the budget. These are excellent stakes.

Judy doesn’t care about the cost to the government — why should she? — but she does care about the cost to her community. A seasoned and dogged activist, most of the people in Judy’s life are disabled in some way, and it’s her mission to a) wrangle them into action and b) be pretty pushy about it. Heder and her casting directors Bernard Telsey and Adam Caldwell have assembled a wonderful, winning cast around Madeley (herself a wheelchair user), including a number of disabled performers, cast here as icons in their own right. Standouts include Madeline Delp as Kitty Cone (the honey to Judy’s vinegar), Andrew Pilkington as Hale Zukas, Antwan Tolliver as Brad Lomax, “CODA” star Daniel Durant as Steve McCleeland, Roberta Colindrez as Joni Breves, and instant star Charlie Rush-Reese as Dennis Billups.

That Heder would cast actually disabled people in these roles should seem obvious (this is the filmmaker behind “CODA,” after all), but there’s no question that it totally pays off all the same. The wide array of performers on offer here is thrilling, and it’s a treat to see them all settling in so well to this period world, rendered tactile and realistic by smart costuming choices by Danny Glicker and unfussy production design by John P. Goldsmith.

Enraged over the lack of movement on the signing of 504, Judy and her compatriots launch a series of protests around the country, focused on federal buildings that house HEW offices. Califano, stuck back in DC, can only hear about these events as they unfold, utterly stymied but what to do, paralyzed by fear for his job, and intent on reminding people he’s one of the good guys (he supported the Selma marches!). But the world has changed. When Judy somewhat impulsively leads a pack of protesters inside the SF federal building, what follows will only spark further change.

Despite the historical implications that follow — the SF sit-in became one of the country’s largest — Heder doesn’t noodle on the cultural vegetable aspect of this story. Instead, “Being Heumann” becomes something unexpectedly frisky and fun. The sit-in comes with plenty of challenges (beyond the myriad needs of the disabled community, there’s in-fighting to spare, government pressures galore, and deep worries about how it might actually pan out), but there’s also a streak of joy that runs through it. It’s thrilling to see people doing literally whatever they can for their well-being, and having a good time in the process (yes, you’ll get acquainted with their “sex tents” soon enough). There are almost too many colorful characters here, a sprawling ensemble in which everyone deserves their own film, though we occasionally lose some threads along the way.

That isn’t always easy for Judy, though, who remains set in her ways even as she sees real change happening around her. Madeley captures the real Judy Heumann’s energy beautifully; she’s funny and flinty and spiky and smarter than anyone else around her and totally driven by her sense of justice and equality. But that’s not always enough, a lesson that “Being Heumann” is not shy about. Fighting for what’s right involves just that, fighting. Sometimes, that even means fighting your own instincts.

A film like ”Being Heumann” is destined to be called rousing — a call to action that’s every bit as entertaining as it is inspiring. It’s a film about tough choices and even tougher circumstances, but it’s also about the tangible good that can come from people working together. What could be more joyous than that? More biopics could learn from this formula, and from this feeling. Be more like Judy: be tough, but never be afraid of joy.

“Being Heumann” premiered at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Apple will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6 and on Apple TV on Friday, November 13.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. JBL’s Live 780NC over-ear headphones are down to $139.95 from $249.95, a $110 discount that brings them to their lowest price ever, according to price trackers. At this price, you’re getting a feature-rich pair of wireless headphones with active noise cancellation, high-resolution audio support, and battery life that can last through several days of commuting or work sessions. They’re designed for people who like to wear headphones for hours at a time, too, with adjustable metal sliders and earcups that pivot to fit comfortably around your head. The earcups also fold flat to make them easier to pack, although the included soft pouch offers less protection in a bag than a hard case would.

Sound-wise, its 40mm drivers deliver a wide frequency response of 10Hz to 40kHz, while Bluetooth 6.0 support, LDAC, and LE Audio give you options for high-quality wireless listening with compatible devices. The catch is that the default tuning pushes the bass a little too hard (according to this PCMag review), so you may want to spend some time adjusting the sound through JBL’s app—which includes a 10-band equalizer, preset profiles, personalized sound settings, and virtual spatial audio, letting you tailor the listening experience to your preferences.

You also get Bluetooth multipoint for connecting two devices at once, plus a proximity sensor that pauses playback when you remove the headphones. Physical controls handle power, pairing, and volume, while a touch-sensitive surface lets you manage playback and call up your phone’s voice assistant. As for its battery life, JBL claims up to 80 hours of playback with active noise cancellation turned off, or up to 50 hours with ANC enabled. That should be plenty for long-haul flights, extended workdays, or several commutes between charges, although the noise cancellation itself isn’t quite as effective as what you’ll find on some higher-end competitors. The headphones also lack water and sweat resistance, so they’re not the best choice for workouts or rainy commutes.

#3458. MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR looks awesome, but I’m not rushing to upgrade

After five years, Apple released its first major MacBook Pro overhaul since the M1 Pro/M1 Max models, and well… it was a little bit underwhelming from a design perspective. The product is incredible on many merits, but after seeing it, I’m not left feeling like I need to buy one – at least not yet.

The new MacBook Pro is substantially lighter. That’s a major improvement, especially if you’re someone who carries around a 16-inch MacBook Pro. With this new PROLED XDR generation, the 14-inch model reduced in weight by 0.5 pounds, and the 16-inch model reduced by 0.7 pounds. That’s a great deal when you’re carrying it around in a backpack or similar. The new models are also marginally thinner.

For me, though, I find myself a bit surprised by the fact that nothing about the top case design changed. The keyboard, trackpad, speaker, and port layouts all look about the same, and the chassis didn’t change shape besides getting a bit thinner. For every MacBook Pro overhaul in the past, the top case has changed in a meaningful way. With this overhaul, it really feels like more of a display upgrade that’s also accompanied by a lighter chassis.

Was there anything wrong with the current MacBook Pro chassis? Not at all. However, you could also argue the same for most design shifts in Apple’s history. It would’ve been nice to have a slightly different look, beyond the display.

This is more of a personal point. That said, I already have an M4 Pro model, and given the fact that these new MacBook Pros are substantially more expensive ($400 more compared to the miniLED MacBook Pros, which are also $300 more than they were prior to the June price hikes), I’m not particularly excited to buy silicon that isn’t the latest and greatest. The M5 family kicked off last year, and we already know M7 is coming next year.

I fully understand why Apple opted to skip the M6 Pro and M6 Max chips, but it sure does make this MacBook Pro feel ever so slightly more uninteresting.

Apple already alluded to the fact that they have more in the pipeline when it comes to macOS optimizations for touch, so maybe I’ll be wowed in the future. For now though, aside from being able to interact with the iOS simulator with proper touch, I don’t really see much of a need to have touch on my Mac.

It’s great that it’s there, and I’m certainly not disappointed that Apple added it – but I’m not yet convinced I truly need it.

None of this was to bash on the new MacBook Pro at all. In fact, I’ll most definitely be buying one in the future, most likely once it gains M7 Pro and M7 Max chips by this time next year. Hopefully touch feels more important by then. I certainly love the idea of having a glowing Apple logo again, just not quite yet – and it’s not like this product will be going anywhere if I don’t buy it during the first iteration.

I bought a ridiculously overpowered M1 Max with 64GB of memory back when they were first released, and I have zero incentive to upgrade to this day. This machine covers all my needs with ease still.

It’s also worth noting I haven’t yet seen the new display in person. It’s totally possible I’ll be blown away once I see it, but I still think I’ll be capable of waiting. Especially since my M4 Pro MacBook Pro already has a 1000 nit display, so I’m not missing out too terribly from the OLED model.

How do you feel about the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR? Will you be buying one, or are you in a similar boat as I am? Let us know in the comments.

#3457. How To Beat Giovanni In Pokémon GO (November 2026)

Team Rocket is a constant nuisance in Pokémon GO, with their leaders representing challenges that yield great rewards due to their difficulty. No one embodies that more than Giovanni, the criminal mastermind of Team Rocket whose Pokémon are the strongest, especially a stolen Legendary under his command. For November 2026, you have to assemble a team of perfect counters to overcome Giovanni's team.

Finding Giovanni is almost as hard as battling him, as you need to assemble the Super Rocket Radar to track down the criminal leader. Completing Special Research and defeating other Team Rocket members will help you find Giovanni, after going through a couple of decoys first. After October 2026 changed Giovanni's team, Pokémon GO players will have had time to adjust to his challenge for the new month.

Like any other encounter with Team Rocket, Giovanni uses exclusively Shadow Pokémon during the battle, with Shadow Pokémon being stronger variants of what you'd normally fight. Shadow Pokémon in Pokémon GO have higher health and deal more damage, making them just as dangerous as a Mega Evolution or Legendary in some cases. Since Giovanni has a Shadow version of a Legendary Pokémon already, the battle can be tougher than you'd expect.

Multiple events in November 2026 could give you new Pokémon to catch and train for an eventual confrontation with Giovanni. Check out the "Into the Wild" or "Dynamax Trails" this month to see if any new team members catch your eye.

Giovanni's battle follows a specific structure, consisting of three waves with three different Pokémon for you to face. Similarly, players are only allowed to use three Pokémon for the battle as well, limiting your counters for each match-up. Giovanni's first and third wave Pokémon are always the same, but his second wave could be one of three possible choices, which are picked at random.

For November 2026, Giovanni uses the following Pokémon, whose weaknesses and best counters are also listed in the table below:

Ground, Water, Ice, Steel, Grass, Fighting

You should have at least one Fighting-type for this battle, as that will let you at least deal with Giovanni's first Pokémon easily. However, this type of Pokémon also could help deal with Giovanni's Kangaskhan, who is arguably the best Pokémon he has in the second wave. Other types like strong Ice-types in Pokémon GO could help in this battle, as well as Fairy, Psychic, or Water-types as alternate choices.

A great example of a team (that's easier to build) that could help you counter almost every Pokémon on Giovanni's team is:

Following Giovanni's example could help you counter his team, with a Rhyperior of your own being the perfect counter to neutralize Shadow Zekrom's Electric-type attacks. Although the Dragon-type moves from Zekrom are still deadly, Rhyperior and Lucario's defensive types could help them resist attacks long enough to take the Legendary down. At the same time, an Alakazam beats Giovanni's Machamp, while Lucario defeats Giovanni's own Rhyperior.

When you take down Giovanni with whatever team you use, you are rewarded with 5,000 Stardust immediately to spend how you please. Yet, the biggest reward from the Giovanni battle is a chance to catch his Shadow Zekrom for yourself, through a free encounter that takes place after the fight. Players may have already caught Shadow Zekrom last month, but they have a chance of getting more Candy for the Pokémon to make one stronger by doing so again.

Players also get three different item bundles for defeating Giovanni, which can stack together to give players a large collection of the same reward. These three random drops mainly consist of strong battle items, making Raid battles or Gym defenses much easier. The item bundles for taking down Giovanni include:

Incoming events for the game may create more opportunities to use these items, including similar battles with Team Rocket in the future. It's unclear whether another "Taken Over" event will change Giovanni's team this month, but if it does, the Legendary Pokémon could change in these rewards. For now, November 2026 might be the last chance to get Shadow Zekrom in Pokémon GO, as long as you beat Giovanni using the right team.

#3456. 3 Seasons Later, ’Silo’s Best Line Still Defines Apple TV’s Sci-Fi Masterpiece

Of all the science fiction shows in Apple TV's library, Silo might be the standout. Based on a trilogy of novels by Hugh Howey, the seriestakes place in a hellish landscape. Humanity has retreated to "Silos," massive bunkers built to withstand the terrors of the outside world. Nobody knows how they came to live in the Silos, or what turned the world into a living nightmare. Eventually, Juliette Nichols (Rebecca Ferguson), an engineer who keeps the Silo running, starts to learn that everything isn't as it seems. One sentence perfectly captures the web of secrets and danger that's the backbone of Silo.

That quote is spoken in the Season 1 episode "The Relic," when Juliette's former lover, George Wilkins (Ferdinand Kingsley), says, “What if everything you know to be true, everything you’ve been told by the people you love, was in fact just one big lie?" While earlier episodes of Silo established that those in power might be hiding the truth about what happened to the world, George's quote fundamentally reshapes the series' approach. Nearly every character in Silo hides something, and it shapes how they see the world and each other.

From the beginning of Silo, it's clear that not everything is as it seems. The pilot episode "Freedom Day" focuses on a young woman who encounters George and other Silo workers who believe the world outside isn't as deadly as it's been painted to be. That's proven true in the following episode, "Holston's Pick," where law enforcement officer Holston Becker (David Oyewolo) discovers that instead of a war-torn landscape, the outside of the Silo thrives with plant life. Future episodes continue to reveal the depth of the deception; "The Relic" reveals that everyone in the Silo is under surveillance, and that the population is fed drugs that suppress their memories.

On another level, George's quote also shows that nobody in Silo can be trusted. During "The Relic," Juliette encounters an ex-girlfriend of George's who reveals just how obsessed he was with learning the truth, to the point where he was using said ex to procure illegal relics. He said that you can't trust the people you love, which extends to the people uncovering the conspiracy as well as the ones enacting it. Silo doesn't shy away from the fact that Juliette has had to make some hard choices in her quest to uncover the truth, and it doesn't shy away from the price of that truth, either.

The unfolding maze of secrets and lies in Silo keeps fans coming back, and it continues to dominate Apple TV's streaming charts. All good things must come to an end, though, as the fourth and final season debuts next year. Showrunner Graham Yost previously promised Variety that Season 4 of Silo would wrap up every mystery left in the show's run and end on a high note.

"It has been a richly rewarding experience to adapt Hugh’s epic novels with our partners at Apple and we are thrilled to have the opportunity to bring this complete story to the screen over the course of four seasons. With the final two chapters of ‘Silo’, we can’t wait to give fans of the show an incredibly satisfying conclusion to the many mysteries and unanswered questions contained within the walls of these silos."

Silo Season 3 ended with even more answers and a few questions, including the potential cause of the end of the world. Season 4 has a lot of ground to cover, but it could also throw more than a few curveballs in Juliette's way. What if she finds that someone close to her is actually a major part of the conspiracy? George's words about the people you love lying to you loom large; she didn't really know him, and other elements could further muddy the waters of her memory.

What makes Silo so compelling is that nothing is what it seems. The quote from George further highlights this, especially the fact that part of the series' draw is uncovering who everyone is and how they fit into this post-apocalyptic tapestry.

#3454. The Bose Premium Smart Ultra Soundbar Is Now Cheaper Than It Was During Prime Day

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon has dropped the Bose Smart Ultra Soundbar to $649 from its usual $999, taking $350 off and bringing it to the lowest price we've seen so far, according to price trackers. PCMag rated the Smart Ultra "outstanding," highlighting its ability to deliver surprisingly immersive Dolby Atmos audio without requiring a room full of additional speakers. If you don't need Bose's top-tier model, there's a less expensive option as well: the Bose Smart Dolby Atmos Soundbar ($399, down from $429), which sits below the Smart Ultra in the lineup.

The Smart Ultra uses a 5.1.2-channel design with nine drivers, including two upward-firing drivers that bounce sound off the ceiling to create height effects. In practice, that means movies, TV shows, and games feel larger and more spacious than they do through most single-bar setups. Bose also includes its AdaptiQ room-calibration system, which measures your room's acoustics and adjusts the sound accordingly. The process takes a few minutes, but it helps the soundbar perform better across different spaces rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all tuning profile. The soundbar also works as a smart speaker, with Amazon Alexa built in and support for Apple AirPlay 2, Google Cast, Spotify Connect, Bluetooth, and multi-room audio through the Bose app.

Its biggest compromise is bass—for a single soundbar, its low end is respectable, but it can't fully replace what a dedicated subwoofer brings to action movies, concerts, or bass-heavy music. The good news is that Bose allows you to expand the system later with compatible wireless subwoofers and surround speakers if you decide you want more impact. For anyone looking for a premium one-piece soundbar that delivers convincing Dolby Atmos effects, clear dialogue, built-in smart features, and a much larger soundstage than TV speakers can provide, the Smart Ultra remains one of the strongest standalone options available, especially at this price.

#3453. ‘Club Kid’ Review: Jordan Firstman’s Brazen, Funny, and Surprisingly Earnest Directing Debut Is a Wild Party Movie with Heart

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 15, 2026 during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. A24 will release “Club Kid” in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

Ask any gay man with a social media account, and they likely have an opinion about Jordan Firstman. The backlash-courting queer actor/comedian, controversial most recently because of an online flare-up over querying the sexual realism of “Heated Rivalry,” is labeled either candid or confrontational. He also has a record of taking on sexually explicit projects like Sebastian Silva’s suicide-ideating, ketamine-fueled dark comedy “Rotting in the Sun.” His status as a self-aware, hyper-online provocateur may not seem to suggest the makings of a bona fide filmmaker, but just wait. Related Stories ‘Being Heumann’ Review: Siân Heder’s ‘CODA’ Follow-Up Is an Essential Biopic That’s Not Afraid to Have Some Fun Will Brill Won a Tony and Got His First Leading Film Role, but That’s Not How He Measures Success

While that reputation might have Firstman on guard as he debuts his feature writing/directing debut “Club Kid,” as it will certain circumspect corners of the audience, this terrific movie should put any of those nervous feelings to rest. Even his haters won’t be able to resist what’s announced here as a major filmmaking talent with a sensitive side that belies his brash, internet-based persona.

He also stars as the protagonist of his hugely crowd-pleasing, excruciatingly funny, and poignant first film — one that plays to all sides of the room despite being brazenly, unapologetically queer — which will prime Firstman-savvy viewers to immediately interpret “Club Kid” as autobiographical. That’s because it is.

He plays party promoter Peter, now in his thirties after a decade-plus of MDMA-addled revelry, the kind where all the days blur and blot into one long and sweaty night with a coming horizon in the shape of regret. Firstman may not be playing himself this time, but he is playing a version of that self, having, as he says, spent enough years in Berlin to be labeled “the angel of Berghain” by his new friends, but now ready to put the days-that-became-years of GHB, MDMA, and other letters of the alphabet behind him.

“Club Kid” is exactly about what happens when the lights go up on the party, the shameover of the morning after that becomes a way of being, and the need to do it all over again to stave off last night’s aching after effects. But it’s also about — earnesty alert! — family lost and found, not only because of the queer community formed around the now-orphaned Peter, who lives in the rent-controlled Manhattan his mother left him after she died, but because he wakes up one day to find a child he fathered and never knew about, literally on his doorstep.

“Club Kid” was shot on 35mm on location in New York City with a team of backers including “Anora” Oscar-winning producer Alex Coco and nepo filmmaker Olmo Schnabel, and a millennial cast of queer comedians. So it’s hard not to leave the movie thinking all that’s needed here is an A24 logo slapped onto the opening credits, and it’s ready for the world. But no matter; while Firstman’s aesthetic is loudly in A24’s register, it turns out to be an asset rather than a limitation.

Beginning inside a sensually lit, drug-soaked party and ending as one rages on without you from afar, “Club Kid” drops us into Brooklyn 2016. Peter, sing-screaming Rihanna’s “Sex with Me” in a clown car of an Uber ride with his friends, is headed into yet another bender to remember (but also eventually forget). At a club of the sort that now dominates night culture in Bushwick, rising party promoter Peter ends up hooking up — and then really hooking up — with a couple of hyperactive “innit, babes?” British women in the back room. It’s all inconspicuously taking a turn for the sexual when the movie smash cuts to “a decade or so later,” when the proverbial party is still dying down, but Peter is still living in it — albeit more sweaty and tragic 10 years on.

He’s now made a career out of his drug use with his best friend and business partner Sophie (a marvelous, perpetually coked-out Cara Delevingne, who’s two inches from a breakdown at all times). A few days before the one that’s about to change his life, they have an important sit-down coming up with FiDi investors to help expand their New York party empire. But alas, as he couldn’t help himself once again the night before, Peter wakes up drugged to the gills, rushing to the meeting only to nod off at the table, still in a GHB-spiked stupor. (His reaction to a dropper of hot sauce that looks curiously similar to the one he used last night to get high is one of the film’s many brilliantly funny little pratfalls.)

All of that’s to say Peter’s life is still totally a mess, and his arrested development from a decade of partying has now washed him out to the point where sobriety is maybe never part of his day. (A weekend spent dissipated, hungover, jerking off to internet porn and eating Popeye’s in bed rings painfully true.)

Party’s certainly over, though, when one of those British “innit babes” from 10 years ago, Edison (Kirby Howell-Baptiste), shows up from London at his apartment (where Peter lives with an “Azerbaijanian aspiring queer philosopher” who doesn’t pay rent) with an eight-year-old boy. “You’ve got a kid! ‘Yay!,’” she tells him while delivering the news that Arlo (preternaturally gifted young breakout actor Reggie Absalom) is in fact Peter’s child with one of the other women from that opening-scene heterosexual encounter, who’s just died. The first and only time Peter fucked a woman, and now he’s fucked himself into having to finish raising a small boy.

Cue the manic panic, more drug use, and resignation to the idea that there’s no sending this kid back to the U.K.

While it’s a bit sudden how fast the switch flips from Peter feeling wildly ill-equipped for parenting to becoming a nurturing caretaker, he and Arlo turn out to have more in common than not. Arlo, for one, has the music taste of someone who grew up on Pitchfork, eagerly taking to the $300 Elliott Smith record Peter buys for him in a later scene. (The soundtrack on this thing, by the way, rules, from Arthur Russell during the film’s melancholy final act to “The White Lotus” composer Cristobal Tapia de Veer’s deeply felt original score.) Their relationship, however quickly, becomes the film’s so-far unexpected sweet center, as Peter starts to really appreciate and eventually love Arlo, who has traumas of his own.

A lot of the success of “Club Kid” rides not only on Firstman’s shoulders, but also on the collaborators he’s working with, including cinematographer Adam Newport-Berra who captures a certain lost-era grit in New York as well as in the chaos-packed nightclub sequences. “Club Kid” also takes advantage of New York City as not just a backdrop but a central character in the storytelling, using the city in a way that feels rare onscreen these days.

“Club Kid” freewheels and unwinds like a head rush of a zippy party movie until Arlo’s introduction brings the comedown. It turns out he feels more at home among Peter’s “found family” of queer revelers, discovering his own DJ skills in the process, than he ever did in London. Could Peter really warm to fatherhood? Real emotional stakes start to heighten as he begins recognizing the unexpected realities of his new arrangement, like getting Arlo into school, or keeping the boy shielded from the drug use of his friends while Peter’s own finally starts to diminish. A nervous, tentative romance comes into view with child psychologist Oscar (Diego Calva), and on a date where a namecheck of Gregg Araki’s “Mysterious Skin” becomes not just a tender confession, but a turn-on.

“Club Kid” takes a sharp dramatic turn, in which the nature of Arlo’s living situation becomes even more dire and probably illegal, that almost shouldn’t work in a comedy like this — but it’s a turn that feels inevitable given how “Club Kid” is structured like the rise and fall of a drug experience, a high that crashes down into despair. The emotional arc bends toward “Kramer vs. Kramer” territory with a cathartic (and well-played by Firstman) courtroom oner. Peter may be insecure about his own place in a world where only parts of it have room for him, but as a storyteller with an eye, Firstman is anything but.

Firstman is by now an established comedic voice, but his work on all sides of the camera here leaves pretty of room for revelation, for him to become a genuine discovery beyond an audience of gay, internet-addled millennials. “Club Kid” has real potential to break out bigger than its seemingly niche scope would suggest, with Firstman finally shirking the ironic pose he’s taken online for years to emerge as a sincere storyteller with heart as much as humor.

“Club Kid” premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. It is currently seeking U.S. distribution.

#3452. Indie App Spotlight: ‘Pumpkin Lights’ adds a fun jack-o-lantern to your Mac’s menu bar

Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact.

Pumpkin Lights is a nifty little menu bar app for Mac that lets you quickly toggle between light mode and dark mode with a ray-traced jack-o-lantern that drops down from the top of your screen. It’s completely free, and very fun to utilize.

If you remember the Festivas menu bar app from Mac year, Pumpkin Lights is very similar in concept.

Pumpkin Lights brings a jack-o-lantern to your menu bar, just in time for halloween. It’s a nice decoration, and there’s plenty of different ways to customize it. You can “grow” many different pumpkin designs, as well as pick between four different color variants.

When you click on the pumpkin or pull on it, your Mac will toggle between light and dark mode – at least by default. Pumpkin Lights also has the option to open an app/website, keep your Mac awake, mute a sound, run a command, or run a shortcut of your choice.

The jack-o-lantern does have proper physics, so you can actually toss it around a bit and move it around in a novel way. You can customize the rope it hangs from, and much more. There’s also an option to have a hanging light bulb that serves a similar purpose.

Why Pumpkin Lights? Here’s what the developer has to say:

The idea came from something most of us do every day without thinking: switching between Light and Dark Mode. It’s always a toggle buried in Control Center or System Settings, and it never feels like anything. I wanted it to feel like touching a real object. So instead of a flat icon, the pumpkin and the bulb are real 3D models, ray-traced in real time, hanging on cords you can swing and spin. When the candle lights, its glow comes through the carved face. I spent most of my time on small details like how the cords move and how light falls on the pumpkin, because I wanted it to still feel delightful the hundredth time you use it, not just the first.

Pumpkin Lights is a completely free utility. You can download it from the developer’s website here, and it’s available for any Mac running macOS 14 Sonoma or later. You can also follow the developer on Twitter.

#3451. The Brutalist Ending Explained: What Happens To Harrison & Laszlo

Brady Corbet's The Brutalist offers an ending with dense thematic material to examine. Adrien Brody leads The Brutalist's cast as László Tóth, a Hungarian-Jewish architect separated from his wife during World War II. He arrives in America and finds himself under the employ of Harrison Lee Van Buren, a wealthy man fascinated by Tóth's innovative architectural talent, who commissions him to construct a landmark community center in memory of his mother.

The movie's ending sees Harrison reach out to László to kick off construction again. On their trip to Italy, Harrison rapes a drunk László to demonstrate his power over him. This causes László to spiral, lashing out in anger at his friends and employees. Eventually, his wife Erzsébet runs out of medication, and László injects her with heroin to help with the pain, causing her to overdose. At his home, Harrison disappears after being accused in front of family and colleagues.

The Brutalist's epilogue occurs in 1980 at a Biennale for László Tóth, exhibiting his architectural work over the past two decades and celebrating his life. It's a shocking moment, given how desperate matters were becoming for him at the end of the film, but it seems like Erzsébet's trip back to Pennsylvania ended up being fruitful for his career. However, it's unclear how exactly László became a renowned architect. The Van Buren community center is mentioned as one of his accomplishments, so he was credited for the work.

Adrien Brody’s historical epic, The Brutalist, has garnered an impressive Rotten Tomatoes score, making many wonder what makes the film so incredible.

At the event, Zsófia gives a speech about László Tóth's life, summarizing her uncle's career and demonstrating a side of his character that the audience hasn't really been directly acquainted with, as László hasn't shared the inspiration for his work. She describes how his personal life influenced his creative process, inspiring different aspects of the community center. Notably, the interiors of the community center were made to resemble the concentration camps László was subjected to, meaning his trauma was developed into his work.

Zsófia's speech names the camps behind the design: Buchenwald and Dachau, where the Tóth family suffered. She frames the community center as an artistic trap, a sort of architectural Trojan Horse. László used Harrison's money to build a structure that repudiates the kind of power and comfort Harrison and his family embody. The film's very last shot is a flash of a young Zsófia in a concentration camp.

Her point is to suggest that László went through hell to achieve his artistry, but the end result is ultimately what mattered.

There's one statement Zsófia makes that's perfectly reflective of the narrative. She closes the speech saying, "No matter what the others try and sell you, it is the destination, not the journey." Her point suggests that László went through hell to achieve his artistry, but the end result is ultimately what matters. His personal life was continuously riddled with conflict and tragedy, yet he accomplished works that eventually came to be respected and admired.

Harrison Lee Van Buren's fate is one of the strangest mysteries of The Brutalist's ending. Despite the importance of his character to the narrative, after Erzsébet accuses him of raping László, he flees the scene. His son and household employees cannot find him on the grounds, and the film cuts away to the epilogue without resolving his disappearance. Furthermore, the epilogue doesn't provide any more information regarding Harrison. Brady Corbet leaves the decision to the viewer.

There are several matters regarding this scene that can be theorized upon. As for Harrison's fate, it's possible that he killed himself or simply fled, hiding from the shame and leaving to begin life anew elsewhere. Another interesting detail in the scene is how his son, Harry, reacts. Harry is a pompous tool throughout the film; this is the scene where he shows genuine despair. Aside from his father being accused of doing something terrible, he's horrified because he believes or knows it to be true.

Another scene in the film shows Harry walking up to Zsófia as she sits by the water in a swimsuit. He asks her if she'd like to go on a stroll, but the scene cuts away before demonstrating what happens. The next time they're shown, Zsófia walks away from Harry, purposefully covering up where she was previously showing skin. The film could imply that Harry attempted something.

Erzsébet isn't present in the epilogue, implying that she passed away sometime in the past twenty years. Luckily, she survived the overdose in 1960, living long enough to move back to Europe with László. She had been diagnosed with osteoporosis in or around 1953, likely impacting her life expectancy. Though she was shown walking on a stretcher toward the movie's ending, her condition primarily wasn't shown to be improving over her seven years in The Brutalist.

Adrien Brody's character, László Tóth, is an entirely fictional figure, though the film is so well-constructed that he feels alive. In an interview with CNN, Adrien Brody discussed how his own life helped influence the creation of the character, saying, "I am fortunate to have an understanding of that immigrant experience and the many parallels of an artist’s journey." Brody's performance, the writing from Brady Corbet and Mona Fastvold, and other talented artists involved in the projection helped develop a fascinating figure to study.

The Brutalist is a post-war epic that examines similarities between immigrants and artists. László is both of these things, and not only is he rejected for differing from the locals in religion and culture, but he's also misunderstood as a creative. He's surrounded by Americans who can't possibly understand any aspect of his life and don't attempt to try. With that in mind, Harrison Lee Van Buren is emblematic of America in its most toxic form: a capitalist who doesn't care to understand László's plight or even the art and yet desires to own it.

The Brutalist's leading man Adrien Brody details his collaborative relationship with director Brady Corbet and reflects on his 2002 Oscars win.

To an extreme extent, Harrison enforces his need for power over László, even sexually assaulting him while reminding him that he isn't living up to his full potential. Harrison is envious of László's creative genius, suggesting that his vast wealth has only resulted in a profoundly shallow existence. The Brutalist is ultimately László's portrait, though, and the movie suggests that, regardless of the tragic journey, he reaches his destination, and the world revels in his creation.

One Reddit thread questioned why The Brutalist ending occurred in Venice when the OP suggested that Israel would have made more sense with Zsófia delivering the speech to a Jewish audience. However, when looking at this, Redditor JamarcusRussell suggested, "It’s not the journey it’s the destination. That it’s in Venice, a place thematically unconnected with the rest of the movie, and that’s we don’t hear him speak or find out if they moved to Israel, is important."

Another Redditor called Constant-Pumpkiin-628 suggested that the time-jump ending was something that played into the idea of how society views history:

"It feels like the filmmakers are holding up a mirror to our perception of the world around us. By skipping all that time and denying us a neatly resolved conclusion—despite how much we’ve invested in the story—it mirrors how we often view history. We see the architecture and admire its grandeur, but we fail to grasp the immense effort, struggle, and suffering that went into creating it."

There was another Reddit thread where fans debated what The Brutalist ending really meant. The OP wrote that they saw the ending as a positive from an artist's point of view: "I expected to leave the theater enraged, but then due to those last few minutes, I left it elated. Tóth and his work will be remembered forever, and that's all that matters." However, others suggested that Zsófia spoke for Tóth, once again stripping him of his agency. In the end, Redditor chesterT3 commented, "Corbet made the ending ambiguous so that you can come to your own conclusions."

The Brutalist follows László Tóth, a Hungarian-Jewish architect and Holocaust survivor who emigrates to the United States after World War II in search of a new beginning. When a wealthy industrialist commissions him to design an ambitious architectural masterpiece, László's pursuit of artistic greatness forces him to confront the personal and professional sacrifices demanded by the American dream.

The Brutalist theme runs everywhere in this movie from the architecture, to the characters, and right down to the sound where everything in the background is amplified and just assaults the senses. Laslo Toth's whole life has been spent trying to realize his vision as an artist and architect against "brutality" from the concentration camp to realizing how difficult life as an immigrant is in America. He finds a benefactor in Harrison Lee Van Buren, a cold and domineering man who envies Toth's artistry despite his wealth. Toth's relationship with Harrison reaches an ugly point that sends Toth reeling. At the end of the movie we see an event in Venice where Toth is celebrated later in life as an accomplished architect where his nice Zsofia speaks for him. She mentions that the destination matters more than the journey in regards to her uncle's success. #3450. The Top 10 Movies Right Now, According to Streaming Data

The most streamed movie in October was Steven Spielberg's Disclosure Day, but half of the month's top ten is made up of season-appropriate horror movies. This year's two most successful horror movies, Backrooms and Obsession, made the list; so did a classic (Halloween from 1978) and an art movie about the genre that Halloween created,Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Perfect double feature. Rounding out the list is the all-around-excellent Hokum. If you're not into horror, you might like Golden Arm, a comedy that refused to die, star-studded comedy The Invite, or ultimate crowd-pleaser Project Hail Mary.

Legendary director Steven Spielberg returns to the extraterrestrials he loves so much with a thriller that's a spiritual sequel to Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Disclosure Day details the events that lead up to the revelation that aliens are among us. Josh O’Connor plays Dr. Daniel Kellner, a cybersecurity expert for a government contractor who uncovers explosive evidence that his employers would kill to keep secret. Meanwhile, a TV meteorologist (Emily Blunt) begins speaking in an alien language. It all sets the stage for a series of set pieces and chases leading to the biggest revelation in human history. Stream Disclosure Day on Peacock.

Director Kane Parsons' analog horror breakthrough is proof that atmosphere, mood, and a fascinating story is scarier than CGI monsters every time. Based on the viral YouTube series of the same name, Backrooms tells the story of Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a store owner who discovers a labyrinthian liminal space in his furniture shop's basement. Renate Reinsve plays his therapist, who goes downstairs for a visit and does not find it easy to return. A hit with critics—Backrooms is sitting at 86% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes—and audiences, Backrooms is a delicious Halloween treat for horror fans. Stream Backrooms on HBO Max.

Director Curry Barker is still in his 20s, but his debut theatrical feature is the kind of horror film that changes the entire genre. Obsession is a classic "be careful what you wish for" story that feels fresh thanks to its talented young cast, unpredictable plot, and careful pace. Michael Johnston plays a young man too scared to tell his crush how he feels, so he wishes she'd fall in love with him instead. The result is a nightmare embodied by Inde Navarrette, whose portrayal of the villain/victim is at once harrowing, terrifying, and heartbreaking. Obsession is the best horror movie I've seen in years. Stream Obsession on Peacock.

This comedy-drama from A24 is packed with heavy-hitting actors. Olivia Wilde, who also directed the film, plays Angela, and Seth Rogen plays her husband, Joe. With the straight-laced couple's marriage on thin ice, Angela and Joe invite their more, uh, open-minded neighbors Piña, played by Penélope Cruz, and Hawk, played by Edward Norton, over for dinner. The evening unravels in hilarious ways, changing everyone's life. If you're a fan of smart, honest comedy, you will really like The Invite. Stream The Invite on HBO Max.

With Hokum, Director Damian McCarthy (Oddity, Caveat) carefully builds a suffocatingly creepy story around Adam Scott's portrayal of Ohm Bauman, a celebrity novelist and unmitigated jerk who travels to the isolated Bilberry Woods Hotel in Ireland to scatter the ashes of his parents and finish his book. Bauman soon learns that the lore of the hotel includes an ancient witch who feeds her victims to the creatures of hell, and she might be more than just a local legend. Hokum is a horror movie for fans of dreadful atmosphere and careful pacing instead of gore or jump-scares. Stream Hokum on Hulu.

With a title like this, it's not going to be a normal movie. Director Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow and We're All Going to the World's Fair are two of the most fascinating, fiercely original horror movies of the last decade, and their third film follows in those strange footfalls. While it's technically a meta re-imagining of the slasher genre, Miasma goes way deeper than Scream ever could. It's a postmodern exploration of why the slasher genre's cocktail of sex, death, and subversion casts such a strong spell on interesting, weird people. Definitely see this movie. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

When Golden Arm was released in 2021, not many people paid attention—with the pandemic in full swing, people didn't seem to have room for a quirky, indie comedy about a woman's quest to win the ladies' arm-wrestling championship—but it's a new age, and you should stream Golden Arm. It's sitting on a perfect score at Rotten Tomatoes, the movie's stars, Mary Holland and Betsy Sodaro, are charming and hilarious, and you can catch Golden Arm on Fandango, a free streaming service. What's not to love? Stream Golden Arm on Fandango or Prime Video.

In this crowd-pleasing sci-fi flick, Ryan Gosling stars as Ryland Grace, a middle school science teacher who is blasted into the firmament in a last-ditch effort to save the world. Grace is the only person on Earth who might know how to protect the sun from a cosmic infection that threatens all life, but he's definitely not an astronaut and doesn't see himself as a hero either. Will he rise to the occasion and learn something about his inner strength and resilience while saving us all from death? My money is on, "yeah, probably." Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+, Prime Video, and Philo.

Hundreds of slasher movies have been released since Halloween came out in 1978, but none have surpassed the original. Michael Myers' expressionless visage and the synthesizer theme have become universally recognized cultural signifiers for "horror movie," and every shot in Halloween has been stolen countless times, but the movie is so good, it's still scary. Watch or re-watch Halloween now! Stream Halloween on Philo, AMC+, and Prime Video.

Directed by and starring Ben Affleck, Animals is a thriller that tells the story of Mark Kimball, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped and held for ransom. Having spent every dime on his outsider campaign, Kimball is forced to turn to extreme methods to guarantee his son's safe return, even if it conflicts with his public persona as a man of the people. Animals is a taut, expertly directed movie that should more than satisfy fans of political thrillers. Stream Animals on Netflix.
