#3449. Billy Bob Thornton’s ‘Landman’ Suffers a Major Streaming Setback Following Season 3 Delay

Taylor Sheridan is no stranger to putting together a show that doesn't just entertain viewers but also pierces a hole in the cultural consciousness, and finds the exact thing that makes people tick. That's why he's been as successful as he has to date. But while one of his shows has been breaking records, ahead of a huge blow for its momentum, another hit has come and it's one that suggests perhaps its popularity is starting to wane the longer it's out of the public eye.

Landman, the hit Paramount+ drama starring Billy Bob Thornton, and based on the podcast Boomtown by Christian Wallace, has officially dropped out of the platform's U.S. Top 10 television chart after spending more than 400 consecutive days among its most-watched shows. The achievement becomes even more impressive when compared with some of the streamer's other biggest hits. South Park has previously managed a 467-day streak, while Ghosts reached 581 days, Everybody Loves Raymond achieved 837 days, and NCIS managed an extraordinary 980 days. No other Sheridan series has reportedly come close to matching Landman's run. The official series synopsis states:

Set in the proverbial boomtowns of West Texas, Landman is a modern-day tale of fortune seeking in the world of oil rigs. The series is an upstairs/downstairs story of roughnecks and wildcat billionaires fueling a boom so big, it’s reshaping our climate, our economy and our geopolitics.

In season two, as oil rises from the earth, so do secrets — and Tommy Norris's breaking point may be closer than he realizes. Facing mounting pressure from M-Tex Oil, Cami Miller, and the shadow of his kin, survival in West Texas isn't noble - it's brutal. And sooner or later something's got to break.

The show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

The cast includes Thornton (Sling Blade) as Tommy Norris, Demi Moore (The Substance) as Cami Miller, Jon Hamm (Mad Men) as Monty Miller, Colm Feore (The Umbrella Academy) as Nathan, Mustafa Speaks (Power) as Boss, Bobbi Salvör Menuez (Under the Silver Lake) as Paigyn, and Francesca Xuereb (Room 104) as Cheyenne. Season 3 will also introduce Michael Kelly (House of Cards) as the head of a global oil investment firm.

Both seasons of Landman are streaming now on Paramount+. Season 3 is in development, although an official premiere date has not yet been announced. Stay tuned to Collider for all the latest news and updates on Landman.

In the rugged terrain of West Texas, a team of landmen work to secure oil and gas leases, acting as intermediaries between landowners and energy corporations. The narrative centers on a driven landman whose ambitions in the energy sector lead him into complex negotiations and moral quandaries. The show explores the intense competition and the far-reaching consequences of the landmen's deals, highlighting the intersection of personal ambition and the broader effects on the community and the natural world.

#3448. Here’s how the new MacBook Pro and macOS 27 are optimized for touch

Apple just unveiled the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR, its first MacBook with a touch display. While Apple already added a handful of touch optimizations to macOS 27 Golden Gate earlier this year, there’s also a number of new optimizations that were unveiled alongside the new MacBook Pro. Here’s what Apple worked on.

With the new touchscreen MacBook Pro, the traffic light icons in the top left of an app window will get bigger when you’re tapping them, making the touch targets a little bit larger.

Gestures that you can normally perform on the trackpad can also be performed on the screen. Whether that be a three-finger swipe up for mission control, three-finger swipes to switch spaces, pinching to zoom, or scrolling on a web page. You can also access Spotlight from the Dynamic Island, similar to how iPhones handle it on iOS 27.

If you’re an app developer, you’ll really appreciate this change: with the new MacBook Pro, you can fully navigate the iOS simulator with touch. No need to try to replicate touch gestures on a trackpad.

When you interact with a context menu in the menu bar, each of the items within a menu will get a little bit larger for touch. Additionally, most optimized apps will have larger touch targets, even if the buttons don’t necessarily appear bigger.

All in all, there’s a handful of optimizations already in macOS 27 Golden Gate for the touchscreen MacBook Pro. On top of what was named here, Apple also added pull to refresh in Safari and slightly larger spacing between menu bar items to all Macs with macOS 27.

Yeeeeeeeah no. Interactions with any of the onscreen elements are incredibly tedious, sporadic, and glitchy. This isn’t the company Steve Jobs started, it’s just Microsoft with an Apple logo.

Apple also says there’s more to come on the Mac when it comes to touch optimizations, so we’ll likely see much more in store at the next WWDC.

What do you think about touch support on the new MacBook Pro? Are you looking forward to it eventually trickling down to every Mac? Let us know in the comments.

#3447. ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight on How Live-Action Filmmaking Shaped His Stop-Motion Animated Adventure

Many scenes in “Wildwood” are designed to look spectacular. Even if each frame weren’t already rendered with the meticulous detail and artistry of stop-motion animation, the Laika Studios film is full of complex, chaotic battle sequences, a forest writhing with eldritch magic, and giant eagles soaring through the sky.

But some of the most technically challenging scenes, according to director Travis Knight, aren’t the ones that look the most majestic. They are — true to the spirit of the film and the lesson learned by its stubborn, caring protagonist Prue (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) — the simple magic of everyday life. Related Stories ‘Club Kid’ Review: Jordan Firstman’s Brazen, Funny, and Surprisingly Earnest Directing Debut Is a Wild Party Movie with Heart ‘Being Heumann’ Review: Siân Heder’s ‘CODA’ Follow-Up Is an Essential Biopic That’s Not Afraid to Have Some Fun

In fact, Knight told IndieWire on an episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast that one of the most challenging sequences in “Wildwood” was simply getting its hero from one end of her bedroom to the other. Laika prefers Canon cameras mounted on large motion-control rigs, which offer the flexibility needed to capture puppet movements adjusted one frame at a time. But when the camera moves, it also has to do so one painstaking frame at a time.

Knight, who’s now directed live-action features “Bumblebee” and “Masters of the Universe” in addition to his Laika work on “Kubo and the Two Strings,” wanted “Wildwood” to have the same camera language as a live-action film. He wanted the intimacy and wordless visual storytelling of a camera tracking Prue as she huffs across her bedroom, where the camera movement helps us see the decor shift from the artifacts of a carefree kid to those of a more disaffected teen.

“I still wanted it to feel like it was shot like a live-action film, with that kind of intimacy with the camera. But a camera on a motion-control rig is the size of a Ford F-150 in our [puppet-scale] world. It’s huge. And so if a camera is moving, you have to create space for the camera on set,” Knight said.

This is on top of creating space for the animator, who is roughly the size of a Kaiju in comparison to the fifth-scale the humans on either side of the Impassable Wood live at. The Prue puppet is roughly 10 inches tall. Being able to move that puppet and a camera at least as large as her bedroom that the puppet is moving through? That is a particularly gnarly feat of physics.

“We essentially had to deconstruct the set,” Knight said. “It was almost like it was a clamshell. It would open to make room for the camera, and then it would close up again. It was such a complicated engineering feat, when all it is [for] is a camera panning across a room. Those are the kinds of challenges that the team has to figure out, which is stupid, but it’s what it requires if you’re trying to tell a story like this.”

There is much to be said, and rightly, about the awe-inducing moments of spectacle in “Wildwood.” The Laika team had to figure out how to make giant puppets out of fabric and feathers instead of standard-issue silicone to simulate flight compellingly, accurately, and tactilely. Combat sequences required enormous attention to detail. But when Knight watches the film, he’s just as struck by the invisible work that makes “Wildwood” feel like a live-action epic — the thankless but involving work that viewers aren’t ever meant to see.

“I learned a great many things about what to do, what not to do [working in live-action]. It fundamentally changed my relationship with the camera, which is one of the reasons why ‘Wildwood’ looks so different. It’s because I wanted it to feel as if it were without the inherent limitations you would typically find in stop-motion cinematography,” Knight said. “When I see this movie, I am seeing all these little miraculous moments of engineering and artistry and human creativity at play on the big screen, and that’s one of the reasons it moves me so much.”

#3445. The Top 10 TV Series Right Now, According to Streaming Data

October's ten most-streamed series are packed with your future favorite shows. There's a couple of modernizations of horror franchises for Halloween (Carrie and Crystal Lake), as well as new horror series Below and Phony. There's an excellent new superhero series Lanterns, sprawling family drama East of Eden, and new seasons of favorites Ted Lasso, Slow Horses, The Diplomat, and Mobland. So don't even try to tell anyone there's nothing on.

Horror master Mike Flanagan (Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass) re-imagines Stephen King's tale of teenage telekinesis, taking the story from the 1970s to now, complete with cyber bullying, smart phones, and a modern sensibility. The core of the tale, though, remains the same, as does the titular character's bloody coming-of-age. Powered by a talented young cast that includes Siena Agudong as Susan and Summer H. Howell as the title character, Carrie is a trick-or-treat for horror fans. Stream Carrie on Prime.

Based on John Steinbeck's pillar of Western literature, East of Eden follows three generations of the hardscrabble Hamilton family and the upscale Trask family, farming and ranching clans in California's Salinas Valley. The show's production is a multigenerational story too: It was written and created by Zoe Kazan, whose grandpa Elia directed the 1955 film version of East of Eden. All respect to Elia Kazan, but Steinbeck's story is so massive, it needs a seven-part mini-series. East of Eden is the kind of sprawling, melodramatic story that episodic television was made for. Stream East of Eden on Netflix.

Like Carrie, Crystal Lake reimagines a horror classic—in this case, Friday the 13th—and expands the lore even beyond the 12 films in the franchise. If you've ever wondered how Pamela Voorhees, played here by Linda Cardellini, became a serial murderer, and how her son Jason ended up a relentless, camp-counselor-killing-machine who lives at the bottom of a lake, Crystal Lake has all the answers. In a lot of ways, this show is better than all of the movies. Stream Crystal Lake on Peacock.

Apple TV's Slow Horses delivers a realistic, nuanced take on espionage by detailing the lives of the losers of British Intelligence. Instead of chiseled good guys and gals saving the world, the agents of Slough House are a team of dysfunctional, troubled souls trying to do the right thing (usually) in a morally gray world, just like real agents. Their leader, gruff, obnoxious Jackson Lamb, is played to perfection by Gary Oldman. Slow Horses has an almost perfect Rotten Tomatoes score over its first five seasons, and season 6 is setting new records. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV+.

DC's TV revamp of Green Lantern details what happens when experienced Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) trains the new guy, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), on how to wield the mysterious and powerful Green Lantern Ring. It's a reserved, neo-noir style take on the comic mythos, as the heroes investigate a series of murders tied to an extraterrestrial threat. Lanterns is pulling in a better than 90% fresh ratings from Rotten Tomatoes, so it's definitely worth a stream. Stream Lanterns on HBO Max.

Created by Jesse McKeown and starring Josh Hartnett, Charlie Heaton, and Mackenzie Davis, Below is set in a Newfoundland fishing village beset with aquatic horror. When the Canadian government offers the residents of Snooks Arm a ton of money to relocate, no one really knows why, but ice fisherman Calvin Penney (Hartnett) suspects it has something to do with the monster he saw under the ice when he was a child. If you like taut creature feature style horror, check out Below. Stream Below on Netflix.

Season four of Ted Lasso sees the title character, played by Jason Sudeikis, returning to the UK to take on a new challenge: coaching the Lady Greyhounds, AFC Richmond's second-division women's football team. This multiple Emmy Award-winning series still has all the heart, humor, and positivity of the original run. Stream Ted Lasso on Apple TV+.

The mystery that drives creepy coming-of-age drama Phony is killer: Sonny Cooke, played by Sam Nivola, is a teenager with a very close relationship to his devoted single mother Ellen, played by Connie Britton. After a freak car accident, he wakes up convinced that his mom is an impostor. She looks the same, but there's something off about her in a way that Sonny can't describe, so he sets out to solve the mystery. Phony is rated over 90% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Stream Phony on Hulu.

In season four of political thriller series The Diplomat, the Kate Wyler, played by Keri Russell, finds that diplomatic relations between the U.S. and the UK are starting to crumble, and so is her marriage. Meanwhile, U.S. president Grace Penn, played by Allison Janney, and VP Hal Wyler, played by Rufus Sewell, continue their conspiracy to steal a Russian super-weapon, nudging the nation toward war with our longtime adversary. In other words, it's an international mess, with a few powerful people keeping the world from descending into chaos. If you like political intrigue, this is the series for you. Stream The Diplomat on Netflix.

Who doesn't love a sprawling organized crime drama? In Mobland, the crime is being organized in Great Britain, where two warring London crime families, the Harrigans and Stevensons, are locked in a battle for underworld power. In the middle of the crossfire is Harry Da Souza, a gritty fixer played to gruff perfection by Tom Hardy. Season 2 finds Da Souza in the unenviable position of holding together the Harrigan family on the verge of civil war. If you like backstabbing, scheming, murder, and other tropes of high-stakes crime thrillers, you'll like Mobland. Stream Mobland on Paramount+.

Of course, the biggest selling point is the versatility of it all. #3443. ‘The Ballad of Lieutenant Dan,’ Documentary About Gary Sinise’s Work with Veterans, Acquired by Freestyle Digital Media

Freestyle Digital Media, the digital film distribution division of Byron Allen’s company Allen Media Group, has acquired VOD rights to the documentary feature “The Ballad of Lieutenant Dan.”

The documentary follows Oscar-nominated and Emmy-winning actor Gary Sinise‘s decades-long mission to honor America’s fighting men and women, support injured veterans, and stand beside Gold Star families. It’s a calling that was inspired by Sinise’s work playing a Vietnam vet in “Forrest Gump.”

“The Ballad of Lieutenant Dan” will be available on North American digital HD internet, DVD, cable, and satellite platforms starting on November 10, 2026. It features interviews with Sinise, as well as Jay Leno, Tim Allen, Joe Mantegna, Chip Foose, and Mykelti Williamson. Sinise is also known for his work in films such as “Ransom” and “Apollo 13,” as well as the TV series “CSI: NY.” He starred in “George Wallace,” winning an Emmy. Related Stories ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight on How Live-Action Filmmaking Shaped His Stop-Motion Animated Adventure ‘Club Kid’ Review: Jordan Firstman’s Brazen, Funny, and Surprisingly Earnest Directing Debut Is a Wild Party Movie with Heart

The film also follows Sinise as he grapples with personal tragedy after his son, Mac, dies of cancer at the age of 33. The documentary looks at how Sinise is motivated by the credo: “We can always do a little more.” “The Ballad of Lieutentant Dan” was directed by Steve Mitchell Beebe and produced by Bud Brutsman.

“’The Ballad of Lieutenant Dan’ looks into the world of actor and humanitarian, Gary Sinise, and explores how his commitment to veterans and first responders created a community that supported him through a difficult period in his life,” said Beebe. “This is a story about selfless kindness and, I hope, will inspire all of us to do what we each can to uplift our friends, neighbors and communities.”

Freestyle Digital Media negotiated a deal to acquire the documentary directly with the filmmakers.

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Chrome is making it easier to autofill online forms with more than just contact information and credit card numbers. For users with Personal Intelligence enabled, Gemini will now suggest items like order numbers, tracking information, membership IDs, and booking confirmations from Gmail messages when completing forms in Chrome.

Chrome's expanded autofill capabilities use Gemini to read your emails and surface suggestions, meaning you don't have to click back and forth between tabs or manually search for codes or confirmations in your inbox. When you click a form field that has a corresponding piece of data, a pop-up menu appears and indicates that an item is "Suggested by Gemini." You can click this to autofill the suggestion as well as open an additional menu to see the specific source (the original email) or remove the suggestion. The latter doesn't delete anything from Gmail; it simply dismisses the suggestion in Chrome.

As Android Police reports, Google started testing enhanced autofill in Chrome this summer using data from other connected apps like Google Photos. The feature currently rolling out is specific to Gmail and is coming first to U.S. users who have Personal Intelligence enabled on desktop as well as in the Android and iOS apps when using Gemini in Chrome.

In the blog post announcing the enhanced autofill feature, Google states that "sensitive data is encrypted" and that users can manage autofill, including enabling or disabling enhanced suggestions, via Chrome's settings.

If you’re like me and bought an iPhone Duo, you’re likely a bit disappointed by the options on the market to prop it up on a table. Apple’s official $129 folio with kickstand is expensive, flimsy, and gets in the way of the outer display. MagSafe wallets that turn into kickstands are too tall for the back of the phone, and there aren’t many good third party cases yet.

That said, the perfect option for an iPhone Duo kickstand might’ve actually been hiding in plain sight all along.

This PopSocket has a few strengths on iPhone Duo:

On the last point, you might’ve heard from some iPhone Duo reviewers that the phone can’t really work on a MagSafe stand while unfolded, because the weight of the left half of the phone drags it down. #3440. Dune 3 Book Changes Endorsed By Stars: "You're Crazy" If You Find Fault With It

Dune 3’s actors are standing behind some major changes the movie is making to its source material.

After adapting Frank Herbert’s original Dune novel across two movies, director Denis Villeneuve is returning with the officially-titled Dune: Part Three, which adapts 1969's Dune Messiah. This will serve as the final installment of Villeneuve’s Dune trilogy, picking up almost 20 years after Timothée Chalamet’s Paul Atreides overthrew Emperor Shaddam IV and seized control of the Imperium. As with any adaptation, Dune 3 has tweaked the Messiah story to make it more palatable for cinematic audiences and conform to Villeneuve’s vision.

In an interview with The New York Times, Zendaya, who reprises Chani, acknowledged that while there’s “a lot” in Dune 3 that "is very true to the source material,” there are also “departures.” Robert Pattinson, who plays Scytale, added that, “You got to be kind of crazy if you’re going to be picking fault with this one [over the changes to the books],” then said:

The script was really cool, but it was quite complicated. And watching the film, it’s not about what I thought it was going to be about at all. It reads as much more of a grand political, moral fable, and the movie is so much more emotional. A lot of it is about parenting, and I just thought it was so moving.

Chalamet also said during the interview that he was “absolutely” satisfied with how Villeneuve wrapped up the Dune trilogy, noting that he “didn’t feel like the bar dropped at all, Denis just changed the location of the bar. This movie is its own thing.” The gap in time between Dune: Part Two and Dune: Part Three is one of the biggest changes in the movie, as Dune Messiah took place 12 years after Dune. Zendaya’s Chani is also being depicted as one of the conspirators against Paul, whereas in Messiah, she remained loyal to him.

Dune 3 sees Paul Atreides facing the consequences of his ruthless reign across nearly two decades, as a movement grows from the shadows to remove him from power. Other familiar faces from the previous movies include Rebecca Ferguson as Lady Jessica, Florence Pugh as Ireland, Charlotte Rampling as Reverend Mother Mohiam, Anya Taylor-Joy as Alia Atreides, Javier Bardem as Stilgar, and Josh Brolin as Gurney Halleck. Jason Momoa also returns as Hayt, a ghola who looks like the late Duncan Idaho.

#3439. 6 Banned Horror Movies That Are Now Considered Masterpieces

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

Imagine hearing about a horror movie for years, only to discover that the version available in your country has entire scenes missing. Someone has decided which images you're allowed to see, which sounds are too disturbing, and whether the film deserves to reach audiences at all. That sounds absurd now, especially when some of those supposedly dangerous movies have become essential viewing for anyone who loves cinema.

This impulse to censor horror is nothing new. While authorities banned some of these films outright and locked others away for years, they completely underestimated the filmmaking behind all that controversy. These six movies survived the outrage, and their reputations have only grown stronger.

A divorce is supposed to mean paperwork, slammed doors, the terrible quiet after someone says they’re leaving. However, in Andrzej Żuławski’s Possession, it becomes something far more frightening, a marriage convulsing until its grief seems to grow teeth. The story follows Mark (Sam Neill), who comes home to Berlin to find Anna (Isabelle Adjani) demanding a separation, then watches suspicion curdle into obsession as her absences and lies gather around a secret in a vacant apartment.

The subway breakdown is the moment that burns itself into memory. Anna flails, gasps, spills, and screams with such frightening abandon that the body seems to be suffering before the mind can explain why. The restless camerawork never gives the panic room to settle as it lunges and circles, while the cramped spaces seem to close around everyone in them. The creature is grotesque, but the marriage is the wound. This is a genuinely unhinged performance in a chaotic masterpiece that refuses to be made tame, or made twice.

You know the setup, five college friends, a cheap weekend away, and a cabin in the woods. The Evil Dead knows you know it, and then sends the forest itself racing at the door. A recording from the Naturom Demonto wakes something hungry, and the group is picked off by possession until Ash (Bruce Campbell) is left alone with the blood-soaked work of surviving the night.

An unseen perspective skims over the forest like a thing with its own appetite. Inside, every groaning board and trembling hand makes the cabin feel smaller. The film turns limited means into an assault of splashing blood, rubbery bodies, and jolting movement. In fact, these effects have the grubby, handmade conviction of a nightmare assembled in somebody’s garage. That texture is the point. Ash is exhausted, terrified, and losing pieces of his world by the minute. The film’s history of censorship only sharpened its outlaw reputation. Its raw energy remains completely alive, a low-budget miracle no polished remake can manufacture.

Before the first scream, the heat has already got you. The Texas Chain Saw Massacre made a blueprint for the slasher, but its real terror is how little it feels like a movie with dust in the van, flies at the farmhouse, and the hard white glare of a Texas afternoon. Sally Hardesty (Marilyn Burns), her brother Franklin (Paul A. Partain), and their friends drift toward a house they should never have entered. Then Leatherface (Gunnar Hansen) appears, and the day becomes a hunt.

The chainsaw’s metallic drone swallows the air completely. Sally runs through thorny brush in full daylight, dirt under her nails, and breath breaking as the sound follows right behind her. The movie builds dread from bone decorations, sweat, and frantic movement, leaving the violence to the audience’s imagination. That restraint is part of why the film feels so punishing because there is nowhere cool or safe to look. Banned and cut in several places, it outlasted the outrage. The film remains locked in its grimy 1970s world, a nightmare that seems to leave dust on your skin.

Father Urbain Grandier (Oliver Reed) is a deeply flawed horror protagonist. He is vain, sensual, and politically inconvenient, which in The Devils makes him an immediate threat to the men who want Loudun under their control. When Sister Jeanne des Anges (Vanessa Redgrave) accuses him of witchcraft, the convent’s fits become a spectacle the state can use. Grandier is arrested, tortured, and pulled into a machinery of power that has already decided what his guilt should look like.

The film stages that machinery in glaring white rooms, where black robes and contorting bodies turn the convent into a public arena. Its religious imagery was shocking enough to provoke cuts, bans, and decades of controversy. However, the spectacle has a sharp edge because beneath the blasphemy, the movie cuts into political greed, censorship, and the ease with which institutions make cruelty look righteous. The film asks us to watch a flawed man be dismantled by people with power rather than mistaking him for a saint. What scandalized audiences has become a tragic masterpiece about integrity under attack.

The Exorcist follows Chris MacNeil (Ellen Burstyn), who has a comfortable home, a daughter she loves, and access to doctors who should be able to explain what is happening. Then Regan's (Linda Blair) illness begins, and every test brings another answer that fails. The horror gathers inside a bedroom, a child’s bruised skin, a bed shaking violently, a guttural voice where her daughter’s should be. Chris can only watch, plead, and search for help.

The famous images still shock, but they are not the heart of the film. That is Chris’s helplessness, the mother standing beside the bed, trying to stay steady while the room turns cold enough for breath to show. Father Karras (Jason Miller), whose faith is already cracking, joins the elderly Father Merrin (Max von Sydow) to perform an exorcism as medicine reaches its limit. The film provoked bans and fierce condemnation, yet its force is more intimate than its reputation suggests. The body horror pulls you close, grief keeps you there. Its balance of medical realism, parental despair, and theological dread remains completely formidable.

Psycho begins as a crime story. It follows Marion Crane (Janet Leigh), who steals $40,000, drives through rain with the money weighing on her, and stops at the quiet Bates Motel. You settle into her fear of being caught. Then Alfred Hitchcock kills his star halfway through the film, and the ground gives way beneath the audience, too.

The shower attack is almost all sound and suggestion, shrieking violins, a shadow, a curtain, water spiraling toward the drain. The violence lasts seconds, the shock seems to last the rest of the movie. Norman Bates (Anthony Perkins) is all nervous stutters and careful sandwiches, with taxidermied birds staring from the parlor as Marion’s sister and a private investigator try to piece together what happened. The film met censorship fights and restrictions, but its boldest cut was to audience expectation. Hitchcock turns a stolen-money thriller into something colder, an inquiry into identity, trauma, and the stories we tell ourselves about who is safe. It remains the definitive psychological thriller, a film that changed how viewers watch.

#3438. Three new iPad models are reportedly launching early next year, here’s what’s coming

After debuting the refreshed iPad mini with OLED this past week, Apple still has more in the pipeline for the rest of the iPad lineup in the first half of next year. That includes a new iPad Air, a new base iPad, and a new iPad Pro, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman.

To follow up the iPad mini refresh, Apple’s next iPad Air refresh will also gain OLED. It’ll likely stick with a 60Hz panel, and likely won’t make the switch from Touch ID to Face ID – but it’ll bring a nifty display upgrade to the iPad Air, a product that hasn’t had a major refresh since 2020.

In terms of chipset, while not confirmed, a jump from the M4 chip to the M5 chip is rather likely. It’ll also likely come with a higher price, likely around $799-899 for the base 11-inch model.

Next year, Apple will also finally update the base iPad for the first time since early 2025. It’ll upgrade it to the A19 chip and 8GB of RAM, finally enabling Apple Intelligence support on Apple’s cheapest iPad. It should also gain the N1 chip and the C1X modem for improved networking performance.

There shouldn’t be any screen or design upgrades with this iPad, at least as of now – though it could potentially see some refreshed color options.

With the iPad Pro, Apple will be adding a vapor chamber to the device, a feat it started last year with the iPhone 17 Pro. It probably won’t have any meaningful changes otherwise, except for a new chipset – likely M6 or potentially M7.

Hopefully, there’s some surprises in store with this device. The iPad Pro now starts at $1199 for an 11-inch model and $1499 for a 13-inch model. It’ll have been around 3 years since the last major revamp by the time Apple introduces the M6 model, and the company should probably do something to make it a more worthwhile refresh.

45W alone is plenty for fast charging any iPhone, but it also supports up to 60W dynamic charging with AVS, which’ll unlock the fastest charge speeds on iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max.

Cassandra Clare’s The Shadowhunter Chronicles has multiple possible reading orders, so we’ve created a reading guide for new readers and seasoned Shadowhunters fans alike. The Shadowhunter Chronicles by Cassandra Clare is one of the longest-running YA series of this century, with 18 main books split up into multiple sub-series, plus short stories and novellas. However, it’s officially the beginning of the end for Clare’s beloved YA fantasy series. The Last King of Faerie, the first book in the final trilogy, The Wicked Powers, is out now.

Between the beautiful cover art and the increased interest in fantasy romance, The Last King of Faerie may convince you to try out the series for the first time. Alternatively, it could be a reminder to catch up on or revisit the world of the Shadowhunters.

Because the book series so expansive, new readers can feel intimidated and unsure where to start. There are four main ways to read The Shadowhunter Chronicles: Cassandra Clare's recommendation, grouped by series, publication order, and chronological order. No matter whether you're diving into the books for the first time or revisiting the series, I'm here to help. I'll outline the pros and cons of each reading order so you can choose what fits you best.

Limited-edition releases, such as Seasons of Shadowhunters and Classics Reimagined in the World of the Shadowhunters, that haven't received wide releases aren't included on the lists. Similarly, Shadowhunters and Downworlders, which wasn't written by Cassandra Clare, and graphic novels don't appear.

*No explicit recommended location from Cassandra Clare

Because Cassandra Clare is the brilliant mind behind the Shadowhunters books, readers value her opinions highly. Luckily, they can experience the books the way Cassandra Clare recommends. On her 2019 website (accessed via The Wayback Machine), she outlined the ideal order. Her current website also makes suggestions for when to read newer books.

She explicitly recommends waiting for Tales from the Shadowhunter Academy, The Eldest Curses, and The Bane Chronicles after finishing The Mortal Instruments. She also suggests reading The Infernal Devices ahead of Ghosts of the Shadow Market, though she doesn’t specify whether to read it immediately after or wait. I’ve taken a little liberty by placing it after The Dark Artifices since reading it sooner would include spoilers. A few other Shadowhunter books don’t have an explicit recommendation, so I’ve placed them in the best narrative spot.

Clare’s suggested order does a good job of breaking each story into consumable bits, preventing burnout. What’s more, reading The Infernal Devices mid-The Mortal Instruments introduces audiences to characters and details that show up in the second half of the six-book series. The order breaks up The Infernal Devices and its sequel, The Last Hours, similar to how it breaks up The Dark Artifices and its sequel, The Wicked Powers. The main downside is that it requires switching back and forth between groups of characters, time periods, and settings. This can feel impossible with so much forward momentum. The back-and-forth can also make it difficult to stay invested in a single story. The writing quality also varies in this order.

While Cassandra Clare proposes a different order, I personally recommend reading The Shadowhunter Chronicles in release order for folks entering the Shadowhunter world for the first time. It’s virtually the only way to prevent spoilers for future stories. Plus, it means getting to revisit Magnus Bane and Alec, a fan-favorite ship, later on. While both characters show up periodically in later series, the couple primarily appears together in The Mortal Instruments and The Eldest Curse.

However, this order isn't without its issues. The back-and-forth between 21st-century New York and 19th-century Victorian London can be jarring. It disrupts the momentum of The Mortal Instruments series multiple times instead of just once, like in Cassandra Clare's recommended order. On top of that, readers either have to read all the short stories in their book collections, which were published months to years after they debuted online, or track down a plethora of links.

Anyone who wants to complete a full story before moving on to the next will struggle with both Cassandra Clare’s recommended reading order and the release order. The former’s a little less jarring about it, but both weave The Infernal Devices into The Mortal Instruments. Luckily, you can also read The Shadowhunter Chronicles in series order.

Technically, any first book in a series can be a starting point, but this reading order recommendation starts with The Mortal Instruments, as it was the first one published and does the best job of introducing the rules and dynamics of the Shadowhunters world. Then, it follows publication order, for the most part.

Because The Eldest Curse centers on Alec and Magnus, central characters in The Mortal Instruments series, it’s better to read it after the first series but earlier in the publication order. Similarly, it’s a good idea to read Tales From the Shadowhunter Academy after The Mortal Instruments because it’s essentially the unofficial seventh book, and it includes foundational information for The Dark Artifices.

Unfortunately, the series reading order includes some spoilers for The Infernal Devices because The Mortal Instruments part 2 and The Infernal Devices were published in an alternating order. Additionally, it can be hard to place the standalones and short story collections because almost all of them feature characters from multiple series and/or take place in different timelines. The only logical conclusion is to read them at the end so they won’t feel out of place in one series or another. However, that means revisiting old storylines and characters later on.

Note: This list will be significantly longer than the others because it breaks down the major short story and novella collections in the Shadowhunters timeline.

The Bane Chronicles: What Really Happened In Peru

The Bane Chronicles: Vampires, Scones, and Edmund Harondale

Tales From The Shadowhunter Academy: The Whitechapel Fiend

Tales From The Shadowhunter Academy: Nothing But Shadows

Ghosts of the Shadow Market: Cast Long Shadows

Ghosts of the Shadow Market: Every Exquisite Thing

The Bane Chronicles: The Rise of the Hotel Dumort

Ghosts of the Shadow Market: Learn About Loss

Ghosts of the Shadow Market: A Deeper Love

The Bane Chronicles: Saving Raphael Santiago

The Bane Chronicles: The Fall of the Hotel Dumort

Tales From The Shadowhunter Academy: The Evil We Love

The Bane Chronicles: The Last Stand of the New York Institute

Ghosts of the Shadow Market: The Wicked Ones

Ghosts of the Shadow Market: Son of the Dawn

The Bane Chronicles: What to Buy the Shadowhunter Who Has Everything (And Who You’re Not Officially Dating Anyway)

The Bane Chronicles: The Voicemail of Magnus Bane

Tales From The Shadowhunter Academy: Welcome to Shadowhunter Academy

Tales From The Shadowhunter Academy: The Lost Herondale

Tales From The Shadowhunter Academy: The Whitechapel Fiend

Tales From The Shadowhunter Academy: Nothing but Shadows

Tales From The Shadowhunter Academy: The Evil We Love

Ghosts of the Shadow Market: Forever Fallen

Chronological order is an appealing way to read book series for many. The linear direction means the time periods pass in a familiar way, and folks don’t have to worry about keeping track of different timelines. However, I only recommend the books and short stories in this order for those who have already read the series and know the Shadowhunters lore.

For starters, this order requires folks to have access to all the books so they can jump in and out of the short story and novella collections. Additionally, The Bane Chronicles won’t be as enjoyable of a starting point for those who don’t already know the dashing High Warlock. That’s half of the appeal of the short story collection. On top of that, you need to do a lot more legwork to understand the world and story without the foundation of The Mortal Instruments.

The Infernal Devices is arguably a better series than The Mortal Instruments. Clare’s writing has continued to get more polished and engaging with every series in Shadowhunters. However, it has a weaker world-building introduction, and readers may take longer to grasp what’s going on. That said, the chronological approach is an interesting way to engage with the franchise for those who have read The Shadowhunters Chronicles. I know I plan to revisit the stories in this order while waiting for The Last Prince of Hell, expected in Fall 2027.

#3434. This Handheld Vacuum Fixed My Biggest Problem With Cleaning

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

I may not be “messy,” exactly, but no one would describe me as “neat,” either. One of my biggest issues is that I tend to wait for a mess to get big enough to justify dragging out a full-size vacuum before I deal with it, because a full-size vacuum means finding the cord or the charger, wrestling it out of the closet, going room to room, and then putting it all away again. When the mess in question is still only a few cracker crumbs? Forget it—I'm just too lazy.

The solution to my laziness has been removing all the friction and hassle of my full-size vacuum, and instead keeping a handheld vacuum always within reach.

Though there are many handheld vacuums out there, I use the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, which I got from Target. It's great for quickly sucking up crumbs and everyday messes, and that's exactly the job I need it to handle. The "dual air" part is what makes it more interesting than your average handheld: It's both a vacuum and a blower, so it can pull debris in or push it out, depending on what you're dealing with. I didn’t expect to need the blower at all, but I’m surprised how handy it is for blasting crumbs out of keyboard keys or loosening up stubborn debris before I suck it up.

The result is that my apartment is simply cleaner. Not because I'm spending more time cleaning overall, but because I'm no longer letting small messes pile up into big ones. When my monthly (or quarterly) deep clean does roll around, it's far less painful, because there's so much less to deal with. Perhaps this is the real upgrade: cleaning up messes the moment they happen instead of saving them up.

I love the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, but there are plenty of similar cordless handheld vacuum and air duster combos out there, and they tend to land in a pretty similar price range. If another one catches your eye, or goes on sale, or has a design you prefer, go for it.

When comparing models, here are my handheld vacuum musts:

It should offer both vacuum and blower modes.

It should be both cordless and rechargeable. If it needs an outlet, you'll have another barrier to using it, and that defeats the purpose.

It should be lightweight and slim. You want something you can grab and use one-handed without thinking about it.

The dust cup should be easy to empty. If emptying it is a hassle, you'll use it less.

You should be able to keep it in plain sight. The closer it lives to where messes happen (the kitchen, the entryway), the more you'll use it.

I used to think a clean apartment meant big, scheduled cleaning sessions. Now I think it's mostly about making the small stuff effortless. A handheld vacuum and blower won't replace your regular vacuum, but it will make you far less likely to need it as often. If you've been waiting for the next big mess, or the next big clean, to get things tidy, consider changing the system instead.

Rowling originally published the Cormoran Strike novels under the pen name Robert Galbraith for the release of The Cuckoo's Calling, hoping to establish a new writing career without the impossibly high expectations set. An investigation discovered more than 400 apps, apparently created by a single Chinese organization. The apps allow users to upload photos and then generate sexual and violent deepfakes which could be used to humiliate or threaten victims …

A Wired investigation discovered a network of more than 400 connected domains and apps with hidden abusive functionality.

Apps like Viefur [ostentibly used to add clothing to pet photos] often claim to be everyday services—such as language tuition or AI workout coaches. When accessed under certain conditions, however, apps in the network stealthily load a web interface allowing the generation of explicit AI sexual images and videos using photos users upload. The apps include AI scenes such as “bedroom rape” and “threatening knife,” where a man holds a knife to a woman’s neck.

I feel like this going to be a never ending cat and mouse game. Much like Apple has always had with jailbreaks.

Wired says that the network is “hiding in plain sight,” thanks to thousands of video ads for them published on Facebook and Instagram. Some of the apps have been around for a year and have passed review by Apple, Google, and Meta despite each having clear policies prohibiting harmful deepfake content.

Bait-and-switch tactics were used to pass app review. The apps normally show benign content, but a server check can activate the hidden features. Downloading the app after tapping an ad for the deepfake functionality on Meta platforms appears to be one of the triggers. Dozens of pornography photo and video templates can then be downloaded, with credits purchased to generate deepfakes from user-uploaded photos.

Apple removed 19 apps after Wired shared details.

We review every app before it’s published, and these apps complied with our rules when we reviewed them. After approval, their developers changed the website the app pulls its content from, replacing what we approved with pornographic content, and promoted it through pornographic ads hosted on a third-party platform.

The company recently strengthened protections against this approach. Meta says it has taken action against more than 10,000 ad accounts linked to domains associated with these apps.

#3426. Marvel Really Wants Fans To Forget Fantastic Four's Biggest Retcon

Who retcons the retconners? Marvel fans know that the true history of their favorite characters isn't written by the victors of some great canon conflict. It is a much messier process than that. Continuity is ultimately what sticks out of a mess of contradictions, as Jonathan Hickman once put it, and now Marvel has effectively said, "You know what? We're not sticking with that big change to The Fantastic Four's origin story we made a few years ago, so forget it ever happened."

Even the most casual Marvel fans are at least passingly familiar with the basic beats of the Four's origin. A team of astronauts, led by Reed Richards, go on a dangerous mission into space, where getting blasted by cosmic rays gives them superpowers. In the 65 years since, a core part of Reed's character has been the immense guilt he harbors over this inciting incident, especially for how it transformed his best friend Ben Grimm into the Thing. (So much so that it has contributed to at least one version of him going utterly insane. Looking at you, the Maker.)

Except in 2019, during a storyline appropriately titled "Point of Origin," Marvel tried to absolve Mr. Fantastic of this progenital guilt, rewriting the very foundation of Fantastic Four lore in the process. The change wasn't well received by fans, and hasn't come up much, or at all, since. Now, as a divide between Tony Stark and Reed puts Marvel on the precipice of Civil War 3, a contentious callback to the Four's first mission confirms the 2019 retcon can effectively be considered non-canon.

Warning! Spoilers ahead for "Invincible vs. Fantastic"!

Iron Man #11 is a masterclass in tension. Reeling from the events of the Armageddon crossover event, Tony Stark (with a civilian plus one in tow) joins Reed and Sue Richards for dinner. Which quickly devolves into a dark game of "What if?" What if the Invincible Iron Man and the Fantastic Four had to fight each other? Before that, things start getting dicey when Tony immediately goes for the low blow: "Why don't I ask Ben Grimm how he feels about your past choices?"

"This whole life you lead now started because you launched your family into space," he tells Reed. And neither he nor his wife go, "Wait, did we never tell you about that whole thing with the Overseer?" They accept it at face value. And for good reason. The Fantastic Four's 2019 origin retcon was worth a shot, but it didn't pan out. Not because the "Point of Origin" arc was bad; in fact, it's a pretty fun story taken at face value. It just wasn't the right creative choice for Reed Richards.

In "Point of Origin," the Fantastic Four found themselves on the planet Spyre, ruled by a character called the Overseer, whose powers were derived from the same kind of cosmic radiation as the team. In a huge reveal, it was made official that it wasn't Reed Richards' hubris, or his miscalculations, or the failure of his technology that led to the accident that changed everything for the Four. The Overseer directed the cosmic radiation at them to try to prevent them from reaching Spyre. He was successful, for a time, but with the side effect of empowering his targets.

Marvel meant for this to be an "Egads! Everything I knew about The Fantastic Four was wrong!" moment for readers. Instead, the reaction was much more tepid. The change was regarded as too destabilizing to the team's lore. Especially for Mr. Fantastic, because endlessly trying to make up for his first, greatest failure is intrinsic to his character.

So, Marvel has rightfully let that change get buried by the sands of time. At least for now. A future story could come along and reintroduce the Overseer plot point, and legitimize it if the end result is great enough. For now, though, Marvel woud clearly prefer to memory hole this particular retcon and leave the classic Fantastic Four origin story untouched.

Iron Man #11 is available now from Marvel Comics.

Prime members can choose to download one free e-book every month from a rotating list—though some months that number is bumped up to two, usually with a free short novel—and non-members get them for a discounted price. Issues around daylight saving time switches date back to the Apple Watch Series 4 in 2018. Apple applied a fix, but a similar problem emerged in 2021 and it has occurred again for some Apple Watch owners over the past week.

Time changes in the fall see clocks move back by an hour. #3421. Netflix’s ‘Detective Hole’ Officially Returns This Week

Book adaptations are all the rage nowadays, with streaming services like Apple TV and Prime Video cornering different genres. The former has excelled in crime thrillers, while the latter has the romance genre figured out. Adapting books carries a certain risk because it could clash with the image viewers have of the character, but when it works, it is great. Netflix hasn't been left behind and occasionally debuts a book adaptation, although the streamer doesn't have a genre lane.

Earlier this year, it debuted the TV adaptation of Jo Nesbø's famed detective Harry Hole, and the risk paid off. The series was a hit with critics and fans, scoring a 91% on Rotten Tomatoes from professional reviewers, and Detective Hole spent four weeks on Netflix's top ten non-English shows. The first season was based on Nesbø's fifth book, The Devil's Star. In it, Harry (Tobias Santelmann) investigates crimes while dealing with a colleague he deeply distrusts. Detective Tom Waaler (Joel Kinnaman) has started breaking the law instead of upholding it, and Harry wants to bring him to justice.

Even though there are more books in the Harry Hole series, Netflix has not yet expressed interest in more seasons. But for fans who still crave more, a new Detective Hole release is officially coming on November 5. Vintage Publishing has released the fourteenth book in the Nesbo series, titled Kill Shot. The 544-page thriller is available to buy online for about $13.50. Seán Kinsella translated the English copy. Kill Shot is also available as an audiobook, published by Random House and narrated by Sean Barrett. The hardcopy version is expected to be released next year on February 23 and costs $35.

A great detective is really just a personality with a method attached, which is why we keep remaking the same four of them. Here is yours, what it says about you, and the case for them being the best in the business.

You let people think you are not a threat and then you simply never go away. Columbo is the only major detective show that tells you who did it in the first ten minutes, because the pleasure was never the puzzle, it was watching a rich man slowly realise he is in trouble.

You are the most interesting person in the room and you know exactly how to use it. Rian Johnson built Blanc as a gentleman detective who is also an outsider everywhere he goes, which lets him be charming at people who would never otherwise talk to him.

Everybody tells you everything, and you have never once asked them to. Jessica Fletcher is a crime novelist from a small town in Maine who is so warm and so obviously trustworthy that suspects confess to her essentially as a social courtesy.

You expect to be lied to and you are almost never disappointed. Chandler wrote Marlowe as a man with a rigid private code in a city that has none, which is why he takes the case, solves it, gets nothing out of it and takes the next one.

The jump from the events in the fifth book to the fourteenth finds Harry at a different stage in life, no longer a detective. There is a new killer in Oslo, and they are staging murders inspired by iconic movie scenes with escalating shock. Evidence points towards the city's biggest film set, and Oleg, Harry's stepson, is investigating. Harry knows he should keep his distance, but instincts he's sharpened throughout the years keep pulling him in, so he finds himself working with his team again. It is a race against time to stop the killer before he racks up more bodies, but Harry is struggling with separating the professional from the personal. Meanwhile, the killer is saving their best scene for last. The book features a final twist that will leave readers gobsmacked.

Jo Nesbø's Killshot is now available for purchase. Stream all nine episodes of Detective Hole on Netflix and stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#3420. Affinity for iPad all-in-one design app now available, free for individuals

Design app Affinity has long been popular with Mac users, and a long-awaited iPad version has launched today. Canva promises that Affinity for iPad offers “the same pro-level power” as the Mac app.

It’s been a year since the company’s vector, photo, and layout tools were unified into a single app on Mac, and the same is now true on iPad …

Created specifically for the touch-first interface and unique capabilities of iPad and Apple Pencil, the app brings professional sketch, vector, photo and layout editing together with the same pro-level power of Affinity on the desktop […]

With Affinity for iPad, creatives can take a project from first sketch with Apple Pencil to print-ready file on iPad alone. And it’s free for individuals, just like Affinity on desktop, which has recorded more than seven million sign-ups since launching a year ago.

“Creative work doesn’t stay in one discipline, so your tools shouldn’t either,” said Duncan Clark, CEO of Pro Design at Canva. “Since we brought Affinity together on desktop, our biggest user request has been the desire to bring it to iPad. Today we’re delivering it: a fully-fledged, professional app built for touch.”

Being able to carry out all of the work within a single app on a single file is a key attraction of Affinity. The integrated app replaces the separate Affinity Photo, Affinity Publisher, and Affinity Designer apps.

Sketch: Rough out concepts the moment they land, with the unique capabilities of Apple Pencil like pressure and tilt in every mark, thick where you press and soft where you tilt. A full brush library comes with controls to shape each brush into the exact tool you need. Sketches stay live in the file to build on, rather than trace again.

Vector: Responsive, smooth and under control. Build a full logo or icon system with real curves and precise nodes, or bring a rough drawing through from Sketch. Sketch to Shapes turns hand-drawn forms into clean vector shapes.

Photo: Fine-tune RAW files, make intelligent selections, retouch in real time and build full composites at the shoot or on the go. Users can even sketch over a photo first to plan where a subject or prop should sit. The Mask Tool finds the boundary as the Apple Pencil pixel precision runs along a challenging edge, so hair, fur and foliage take a stroke rather than an afternoon. Every mask, grade and retouch stays live and undoable, even thousands of layers deep.

Layout: Create multi-page documents such as ‘zines, lookbooks and photo books, with text and images flowing across pages; master pages and grids keep everything consistent, and typography exactly right. Projects go all the way to a print-ready file with proper colour handling.

Canva says the app supports all of the advanced capabilities of Apple Pencil Pro: pressure, tilt, barrel roll, squeeze, and hover. AI features include generative expand, upscaling resolution, and adding attributes like motion blur. A Decompose Layer feature even splits a flat image into editable layers.

Affinity for iPad is a free download from the App Store.

#3417. All the Health and Fitness Products You Didn't Realize You Could Buy With HSA Funds

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), it's that time of year: Use those funds, or you'll lose them. Luckily, there are plenty of clever ways to spend your remaining FSA funds on qualifying healthcare costs—some that you may never have considered as "qualifying."

For instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch (even the latest Fitbit Air). At least, that's what plenty of brands like Whoop, Oura, and even Nike want you to think. Is the process really as straightforward as the marketing suggests? Here's what to know about all the unexpected ways you can spend your FSA funds before the end of the year.

Right off the bat, when it comes to most of these fitness trackers and smartwatches, your HSA/FSA dollars won't be able to cover the entire purchase; instead, you'll save an average of 30% on eligible health purchases.

There is some more fine print, although it’s not as tricky as you might think. For the most part, if a device is necessary for treating or monitoring a specific medical condition—and not just “general wellness”—it could be eligible to purchase with those pre-tax health dollars.

The main “catch” here (as I’ve previously explained) is proving that device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN). Your LMN is basically a doctor's note required to classify certain purchases as qualified medical expenses under IRS guidelines, proving that the device will be used to treat a legitimate medical condition, such as obesity or a heart condition. Let’s take a look at what you can actually expect if you want to get a fitness wearable approved as a medical necessity.

When it comes to securing your LMN, you might not even need to make a doctor's appointment, thanks to third-party players like Truemed. When you browse sites like Coros, Amazfit, and more, you'll see the option to “Pay With Truemed” at checkout. From there, you'll be asked a few questions about your health circumstances, and you’ll be matched with a provider to determine your eligibility. If you qualify, you’ll get an LMN that will allow you to use your HSA or FSA funds to complete your purchase—all without ever having to meet with your primary doctor.

Truemed is one of the most popular payment platforms in this space, with the company claiming on its site that “90% of LMNs are issued within seven hours.” I spoke with Truemed’s co-founder and CEO Justin Mares to find out how it works behind the scenes. After you take that short survey about your health, an independent licensed provider reviews your answers before deciding whether the purchase looks medically necessary. If it doesn't, Truemed won't bother forwarding the request at all. Because Truemed screens your case before it has a chance of getting denied, those approval numbers get to stay mighty high. And the reality is, most Americans will have at least one health marker—like weight or cholesterol levels—that they can self-report to prove that, say, a Fitbit Air is necessary tool for prevention and maintenance.

For the purchases that do go through to a medical professional, approval turns out to be surprisingly straightforward. It comes down to the idea of "standard of care" in general. “If you go into a doctor's office and say your family has a history of high blood pressure,” Mares says, “your doctor probably is not going to ask for lab work before they'll talk to you about it. They simply take you at your word and help you manage the risk.” Proving HSA/FSA eligibility works on that same standard fairly often, according to Mares. You're not submitting a stack of medical records; you're answering a simple intake form about your health history, and a licensed clinician uses that, plus their own judgment, to decide whether a given product is appropriate for you.

Before you get your hopes up too high, FSA/HSA eligibility for wearables is still far from a free-for-all. An LMN only covers you, personally, for a specific product from a specific merchant, and it's usually tied to a specific condition, like cardiovascular risk, pre-diabetes, sleep issues, chronic pain, and so on. Some employers' FSA administrators scrutinize wearable purchases more closely than others, and even a fully compliant LMN doesn't guarantee your plan will approve the claim. Some companies (like Coros, for one) are more transparent about walking customers through the required medical consultation at checkout, while other brands market "HSA/FSA eligible" prominently without explaining that the LMN step is what actually makes that true. Luckily, I’ve saved you some time and rounded up some of the major wearables—and other unexpected items—that you might be able to prove as FSA/HSA eligible.

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. These tend to draw more scrutiny from plan administrators simply because they're marketed as lifestyle products first, so the strength of your intake answers matters more here than it does for something obviously medical, like a blood pressure cuff.

If cardiovascular monitoring, training load tracking, or heart rate accuracy is relevant to a documented health concern, these watches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches. Sadly, no Garmin watches are HSA/FSA-eligible. Still, the following Garmin-brand products are eligible for an HSA/FSA purchase:

You can filter by HSA/FSA eligibility and browse all eligible Garmin items here.

Think adjustable dumbbells, rowing machines, and connected bikes. It's the same logic doctors use when they tell a patient with pre-diabetes or high cholesterol to start exercising regularly; if a clinician is willing to attest that structured exercise is part of your treatment plan, equipment that enables that can qualify. For instance, here are some HSA/FSA eligible products from Nike Strength:

The common thread across all of these is that the product itself doesn't determine eligibility—your health history does. A Whoop band might be an easy approval for someone managing a cardiac condition, but it'll get more pushback for someone with no relevant health history at all. If you're curious whether something on your wish list might qualify, it's worth filling out the intake process just to see how creatively you can spend those pre-tax health dollars. However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste.

Each episode of “12 12 12” unfolds across three timelines of a heist: the 12 months of planning, the 12 hours of the heist and the 12 days following it. The series follows a disgraced FBI agent (Anthony Mackie) and an American career criminal (Jamie Dornan) as they play a zero-sum game of cat and mouse across Europe. At the center of it all is the daring, epic raid on a bank vault deep beneath the streets of Zurich.

They wouldn’t take Judy Heumann’s phone calls, so she took their building. In 1977, a young disabled woman (Ruth Madeley) and a scrappy coalition of outsiders decide they’ve had enough. What begins as one impulsive act becomes the longest occupation of a federal building in American history, as hundreds spontaneously seize government offices and refuse to leave until the bureaucrat in their way (Mark Ruffalo) takes action. Bringing rebellion in all its forms to the hallowed halls, a movement’s accidental leaders struggle to find their path forward where none has ever been paved for them. Directed by Academy Award winner Siân Heder (“CODA”) and based on true events, “Being Heumann” is the revolutionary, irreverent and deeply human story of the least likely people trying to pull off the impossible and change the lives of millions.

In the latest special under the acclaimed “Snoopy Presents” banner, the Peanuts kids are on their best behavior — but Snoopy has landed on Santa’s naughty list. With just 12 days until Christmas, he sets out to prove he’s not such a bad beagle after all, discovering along the way that the season is about more than gifts.

Middle school has been a nightmare for Marc (Jude Hill), a good kid who’s bullied by his classmates and feels like he’s behind in everything, from academics to P.E. to just making friends. That changes when his injured Uncle Jake (Chris Pratt), a decorated Navy SEAL, comes to spend the summer and recuperate with Marc and his mom, Sarah (Linda Cardellini). To help Marc defend himself, Jake devises an ambitious program he calls “Operation Warrior Kid” based on his SEAL training. Instead of teaching his nephew how to fight, Jake shows Marc what real courage is, facing down his own demons along the way. Based on the bestselling novel by former Navy SEAL Jocko Willink, “Way of the Warrior Kid” is directed by McG (“Charlie’s Angels,” “Terminator Salvation”) from a screenplay by Will Staples (“Without Remorse,” “The Right Stuff”).

#3413. Apple Is About to Release a Touchscreen MacBook Pro (Plus Four More Devices)

Apple has had a busy fall. Head to the company's website, and you'll immediately be greeted by a sea of new products: the foldable iPhone Duo; the iPhone 18 Pro; HomePod mini 2; Apple Watch Series 12; the list goes on. It seems, under new Apple CEO Jon Ternus, the company is ready for a refresh of just about every product it sells. To that point, the company seems far from finished. Just this week, Apple is planning to release five brand new products, each launching on Friday. While four of these are Macs, Apple does have a new iPad in the works, as well. Here's everything new Apple is releasing this week.

Finally. For the first time, the iPad mini is about to ship with an OLED display. Apple's smallest tablet has always come with a standard screen. Despite its price tag, the iPad mini has never come with an OLED display, or even a mini-LED screen, until now. With this new model, there is no backlight. As such, each individual pixel on the iPad's display will be able to shut itself off when displaying dark content. That will benefit the content you watch on this device, as well as the overall contrast of the screen.

Beyond the new OLED panel, the new iPad mini is thinner and lighter than the previous model. It also comes with Apple's newest A20 Pro chip, the same processor the company put in its iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo smartphones. The new device starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, though there are various upgrades, including nano-texture glass (add $100) and cellular (add $150).

Good news: There's a new iMac. Bad news: Not much is different here from the previous model. The biggest change here is the new M6 chip, which Apple says is up to five times faster than the iMac with M4 and up to 12 times faster than the iMac with M1. With that M6 chip, the iMac now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Other than that, this is the same iMac you may already know: It comes with a 24-inch LED display (no OLED, unfortunately), two or four USB-C ports (depending on the configuration), and a built-in 12MP webcam. If you're looking for a new all-in-one computer, or you've been considering upgrading your older iMac, this is likely a great choice. But if you already have an M-series iMac, it's not such an obvious upgrade. (My M1 iMac may be up to 12 times slower, but it's still plenty fast for me.) Apple didn't change the price here: The M6 iMac still starts at $1,499 for two ports, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage.

Similarly, Apple's newest 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't much different from the previous model—save for the new processor. This model also comes with Apple's M6 chip, which Apple says is up to 13 times faster for AI processing than the M1 MacBook Pro. (Apple seems keen on convincing stubborn M1 users to upgrade this cycle.) Now, the company is offering this model of MacBook Pro in three chipsets, depending on use case: M6 for "entry-level" pro work; M5 Pro for mid-tier pro work; and M5 Max for the most demanding situations.

But, like the M6 iMac, this is the same MacBook Pro Apple sold before. It has a 14-inch mini-LED display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz. It comes with three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, an HDMI port, and an SDXC card slot. It, too, has a 12MP webcam for video calls. Apple's newest MacBook Pro starts at $1,999, but you can quickly ramp up that price tag with screen, chip, memory, or storage upgrades.

Apple's most exciting product launch this week is undoubtedly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros. Unlike the M6 MacBook Pro, which only comes in the 14-inch variant, Apple's first touchscreen laptop comes in both 14- and 16-inch options. Apple says this touchscreen lets you scroll, zoom, or draw on the display. That works with basic functions, like web browsing or selecting files, but also with specific workflows, like playing virtual instruments in Logic Pro, or manipulating an object in a 3D modeling app. Like the iPad mini, this laptop comes with an OLED display (Apple calls it PROLED XDR), with up to 1,000 nits of typical brightness and 2,000 nits of HDR brightness. It also brings back the backlit Apple logo, something I've missed on my last two MacBooks.

This MacBook Pro also comes with the iPhone's Dynamic Island for the first time. This replaces the "notch" that other MacBook Pros and MacBook Airs currently ship with. It can function as a basic webcam, but also as a dedicated zone for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI. This machine comes in either M5 Pro or M5 Max variants—no M6 for this model—as Apple seems to be positioning it exclusively for the most taxing situations (particularly AI). The company says the new MacBook Pro has up to 13 more hours of battery life than Intel-based MacBook Pros, and can fast charge up to 50% in 30 minutes. It's essentially a supercharged version of the existing MacBook Pro.

As such, this is Apple's most expensive laptop. The 14-inch M5 Pro version starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. However, you can configure these machines to have outrageous price tags. The maxed-out 16-inch MacBook Pro is $14,549, roughly half of which is the 16TB of RAM.

#3411. iPadOS 27.2 adds convenient new multitasking option on iPad

iPadOS 27.2 launched last week with a variety of new features for iPad, including a convenient change for multitasking.

When iPhone Duo first got into users’ hands, several reviews mentioned how the new Split View system felt more intuitive than iPadOS multitasking ever has.

And in iPadOS 27.2, there’s a convenient new multitasking change that’s likely inspired by iPhone Duo.

Apple hasn’t brought over the entire iOS system to the iPad. But it has made one common multitasking feature easier to set up: Split View.

From the official iPadOS 27.2 release notes:

Side-by-side multitasking is easier to set up with the option to choose a second app whenever you tile apps to the left or right with the window controls or menu bar

Starting with iPadOS 26 last year, setting up two apps side-by-side could fairly cumbersome.

You needed to open the first app, resize it, then swipe up from the bottom of the screen to see your other apps, select one, and in many cases manually resize the second app too.

But in iPadOS 27.2, any time you use Apple’s window resizing controls to tile an app left or right, you’ll immediately see the Home Screen and be able to tile a second app with a single tap.

FTA: "Once you master the built-in keyboard shortcuts for app tiling, it becomes even quicker and easier to set up your apps side-by-side."

Ok, great, but…then no one lists these keyboard shortcuts. Sure would have been helpful to paste them in here when talking about new features.

It’s not identical to the iPhone Duo experience, but it’s a lot closer to it than the old system was.

Once you master the built-in keyboard shortcuts for app tiling, it becomes even quicker and easier to set up your apps side-by-side.

Sources told TMZ ... Erin left behind journals containing personal writings, though it's unclear what was written in them or whether investigators reviewed their contents.

#3409. New report on ‘HomeView Ultra’ product covers features, pricing, more

Apple’s new HomeView product arrives in users’ homes next week, but today a report from The Information outlines what to expect from a larger, high-end ‘HomeView Ultra’ product coming next year.

Today Aaron Tilley at The Information published a report on a forthcoming HomeView product that could be dubbed ‘HomeView Ultra.’

Similar to Mark Gurman’s extensive reporting, Tilley classifies the new home product as a robotics project. He says, “Apple’s new CEO John Ternus wants the company to get serious about robots.”

Per the report, the HomeView Ultra product has “a nine-inch screen that swivels around on an arm and resembles the Pixar lamp.” Tilley writes:

Apple initially began working on the robot in 2019—code-naming it J595—and had modest ambitions for it, envisioning it mostly as a device for video calls. Its robotic arm was intended to allow it to follow someone wherever they were in a room. But hopes for the robot ballooned once Apple executives began wanting to add AI capabilities to it.

The current design for the robot envisions it using a camera and sensors to be fully aware of its environment and act autonomously, allowing it to turn on the lights when someone walks into a room—or perhaps even try to tell a cat to get oﬀ a table. It is meant to be smart enough to avoid accidentally hitting objects around it.

The report notes that much of the hardware for the product “has been finished for around two years.” Software, however, is keeping the device from shipping. This is due to a more ambitious slate of AI-powered features than was originally envisioned.

Pricing is expected to be “around $1,000” per the report, but it may cost more depending on market prices for components. Tilley spoke to several former employees who said they expect Apple to use ‘HomeView Ultra’ branding for the product. As we’ve seen this fall though, Apple has been hesitant to expand its slate of Ultra products.

As for release timing, Tilley says that “Apple hopes to launch the robot next year. It could push the launch out to 2028 though.”
