#3408. Walmart Will Have Three Major Shopping Events This Holiday Season

If you're thinking of picking up any big-ticket items soon—whether for yourself or as a gift for someone on your list— I would advise you to wait until you see what retailers have in store for the holiday sales season, which will kick off in earnest in mid-November. Walmart is the first major retailer to announce its Black Friday and Cyber Monday plan for 2026, and they actually involve three major shopping events between now and the December holidays. H

As it did in 2025, Walmart will hold three sales between Nov. 12 and Dec. 2, as outlined in a recent press release. The sales will be both online and in-store, and will target a mix of Walmart+ members and general shoppers.

The events will take place on three different dates:

Walmart's Black Friday Deals Event 1: Nov. 12–15

Available online and in stores starting at 6 a.m. local time

Walmart+ members get six hours of early access beginning online at 12:01 a.m. ET on November 12

Walmart's Black Friday Deals Event 2: Nov. 23–29

Online only: Nov. 23 starting at 12:01 a.m. ET

Online and in stores: Nov. 27 starting at 6 a.m. local time

Walmart+ members get six hours of early access online beginning Nov. 23 at 12:01 a.m. ET

Walmart's Cyber Monday Deals Event: Nov. 30-Dec. 2

Walmart says that you can expect discounts on electronics, toys, fashion, beauty, home goods, gifts, and everyday essentials. Although the company doesn't provide much in the way of specifics in its press release, last year's sales included discounts on TCL TVs, Dyson vacuums, Dreo appliances, and toys from LEGO.

The holiday season will see major sales from the same list of retailers that compete for your dollars throughout the year—namely, Best Buy, Target, and Amazon. Each will have its own version of Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales. So far, only Walmart has revealed its plans.

In short, yes. Though they aren't quite as impactful as they once were, Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales offer discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. Whether it's a major purchase you've been saving up for or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts, especially on items like appliances and electronics. Last year's sales included categories such as tech, home improvement, and fitness.

Black Friday used to be when major retailers offered their best deals on expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Now, however, the distinction is almost meaningless: Every major retailer offers sales on both days, which means the smart move is to know what you want, use price trackers to monitor the deals, and refer to our Black Friday coverage, where we do all the searching, curating, and price tracking for you.

To Nicoletto’s right, TVs set to Fox News flashed undeniably dismal numbers: Republicans down in Ohio, in Michigan, god — even in Texas. Nicoletto went on, telling the few dozen club regulars in attendance that he would “spend every waking moment” in the coming years signing up new Republican voters. “We are going to take the city back in 2028!”

There was a smattering of applause, a few hoots. The TVs were all on mute, and silence crept into the room. “Let’s get some music on!” Nicoletto said, relinquishing the mic.

At 25 years old, Tuesday night was Nicoletto’s first real taste of defeat. In one of the most disastrous midterm elections in history, Donald Trump’s Republican Party was wiped almost entirely off the map in several states. As of Wednesday morning, Senate seats in Maine, Iowa, Ohio, Texas, South Carolina, and North Carolina have flipped blue, and the president has been stripped of his majority in both chambers of Congress. Almost immediately, Trump lashed out, placing the blame for the catastrophe anywhere but on himself — despite the war in Iran, brutal tariffs, a stagnant economy, and skyrocketing gas prices. Young people everywhere, including several I spoke to on election night, call this multi-faceted clusterfuck “the affordability issue.”

As results started to come in, I chatted with Alexis, a young woman who had joined the club a few years ago.   Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

“I’m 26. I wanna buy a house, I want to have a family — I can’t do those things,” she said. “I’d like to see the party just talk about that more — and more than just talk about it, figure out a way to help us!”

Alexis thought that Donald Trump had done a great job of this in the 2024 election. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, she said, a Democratic Socialist, had also focused on affordability and won big from the other side. But in 2026, she says, Republicans were at a loss for any kind of coherent message.

“The immigration thing, it indirectly helps,” Alexis said, referring to Trump’s deportation agenda. “That’s great, that’s cool… but then we’re going to war with Iran! I wish I could be in the room when they made that call to do that. It’s just like, ‘What the hell were you thinking?’”

I couldn’t blame Alexis for her exasperation. She’d spent most of the night thus far running a gauntlet of press — at least three different Scandinavian writers and a Japanese TV crew — all of whom wanted to know “how she was feeling.” I didn’t bother to ask that question, as the vibes in the room basically spoke for themselves. The people who were watching the TVs looked glum. Everyone else was mostly focused on drinking, and looked to be having a fine time.

The question I was asking was what comes next. Trump has two more years in the White House, and then the GOP has to make a choice. Republican strategists I’d talked to last month — the older, sober, grizzled types, at least — had predicted this kind of blowout loss and warned that the party was headed for a “reckoning.” Some seemed gleeful that the Trump era was ending, the siren song of neo-conservatism once again sounding faintly on the wind. But the young people in the Manhattan clubhouse were part of a different movement — MAGA — and no matter how bad their losses got, they weren’t ready to let it, or its leader, take the blame. “Life takes all of us at a certain point,” says Becky Oliveira, 25, the club’s design chairwoman and “first lady” who is engaged to club president Stefano Forte. “I see no reason to push him out the door when there’s still work to do. This donor class, these old-guard advisers, this old-guard ecosystem that exists around him, is what needs to be taken out.”

Like many of her peers, Oliveira is protective of Trump — after all, he has been the singular figure of conservative politics for her entire adult life. The dismay in the room, then, stemmed less from the electoral losses than the existential fear that their wing of the party — the brash, radical, Trump-loving new right — would find itself cast back into the wilds, alone and adrift as their political party was reclaimed by the kind of neo-con wonks who dominated the Republican side of the swamp until 2016.

This is the secret of the young Republican movement. For every die-hard ideologue, there are more than a handful of people who really just want to be able to hang out with likeminded friends: people who like the same memes and laugh at the same jokes that might rub people in New York’s overwhelmingly liberal young adult monoculture the wrong way. Sure, some of them are deeply devoted to a specific (and sometimes dark) vision of right-wing governance, but a lot more just want to be able to talk shit about their annoying coworkers and mainstream Democrats in a city famous for libbing out.

“I don’t know how many people I’ve met [through the club] that are like, ‘Oh my gosh, I can’t believe I can have normal conversations,’” Oliveira said. “That doesn’t change regardless of who wins nationally. When they come here they find kinship and solace.”

In two presidential elections, at least, Trump turned that sense of belonging into massive electoral success — a sense of purpose, and power, and movement that many young Republicans will do anything to preserve. If the RINOs and fuddy-duddy neo-cons take back the party, the young Republicans will feel cut off from the free-wheeling culture of based memes and swamp-draining that helped them feel, for the first time in most of their lives, as if they had political power and agency.

“I don’t want to get rid of MAGA! If they scapegoat the only thing that’s been getting them votes the past decade, then the party’s going to become irrelevant,” Nicoletto said. “We need to stand with Trump — no matter how bad things get.” Trending Stories Trump's Bizarre Journey Through the Stages of Grief as Democrats Dominated the Midterms Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner Did an AMA About That Shower Scene, His Sniffing, and ‘You Can See Everything’ Dane Cook’s Brother Robbed Him Blind. “I have never seen an election of this scope, and this scale,” he said. “What comes next is a mystery to me.”

#3404. Six Fitness 'Rules' That Don't Actually Matter

I’ve learned a lot in my many years in the gym, and beginner-me would be shocked and appalled by the things present-me does during workouts. With the benefit of experience, I now do exercises I used to think one should “never” do, and I’ve broken pretty much every other rule besides.

I've already explained a bunch of things you can stop worrying about as a beginner, but I’d like to expand on that list with a few more rules that even intermediate-level exercisers can ditch without consequence.

If you can theoretically do 13 bicep curls with a certain weight, how many curls should you actually do? One common misconception is that if you don’t do all 13, you’re leaving gains on the table. The rule kind of makes sense if you have truly no clue where to start; if you go until you can’t do a single rep more, then at least you know you’re not slacking off.

But the downside is that going to failure for every set of every lift is just going to make you exhausted. On bicep curls, maybe not so much, but once you’re squatting pretty heavy weights, you’re going to feel spent if you do every single set to failure, and that fatigue will get in the way of getting a good workout in consistently. What’s better is to follow a program that advises you on when to hold back and when it’s a good time to really push your limits. You’ll find that most of the time, you stop a set at least 2-3 reps shy of failure, and sometimes even more.

Rest days are a convenient tool for making sure you’re not overworking yourself, but that’s all. Organizations like the American College of Sports Medicine recommend leaving 48 hours between intense strength-training sessions for a given muscle, but if you look at where they get that number, it’s meant to be a general recommendation for beginners and for people who are exercising just to stay healthy. Once you’re talking about athletes or enthusiasts, the ACSM acknowledges that training most days of the week is fine if your program manages fatigue effectively. That may mean alternating between heavier and lighter days, rather than taking complete rest days.

The “10% rule” is a not-terrible guideline for figuring out how quickly to ramp up your training. But like many of these other myths, it’s a suggestion, not a commandment to be strictly obeyed.

As running coach Jason Fitzgerald told Lifehacker, “While the adage is to only increase weekly mileage by 10%, this may be either too conservative or even too aggressive depending on where you start from.” When you’re coming back from a short layoff, you can probably increase mileage a lot faster. Same goes if you’re a beginner and your mileage is overall very low; if you took the rule literally, you wouldn’t be able to increase from zero to any other number.

Meanwhile, serious running programs—once again, a program is a wonderful thing—may give you a bigger increase for a few weeks in a row, then cut back and decrease your mileage temporarily before ramping up again. Or they may keep you at the same mileage for weeks at a time before venturing a larger increase. If you were to stick to the 10% rule, you would miss out on the advantages of programs that work this way.

There are pros and cons to lifting before cardio, and to doing cardio before lifting. It’s more of an “it depends” than a rule. So here are some of the ways to decide which makes sense.

Your lifts tend to suffer when you’re fatigued, and doing them fresh is important to you

Cardio is your top priority, and you want to have more energy for it

Your lifts are the kind of thing that can get done even when you’re fatigued

Or you only intend to do a small amount of cardio before lifting

So a cyclist may prefer to do a strength workout after hopping off the bike, but a powerlifter would probably rather get their conditioning in after finishing squats for the day. Either is fine if you don’t care, or if you prefer to mix it up.

There are a few supplements that can help you in your fitness journey, but none of them are necessary. Creatine is one of the best-known muscle-building supplements. It’s understood to be effective, but here’s the thing: Just because it does something for most people doesn’t mean it does very much. If you decide it’s too expensive or just that you would rather not have another thing to remember to take every day, you’re not missing out on any substantial amount of gains.

Likewise, protein powder is a helpful way to get more protein in your diet, but you don’t need to use a supplement; you can just eat more protein-containing foods.

And finally, pre-workout drinks can give you more energy in the gym (it’s mostly caffeine), but the idea that you need it is a very recent development. Even ten years ago, it wasn’t really a thing. People showed up to the gym with a coffee or a coke or with no caffeine at all in their stomach, and worked out just fine.

Look, people have been exercising successfully for millennia, but all of our apps and devices weren't even a thing until the 2000s. Tracking every minute, every step, or every mile of your routine is not actually necessary. You’re still a runner even if you don’t have an app that knows how many miles you ran. You don’t even have to track your sets and reps in your lifting journal if you don’t want to. Your body is what knows how much work you put in, even if your phone were to get wiped overnight.

#3401. Bob Dylan Meets With Pope Leo XIV in a Private Audience

Pope Leo XIV has made time for several revered musicians this past year, including Patti Smith and Bad Bunny. On Wednesday, he also held a private audience with Bob Dylan.

His Holiness showcased his fondness for the revered songwriter in his book, Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift, in a citation. The pope quoted Dylan’s unpublished 1963 protest song “Go Away You Bomb” in the book. “‘I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned an’ man-handled,’” the pope quoted from Dylan. The previously unreleased song’s lyrics, which were typewritten and then corrected by hand, were auctioned by Christie’s in the summer of 2013.

It was written by Dylan in 1963 for Izzy Young of the Greenwich Village Folklore Center. “I asked everyone I knew to write a song about the nuclear bomb,” Young told Rolling Stone in 2013. “Bob Dylan came in literally the next day and handed this to me.”

In the pope’s book, he quoted Dylan’s “Go Away You Bomb” and also commended pacifist Dorothy Day for her work for peace.

According to Vatican News, the pair’s meeting on Wednesday was “brief” and consisted of “greetings and a few lighthearted exchanges.” The pair exchanged gifts: The pope presented Dylan a rosary and Dylan gave the pope his autobiography, Chronicles: Volume One.

In June, Pope Leo met with Bad Bunny and others while both were touring Spain. “If they are confronted with the question do they want to see Bad Bunny or do they want to see the pope, I think many will see Bad Bunny,” Leo acknowledged of the musician’s popularity. “But I think there will also be a few here to see the pope. And that says something.”

Fellow Chicagoan Patti Smith met with Pope Leo in August. “This is a moment that shall forever produce a smile,” Smith wrote on Instagram of the encounter at the time. Amazon has cut the price of its latest Fire TV Stick 4K, dropping it to $24.99 from $59.99 and bringing it to its lowest price ever, according to price trackers. At this price, it's an affordable way to bring 4K streaming to an older television or give a sluggish smart TV a performance upgrade. Despite its small size, it supports 4K streaming over Wi-Fi 6, along with HDR10, HDR10+, and HLG for improved contrast and color on compatible televisions. There's also no support for Apple AirPlay or Google Cast, so sharing content directly from your phone isn't particularly convenient. #3397. ‘This Had Better Work’: Why This Folk-Country Band Sold Their House to Go on Tour

There’s committing yourself to a life of music, and then there’s selling your house, buying a van, and hitting the road. The Minnesota folk trio Wild Horses threw themselves into the latter.

In 2021, the band got booked at the Grand Rapids Riverfest, a regional end-of-summer festival that has featured headliners like Jason Isbell and Wilco. Bolstered by the high-profile slot, Jed LaPlant and his partner Ariana, the husband-and-wife songwriters who founded Wild Horses, sold their home, picked up a 1989 Chevy Astro van, and hit the road.

“We decided this is what we’re gonna do,” Jed says. “We’re going all-in.”

Since then, they’ve spent nearly all their time on tour, playing their own gigs and supporting headliners like Charley Crockett, Trampled by Turtles, and Sam Barber. The LaPlants found that such a nomadic life was the perfect catalyst for songwriting. “Whatever it is — roots or Americana music — is unique, in that the job of it fuels the inspiration,” Jed says, recalling something a peer once told him. “Being out on the road is the fuel.”

Wild Horses took their road experiences and assembled them for The In Between, the group’s second studio album, released in October via Outlaw Foundry/Atlantic Outpost. It’s an autobiographical snapshot of a grassroots folk band trying to navigate an era when selling all your belongings and pursuing a music career sounds, at best, ill-advised.

After releasing their debut album, Runaway, in 2022, Wild Horses upgraded from that Astro Van to a high-miles coach and converted it into a tour bus. The early lineup fluctuated between four and six players — including banjo and trumpet — before they found a path ahead as a trio with bassist Landon Pahl. A longtime friend of Jed’s, Pahl followed his pal’s lead and quit his day job, joining the LaPlants for a life on the bus.

On The In Between, Wild Horses —Jed on vocals and guitar; Ariana on vocals, fiddle, and keys; and Pahl on bass — compile nine tracks, each of them written by the LaPlants. Early single “Sunrise on the Absaroke” gives the album its title. It’s a road-weary tune about making ends meet in close quarters and includes the line, “Livin’ in the in between, trying to beat the desert heat/there’s nothing I could do to keep from crying my way home.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

On “Take It As It Comes,” which plays out over a high-tempo guitar-and-fiddle melody that evokes horses galloping, the LaPlants double down on their life on the run. “There’s a sense of urgency in that song,” Jed says, “that I think came out of playing a lot of really noisy bars in places where we really didn’t belong — trying to win over people. That urgency came from the idea that this had better work.”

Grand Rapids is a town of a little more than 11,000 in north-central Minnesota, named for the rapids of the far northern reaches of the Mississippi River that cuts through downtown. The LaPlants met in town, playing open-mic nights, and fell in love.

“We were both working other jobs,” Jed says. “We were paying for a house and all that. Then, during Covid, I ended up with a broken back, and the construction job I had wasn’t gonna cut it. We were at a crossroads. We started jamming with friends of ours — a bass player and a drummer in town here — just to keep out the cold.”

So far, it’s working. The band have found receptive audiences on the road, especially during an October tour with Trampled by Turtles. In December, they’ll join Sam Barber for a swing that begins in the Midwest and ends on the West Coast.

Jed has a personal goal of understanding how people connect with his songs, and spending time playing before Barber or Crockett allows him the chance to witness firsthand what lyric or melody is moving the needle. #3391. The Votes Are In: Americans Don’t Want Data Centers

Democrats won big in Tuesday’s midterms, not only taking back the House of Representatives and Senate by overwhelming margins, but rebuking Republican candidates down the entire ticket in deep-red states like Texas, Mississippi, and Tennessee. Pundits and politicians are offering plenty of explanations for it — the exorbitant cost of living, the war in Iran, Republican candidates simply not being good enough — but there may be another thing that drove voters to the polls: the public’s deep distrust of AI data centers going up across the nation.

According to the report Data Centers on the 2026 Ballot, published by the firm Redbud Consulting, which has been tracking the initiatives, the election showed a decisive loss for data centers. Since yes and no could mean different things depending on the ballot, Redbud broke it down by votes to “restrict” or “allow” data centers in their analysis. Of the 39 nationwide referendums that have been fully counted, 38 of them enacted new restrictions for potential new data centers.

“For as much as Republicans did poorly last night, the one thing that did even worse were data centers,” says Alex Lundry, founder and CEO of Redbud Consulting. “For the most part, the restrict side has gotten about 77 percent of the vote in each of these races.” This lines up with recent polling: On Monday, Gallup published a survey that showed 70 percent of Americans don’t want data centers near where they live.

The one initiative that didn’t pass so far, Lundry notes, was in the town of Harwood, North Dakota, where an initiative would have imposed “additional significant requirements” on “certain development or building projects within the City.” Though the measure was ostensibly there to target data centers, Lundry notes that the phrase “data center” wasn’t itself present in the ballot language, which could have affected its outcome. “To be clear, there are literally only, what, 430 people voting on this issue in the city of Harwood,” he says. “So it’s hard to read too much into this, but it is interesting.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

#3390. The Out of Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Does 'Code Rot' Mean?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's Out-of-Touch guide takes a look at a phenomena that's probably going to define the lives of generations of young people: Code rot—both actual computer-style code rot, and the more elusive cultural kind. I'm also taking a look at the fake controversy over the "cancellation" of Freddy Krueger, and finally, bringing things home with viral videos of boyfriends dancing.

Expect to hear young people talking about code rot for awhile, maybe for the rest of their lives. It's a concept that's going to affect them more than any previous generation. Code rot, or software rot, describes what happens to a computer program when the hardware and operating system it runs on advance. If older programs aren't updated, they become less stable and glitchy until they eventually become unusable.

The idea of code rot has really caught on in the young people's popular imagination, probably because they're going to spend a lot of their lives dealing with it. They've even taken the idea of code rot into life, and use the phrase to describe anything that is worn out or malfunctioning. If the ice cream machine isn't working at McDonald's, it's code rotted. Bad grades on a report card? Code rot.

Kids are making videos where they demonstrate actual code rot:

or point out physical things that are code rotted, like a cat:

Interestingly, a lot of the online discourse around code rotting concerns the massive video game platform Roblox. Because Roblox games there are made by users, there's often not a lot of incentive for the creators to keep the games current with the platform's changes, so a lot of Gen Z's childhood memories of playing games are sinking into code rot. Here's a video about it:

Another interesting wrinkle is the tone these videos take. Code rot is seen as apocalyptic. While it's mostly hyperbole, I think part of it is the realization that the entire world is code rotted. The old programs that used to run within the "Western Culture" operating system no longer apply and everything is starting to glitch out.

The meaning of "PDF file" depends on the context. If you're at work, it refers to a Portable Document Format file, a format created by Adobe that is famously hard for older people to open. In slang, though, PDF file is algo speak for "pedophile." Because that word is flagged by moderation software online, people say "PDF File" to skirt the censorship.

The run-up to Halloween brought a lot of online discourse about Nightmare on Elm Street villain Freddy Krueger. The supernatural serial murder/PDF File was supposedly cancelled online by overly woke, Gen-Z Tiktokers outraged that he is a child predator. The controversy started with a post from Entertainment Industry Reporter that points out how strange it is that in the '80s and '90s, Freddy Krueger, depicted in 1984's A Nightmare on Elm Street as a child murderer so driven by bloodlust he transcended death, was featured on dolls, board games, and lunchboxes aimed at children. It's a good point, but not a call for "cancellation."

Although the article does say that "Freddy Krueger lunchboxes shouldn’t exist," and that parents "shouldn’t have been buying their kids action figures of a child murderer," this is not a call to action. It's not suggesting cancellation of any kind, and it's hard to even conceive of what cancellation of a fictional character in an old horror franchise would even mean. The article is actually an observation about how merchandising (and low-quality sequels) change the meaning of art. But people online missed the point entirely and invented a scenario where "woke" young people are calling for the cancellations of a fictional villain for doing bad things.

I've been scouring TikTok, looking for even one video where someone is calling for "canceling" Freddy Krueger, and I can't find any, but there are hundreds, maybe thousands of videos like this:

In these videos, people point out how enraging it is that the woke people are calling for Krueger's cancellation and vowing that they won't let it happen. Even though it is not happening. There are even levels to the myths about woke mobs canceling Freddy. Supposedly, younger users were unaware that Krueger is depicted as a "PDF file" as well as a murderer in the 2010 reboot of the franchise, so there are online arguments about whether that's the reason he's being canceled. Even though no one is canceling anything. These anti-woke folks are, ironically, defending a fictional villain from cancellation by creating another fictional villain, the shadowy woke mob that's ruining horror movies. Meanwhile, the real villain is a lack of media literacy. Saying "wow, it's crazy that previous generations made a comedy mascot of such a terrible character and marketed him to children" is not the same as cancellation.

This week's viral videos are of boyfriends dancing. The newest thing on the TikTok is young women sharing video of their boyfriends getting down accompanied by a clip from the song "gay alligations fr. my girlfriend" by TikToker OH MICKEY. Like this:

It's a simple, silly template that maybe doesn't mean a whole lot, but this generation of young men are so messed up when it comes to relationships and masculinity, I'm always happy when a meme becomes popular that indicates that young women want goofy dudes, dudes who know how to dance, and dudes who act silly as boyfriends more than they want red-pilled, manosphere, looksmaxxing types. I don't know if these kinds of messages ever really "break through" to the underground of internet incels, but I like to hope they do, because a lot of young men are not OK.

#3389. New York Times Exec's Alleged Killer In-Laws Defaced His Family Photos, Cops Say

Disturbing new details are emerging after a 40-year-old transgender man was shot and killed by his in-laws last month at a sports complex in Northern California … and now police are alleging his father-in-law had been planning the killing for some time.

According to KRON4, newly revealed court documents suggest 77-year-old Shouyong Zhang had been targeting his son-in-law, Jonathan McKinsey, for a while … with investigators discovering defaced photographs of McKinsey inside the elderly couple's apartment.

Zhang and his 77-year-old wife, Shili Chen, have both been charged with premeditated murder. If you don't remember, here's how prosecutors say it all went down:

McKinsey, a 40-year-old engineering director for The New York Times Games, went to Dublin Sports Grounds in Dublin, California, for a court-mandated supervised visit with his three children.

According to the new court documents, Chen claims she was "in the dark" about what her husband had planned when they met McKinsey at the park. She says she was still sitting in the car when Zhang began firing shots at her son-in-law.

However, surveillance footage shows Chen walking up to McKinsey and firing seven shots as he lay lifeless on the ground.

An off-duty Milpitas police officer was at the park when he spotted an Asian man and woman standing over McKinsey. Within minutes, police located the elderly couple and placed them under arrest.

Legal analyst Steve Clark described the homicide case to KRON4 as bizarre on the surface, adding, "But when you analyze what occurred here, it appears to be a premeditated, personal, revenge style killing."

Chen's attorney, however, claims she only shot McKinsey because she heard gunfire and feared her husband was in trouble.

Her defense attorney wrote, "The prosecution may attempt to argue that Ms. Chen is the actual killer but that would be a strain on the facts here since Mr. Zhang fired so many shots into Mr. McKinsey’s chest and head before Ms. Chen arrived."

Police say Zhang confessed to the shooting, claiming his son-in-law was "violent and aggressive all the time with the kids" and that he feared for his grandchildren's safety.

Another possible motive? McKinsey was in the middle of an intense child custody battle and divorce with his estranged wife, 46-year-old Candice Jang. There were also allegations that McKinsey threatened Chen's life and even hired a hit man to "get rid of" his mother-in-law.

The elderly couple reportedly purchased guns in March 2026 out of an abundance of caution, claiming they feared for their lives.

Chen's defense attorney, Curtis Briggs, said, "(Chen) was essentially a live-in nanny for the family, and Mr. McKinsey was extremely hostile, violent. The divorce continued to deteriorate the dynamics of the family."

Court records show McKinsey and Jang had previously accused each other of child abuse and domestic violence.

Jang described herself as a "stay-at-home mom" who depended on McKinsey financially. She also claimed she slept with a pair of scissors near her bed for protection.

"I and the children have all experienced physical, verbal, emotional abuse from Jonathan. My mother, who helps me watch the children, has also experienced emotional abuse from Jonathan," Jang wrote in a 2025 request for a restraining order against her husband.

We previously reported that McKinsey filed a restraining order against his ex. In court documents, McKinsey claimed Jang attempted to yank medical tubes out of his body during his 2010 transition from a woman to a man. Despite the alleged incident, the couple reportedly tied the knot the following year.

Court records also show McKinsey accused his in-laws of transphobia and allegedly feared his children would be harmed by their mother.

In his filing, McKinsey claimed his mother-in-law called him a "pervert" and a "disgusting queer" after the two had a falling out over one of their children's clothing choices.

And here's where things get even more disturbing …

While executing a search warrant at the elderly couple's one-bedroom apartment following the killing, detectives discovered four photo albums containing photographs with a defaced McKinsey.

"One had black marks and dots drawn on his chest and over his right eye in places that appeared consistent with where he was later shot," the defense attorney wrote.

Zhang allegedly lived alone in the apartment, while Chen stayed at her daughter's home to help care for the children.

Both Zhang and Chen are charged with first-degree murder with a lying-in-wait special circumstance in connection with McKinsey's death. Both have pleaded not guilty.

Chen's defense attorney has now filed a motion seeking her release on bail, arguing she had no knowledge of the planned shooting.

A pretrial hearing is scheduled for November 23, 2026.

Microsoft’s flagship development tool, Visual Studio Professional 2026, reduces much of the friction that used to come with large projects, and it’s on sale for just $29.97 on StackSocial right now, which is far less than what most developers expect to pay for a professional-grade IDE.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a desktop-only Windows product built as a 64-bit application, designed for people working on real-world codebases. Think multi-project solutions, long build times, and code that’s touched by more than one person. In day-to-day use, the biggest benefit is the context the software provides while you work. Visual Studio 2026 supports C#, C++, .NET, ASP.NET, Blazor, and .NET MAUI, so you can move between desktop, web, and cross-platform projects without switching tools. You also get Hot Reload, which helps reduce rebuild time by letting you edit code in .NET and C++ apps and see changes immediately. And CodeLens adds useful context right inside the editor—who last edited a method, which tests cover it, and whether recent changes broke anything—without forcing you to dig through menus or version history. The software’s AI-powered IntelliCode suggestions also feel more restrained than flashy. They tend to fill in logical patterns based on your existing code. It saves time on repetitive work, but you’ll still want to read what it writes.

Collaboration is another area where this version earns its keep. Live Share allows teammates to jump into a debugging or editing session without cloning the repo or matching environments. That’s useful for code reviews or troubleshooting, but it depends heavily on a stable internet connection. System requirements are also worth noting: While it can technically run on 4GB of RAM, 8GB or more is far more realistic, especially for larger solutions, and storage needs can balloon depending on workloads, reaching well over 100GB in some setups. Also, it doesn’t support 32-bit systems and won’t run on mobile devices or Chromebooks. For developers already working in the Windows ecosystem, this is a solid long-term license. For everyone else, those limitations can be deal breakers.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a full-featured, 64-bit IDE for Windows designed for developers working on complex, multi-project codebases, and it's on sale right now for a one-time price of $29.97 on StackSocial.

The Pelican MagSafe Battery Pack is 5,000mAh, which is about one full charge for a standard iPhone and a solid top-up for a Pro Max. It charges via MagSafe at up to 15 watts, and the magnets are strong enough to stay put while the phone is in a jacket pocket or clipped to a backpack strap. It also works with any Qi device, so AirPods or a Samsung phone with a magnetic case will charge on it.

There’s a USB-C port for anything without MagSafe, with USB output and a short cable in the box. Four LEDs on the side show its remaining charge, which is still the simplest way to know whether to grab the battery or the wall charger before you walk out the door.

Two things to know going in. This is a 15-watt battery, not a Qi2.2 25-watt model, so it won’t match the fast-charging speeds you’ll see on the newer MagSafe batteries. For an outdoor MagSafe battery that spends most of its time topping up an iPhone in a pocket, I don’t think that matters much. The bigger one is the recharge speed. It recharges fairly slowly, so plug it in when you get home, and it’ll be ready by morning, but don’t expect to charge it in the car, though

The best MagSafe battery for outdoor life is one designed for the outdoors. The Pelican MagSafe Battery Pack sacrifices some charging speed for a shell that can take a beating without getting damaged.

The Pelican MagSafe Battery Pack is available on Amazon.

#3381. iOS 27.2’s clever new Messages feature can be tailored to your needs

iOS 27.2 launched last week with a convenient new Messages feature called ‘Suggested Actions.’ Here’s how you can customize the feature to your liking.

If your iPhone is running iOS 27.2, you might have noticed a handy addition in the Messages app.

Whenever a message contains actionable information—an event you might want to add to your calendar, or todo you need reminding of—Messages will add a ‘Suggested Action’ right below the relevant message.

Using these new suggestions, with a quick tap you can turn the message into an action. And they’re so small and unobtrusive in the UI that they don’t clutter up the app at all.

But depending on your needs, you might want to enable or disable some of these suggestions. And Apple lets you do that with a surprising level of granularity.

Inside Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Messages -> Suggested Actions you’ll find customization options for the feature.

There are five different types of suggestions that can be enabled or disabled in Settings. By default, all five are enabled.

I’m planning to leave all five enabled, because I’ve found the feature a useful addition. But it’s great to see Apple offer a refreshing level of control like this right off the bat.

Note: Suggested Actions are powered by Apple Intelligence, so you’ll need an AI-compatible iPhone to get the feature.

What do you think of Messages’ new feature in iOS 27.2? Let us know in the comments.

#3380. ‘Euphoria’: What Election Night Felt Like in the Heart of Blue Texas

There’s a sound that carries in it 38 years of dashed hopes, of close calls and complete wipeouts. It’s thousands of triumphant screams and gasps and cries of elation layered into one riotous wall of noise. It’s Democrat James Talarico becoming the next senator from the state of Texas.

Attendees at Talarico’s election night headquarters in Austin wept at the sight of the yellow checkmark over his candidate headshot, declaring him the projected winner over the Donald Trump-endorsed Ken Paxton. They clung to each other and screamed “WE DID IT” at the top of their lungs. Seconds later, any remaining cobwebs of anxiety about how the midterms might go were wiped away as the networks projected the victory of Gina Hinojosa over three-term incumbent Republican Governor Greg Abbott. The crowd, several thousand strong, broke into a “U-S-A” chant, followed by a round of “Si Se Puede” — “Yes, We Can” — a nod to the force of Hispanic Texans, and the state’s first Latina governor.

Campaign staffers and pundits nervously warned that it would likely be a late night. Late polling gave Talarico the advantage over Paxton, but given the deep-red character of the state, virtually all agreed it would be a nail-biter. You could practically taste the anxiety in the November air as results came in on Tuesday evening. “I feel like Charlie Brown,” with “the football” every election cycle, one Talarico supporter told Rolling Stone early in the evening, referencing the running gag from Peanuts.

Republicans have dominated the state’s politics for the last three decades, and every time it has looked like Democrats might break their losing streak, they end up falling on their asses. If Talarico lost despite Trump and Paxton’s combined unpopularity, and the clear momentum behind his campaign, then there was perhaps truly no future for Texas Democrats.

Supporters were hopeful, but no one would have dared to jinx it by predicting a statewide sweep. Paxton was only the first Republican domino that fell over the course of the night, though. Abbott, thought to be in a far more secure position than his AG, was also voted out of office. Democrats took the lieutenant governorship and the state attorney general’s office, both extraordinarily powerful offices in the Texas government. They took the comptroller’s office, railroad commissioner, and agricultural commissioner. They even took control of the state House of Representatives. “I’m hearing Democrats may not even have enough people to staff all the new offices,” one college-aged Talarico supporter told Rolling Stone amid the festivities.  Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Texans did not just pull off a fluke win for a perfect-storm Democratic candidate running under just the right set of conditions — they led the country into a generational blue tsunami. The Lone Star State was the epicenter. Many of the Texans celebrating in Austin have lived their entire lives without experiencing a major Democratic win in their state, and vividly remembered the sting of Beto O’Rourke’s narrow loss in 2018. But Blue Texas was here. Armadillos had learned to fly. Longhorns had broken into song.

Talarico’s watch party, held at the Long Center on the banks of the Colorado River, had the light air of a fair. On the large outdoor terrace holding the majority of supporters, food trucks serving tacos and barbeque — and a long bar — kept attendees well provisioned. Local vendors were selling custom bejeweled “Talafreako” t-shirts, ceramics, embroidered bandanas, and face painting. As the audience waited for Talarico to take the stage and claim his victory, members of the crowd performed the wave. Campaign staffers and volunteers, misty-eyed and grinning from ear to ear, hugged each other in the aisles.

“Talarico was not campaigning by saying ‘I’m representing the Democratic Party,’” David Maxwell, a lifelong Republican, Texas Ranger, and whistleblower against Paxton, told Rolling Stone near the taco line. He, like other Republicans in the state, gave his support to Talarico partially as a rebuke to the self-dealing, corrupt record of Paxton — who has become a pariah within his own party.  “[Talarico] said I’m representing the 31 million Texans,” Maxwell said.  Related Content The Votes Are In: Americans Don’t Want Data Centers ‘Don’t Get Rid of MAGA!’: Some Young Republicans Are Sticking by Trump After Blowout Loss Is Mississippi Really About to Elect a Democratic Senator? How Abdul El-Sayed Overcame the Hate and Won Big in Michigan

It was a message Talarico would reiterate in his victory speech:

“To the Texans who didn’t vote for me, I will be your senator too. I always will. I will always serve you. I will always fight for you. This win is not about the Democratic Party or the Republican Party. It’s much bigger than that. We must bridge the divides between us and repair the ties that bind us. We forged a new kind of politics here in the Lone Star State. In answer to this decade of division, we showed that when working people come together across every dividing line, we can do extraordinary things.”

His supporters have been embracing that message for months now. When asked by Rolling Stone what they hoped would change in Texas under Democratic governance, attendees mentioned everything from corruption, to environmental regulations, to housing affordability and the protection of public education.

Through the early hours of Wednesday morning, after Talarico delivered his victory speech, Texans continued to shout their glee, from the streets, from out of their cars, from literal rooftops. Outside of the Texas Capitol building, a steady stream of revelers blasted music and cheered on vehicles engaging in celebratory honking — in the local fashion usually associated with victories for the San Antonio Spurs, not down ballot Democrats.

One junior Texas legislative staffer described himself as being in a state of “euphoria.”

“I thought this shit would be like 15 years in the future,” he said, as Bad Bunny’s “CAFé CON RON” blasted on a portable JBL speaker, with neighbors clad in all manner of Texas-themed paraphernalia dancing around the Capitol gates. “[I thought] that [winning] would be like a 50-50 squeak … I feel like this is kind of like the end of Trump — or end of MAGA to say the least —- because there’s no way a Democrat wins Texas by 15 points.”

Austin, a young woman from a small, deeply Christian town in rural Texas, told Rolling Stone that she was “so hopeful for America it scares me.”

“It feels even more euphoric than Obama in 2008,” she added.

Chants of “Fuck Greg Abbott” went up just feet away from the governor’s mansion — soon to be occupied by a Democrat for the first time since Texas legend and former Governor Ann Richards finished her term in 1995. Drivers, windows rolled down and sun roofs opened, waved pom poms and signs and shouted “VIVA LA LIBERTAD” as if they had just defeated the Mexican army.

At one point a young man runs through the crowd, frantically holding out his phone to anyone who will look. “ABDUL IS WINNING,” he announces, a temporary town crier bringing news from beyond the borders about Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate race in Michigan, which would be called for the Democrat a few hours later.  Trending Stories Trump's Bizarre Journey Through the Stages of Grief as Democrats Dominated the Midterms Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner Did an AMA About That Shower Scene, His Sniffing, and ‘You Can See Everything’ Dane Cook’s Brother Robbed Him Blind. Now He’s Rebuilding His Life — And Gunning for a Comeback Trump Is Already Crying That He’s Not to Blame for Republican Wipeout

“It finally happened,” another man — speedwalking down the sidewalk — exclaimed at another, not even bothering to stick around to hear his reply.

“It finally happened,” his target practically whispered back in reply, almost to himself, like a reassurance that a blue Texas was no longer just a dream. Democrats no longer have to hope they can carve out a future in the conservative stronghold. As of Tuesday night, they are the state’s future.

#3377. ChatGPT and Work are merging soon, while ChatGPT Classic retires in January

Users who still rely on the ChatGPT Classic app were greeted today with a message informing them that the app will soon be retired. Separately, OpenAI is also preparing to merge ChatGPT and Work into a single interface. Here are the details.

A few months ago, OpenAI released a new ChatGPT desktop app, which brought ChatGPT, Work, and Codex under a single interface. As a result, the regular ChatGPT app was renamed ChatGPT Classic.

The move proved controversial for two reasons. First, OpenAI replaced the native macOS app with an Electron-based version. Second, the new interface was extremely confusing, making it difficult to access regular ChatGPT conversations or even distinguish between ChatGPT, Work, and Codex.

OpenAI was quick to address some of the complaints, restoring direct access to conversations via a prominent Chat and Work toggle at the top of the window, along with a sidebar menu for switching between ChatGPT and Codex. The company has since introduced other changes to make the app easier to use.

The ChatGPT Classic app, on the other hand, remained largely untouched and became increasingly less reliable as OpenAI released new models that were more tightly integrated with features exclusive to the new app, such as the ability to select different reasoning effort levels.

And as much as it felt like the writing had been on the wall for its demise, now we have a date. According to a new message displayed to users when they open ChatGPT Classic, the app will officially be retired on January 30, 2027.

“This app will retire on January 30, 2027. Get the latest features in the new ChatGPT app. Your full chat history comes with you, so you can pick up where you left off.”

Clicking on the banner leads users to the ChatGPT downloads page, where they can download the latest version of the desktop app.

Meanwhile, OpenAI is informing users that it will begin testing a combined Chat and Work experience in the coming weeks.

The announcement comes a few months after OpenAI president Greg Brockman acknowledged that the new ChatGPT interface was “kind of a mess,” and said the company hoped to eliminate the Work tab by the end of the year, with its functionality becoming part of the regular ChatGPT experience.

Now, in an email sent to users, OpenAI explains that the test will start with a small group of users, who will be able to access ChatGPT’s conversational features and Work’s more advanced capabilities from the same interface:

This will enable you to move from exploring an idea to having ChatGPT carry it through, all in one place. You can bring in your files and plugins and ask ChatGPT to build a website, create a presentation, or do things for you on the web, while reviewing and guiding its work. Codex will remain a separate experience in the ChatGPT desktop app.

As part of the transition, OpenAI also plans to introduce a shared usage allowance for ChatGPT and Codex, replacing their separate limits.

According to the company, “most users won’t need to wait for their usage to reset more often than they do today.” OpenAI adds that “usage will depend on model and task, with more advanced models and complex tasks using more of your allowance. Unlimited Instant is included in your plan and will not draw from your usage.”

#3372. How to Try 'Audio Intelligence' on Your Apple Watch Early

It has been a big year for Apple. There's a new CEO, prices have increased across the board, and there's been a seemingly endless rollout of new devices, including two new Apple Watches: the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. All things considered, these watches offer only minor upgrades over the previous models, shipping with new heart rate monitors and the latest S11 processor. But one of the biggest new watch features, "Audio Intelligence," is also the most controversial—and it's rolling out in beta today.

Audio Intelligence is Apple's branding for a new set of features exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4. These features use the new Apple Watches' hardware, along with on-device and cloud-based AI, for tasks like sound and music identification as well as dictation. "Sound Recognition" can alert you to important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, while "Music Recognition" can automatically display songs playing around you—but these aren't the features you'll hear talked about in discussions of Audio Intelligence.

Rather, everyone is up in arms about "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap." These Audio Intelligence features passively "listen" to your conversations throughout the day, and, using AI, deliver summaries of what was said. When you double-click your Apple Watch's crown to use Live Rewind, you'll get a loose transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation it overheard, while Siri Recap can show summaries of all your in-person chats throughout the day. You can even configure a schedule for when your watch is "listening" for recaps—e.g., only run during work hours. Apple suggests each is intended to help jog your memory; maybe you use Siri Recap to remember important discussions you had that morning, while Live Rewind is meant for moments where you forget what someone just said. (As opposed to asking them to repeat themselves, I suppose.)

Apple's claims may or may not assuage your fears, but it seems the company is pushing on ahead regardless. Apple is releasing Audio Intelligence as part of iOS 27.3, which launches in beta on Tuesday. If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you can try it out today, assuming you enroll in Apple's latest beta version.

To do so, you'll need to sign up for the Apple Developer program, since iOS 27.3 is rolling out first for devs. This program used to require a $99 fee, but you can skip it now if you opt for the free account. Once you enroll your Apple Account in this program, you can open your iPhone, head to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, and choose "iOS 27 Developer Beta." Go back one page, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install iOS 27.3 when it's available.

The start of another month brings a wave of new movies and TV shows to the top streaming services, and Apple TV is no exception, with a lineup of fresh titles in November 2026. Thankfully, along with the new, the Apple platform is also welcoming plenty of golden oldies to the streamer this month, with 20 classic titles joining its digital archive, from sci-fi stunners like "Minority Report" and "Interstellar" to iconic comedies like "Anchorman" and Oscar winners like "Forrest Gump."

One of the best '90s movies, Amy Heckerling's coming-of-age comedy is a whip-smart, modern retelling of Jane Austen's 1815 novel "Emma." Alicia Silverstone iconically portrays Cher Horowitz, a Beverly Hills teen socialite with a heart of gold who makes it her mission to help those less fortunate around her. That includes playing matchmaker for a pair of lowly single teachers (Wallace Shawn and Twink Caplan) and making over a naive new student (Brittany Murphy) that Cher takes under her stylish wing.

However, for all of her improvement efforts, Cher soon realizes that when it comes to her own heart, she's actually totally clueless — and maybe in love with her hunky ex-stepbrother Josh (Paul Rudd). We promise, it's way less creepy than it sounds.

Directed by the late, great Penny Marshall, this 1988 fantasy-comedy is one of the most beloved Tom Hanks movies in the actor's extensive filmography and for good reason: It's a warm and funny watch that offered a sweetly thoughtful take on the classic body-swap comedy, with a stellar, star-making performance by Hanks, who earned his first Academy Award nomination for the role.

When 12-year-old Josh Baskin (David Moscow) makes a wish at a mysterious carnival machine, he shockingly wakes up in the body of a 30-year-old man (Tom Hanks). Soon after, he heads to New York City and gets a low-level job at a toy company, all while navigating the stress, responsibilities, and emotional chaos of adult life, including a confusing connection to his new co-worker Susan Lawrence (played by Elizabeth Perkins).

Some movies simply feel like autumn, and "Dead Poets Society" is one such enduring fall favorite, a big-hearted back-to-school classic that will rouse you on top of the nearest desk.

An Oscar-nominated Robin Williams stars as John Keating, the new, unconventional English teacher at Welton Academy, a rigid all-male prep school in 1950s Vermont. Through Keating's teachings, the young students — portrayed by an iconic young cast that includes Robert Sean Leonard, Ethan Hawke, and Josh Charles, among others — learn not only the merits of English literature but also that life is short, fragile, and exceptionally beautiful. If you needed a reminder to "seize the day," this one's it.

#3366. John Ternus addresses iPhone Duo supply constraints, display issue

Today Apple reported record Q4 earnings, which beat Wall Street expectations overall. And in an interview with Reuters, CEO John Ternus addressed current iPhone Duo supply constraints and also referenced units that have been returned for display issues.

Apple’s latest quarterly earnings did not include any sales for the iPhone Duo. That’s because it covered a period running July-September, and the Duo didn’t go on sale until October.

But Wall Street is understandably still very curious about how sales for the foldable are going. Especially as relates to revenue forecasts for the current quarter.

In an interview with Reuters, Ternus addressed two aspects of the iPhone Duo: supply constraints and units that have had display issues.

Regarding supply, it sounds like Apple doesn’t know when it might reach supply-demand balance:

“Duo is constrained as of today,” Ternus said. “The ramp is going well, and we’re working hard to get it to as many customers as quickly as possible, but at this point, we’re not ‌able to ⁠predict when supply and demand will be in balance.”

Currently, shipping estimates from the Apple Store are still set for late January. That’s where they’ve stayed since the first pre-orders immediately sold out on October 16.

On the matter of iPhone Duo screens cracking, Ternus was brief and essentially repeated what Apple had previously confirmed: that the issue is real, but limited to a very small number of units.

Ternus told Reuters that “a very small percentage” of iPhone Duo units had been returned with display issues. Apple is replacing those units with new models.

#3363. Apple spent a record $45.77 billion on R&D in fiscal 2026, up 32%

Apple’s research and development expenses reached a new all-time high in fiscal 2026, climbing 32% year over year to $45.77 billion. Here are the details.

While it may have taken Apple longer than some wished it had to ramp up R&D in the face of growing competition in AI, the company has significantly accelerated its spending over the past year.

As Apple shared in its Q4 2026 results, it spent $11.73 billion on R&D, bringing its total spending for fiscal 2026 to $45.77 billion, a 32% increase compared to the $34.55 billion it spent in fiscal 2025.

During an earnings call earlier this year, former CEO Tim Cook said Apple was “clearly investing more,” adding that R&D was “accelerating much higher than the company” overall. CFO Kevan Parekh also explained that AI-related spending was being added to the investments Apple was already making in its existing product roadmap.

Interestingly, today’s figures also suggest that Apple’s R&D spending may be starting to level off.

While Apple’s Q4 2026 R&D expenses were up 32% from $8.87 billion in the year-ago quarter, they were virtually unchanged from Q3, increasing by just $1 million. As the chart above shows, Apple’s R&D spending jumped significantly at the beginning of fiscal 2026, but has since stabilized at a much higher level than in previous years.

But it was the song choice that boosted the clip: El-Sayed and his team opted for Taylor Swift‘s “You Belong With Me (Taylor’s Version).” The El-Sayed campaign team changed the lyrics of the song to reflect jabs at his opponent, Mike Rogers, and captioned the video to read: “Happy Taylor wedding …err, July 4th weekend” in a nod to Swift’s big day. It shouldn’t come as a surprise that the video racked up 5.7 million views.

Underneath the clip, several TikTok users claiming to be Swift’s fans left comments like, “Michigan Swifties unite!!!! Proudly voting for you sir 🫶☺️❤️,” “LMAO NOT MILLENNIAL SWIFTIE IN MY POLITICS SIGN ME UP,” and “This swiftie will be voting for you. 🫶” El-Sayed clinched the Democratic nomination for the Senate race in August, just a month after posting the clip. While the physician’s policies, like affordability, increased access to healthcare and AI regulation are what mainly brought Michigan voters to the ballot in support of Al-Sayed, his Swiftie status surely didn’t hurt.

Swift may not have endorsed El-Sayed, but the superstar also didn’t try to remove her song from his viral video either. When a constituent asked about Swift’s response to the clip, the Senator-elect pointed out, “Here’s the interesting thing, they never forced us to take it down.” That is interesting considering the fact that the superstar’s music was notably muted when Donald Trump and the White House social media teams tried to use the songs to soundtrack several videos in an attempt to bait a response from Swift. #3358. Why I'd Choose the Oura Ring 5 Over the Cheaper Ultrahuman Pro

Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro is now officially on sale in the U.S., which makes this the perfect time to consider how this new device compares to the reigning champ in the smart ring market, the Oura Ring 5. Here's the short answer: While there’s a lot to like in the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, ultimately I think the Oura Ring 5 is just better at doing its job.

I’ve spent plenty of time with both rings, and admittedly, many of the differences between the two will come down to personal preference—for example, do you like the biohacking concept and the “next best actions” suggestions in the Ultrahuman app, or do you favor the soothing vibes of the Oura app? But when it comes to the devices themselves, there are big differences between them in terms of size, cost, and overall ease of use. Here’s my take on each, and why Oura is still my top choice.

The Oura Ring 5 is impressively small, and when you have to wear something on your finger, size matters a lot—and generally, smaller is better. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I’ve ever worn. I have a ton of photos here comparing it in size to other smart rings (including RingConn, older Oura rings, and an older Ultrahuman); suffice it to say, the Oura Ring 5 wins this category easily.

When it comes to the interior fit, both rings are similar: mostly smooth on the inside, without any intrusive bumps. But considering the overall shape and feel, the Oura Ring 5 is just more comfortable to wear throughout an entire day.

The Oura Ring 5 comes with a plug-in charger, which isn’t very convenient, but will get the job done. You can buy a slim, rounded charging case that easily fits in your pocket for $99. You need to match the size of the case to the size of your ring, and the charging case is not compatible with earlier versions of the device. It’s good for 30 days of charge, according to Oura.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro comes with a charging case that is heavy and bulky with prominent corners, but good for an extra 45 days of battery life. The case fits any size of Ultrahuman Ring Pro, but is not compatible with previous versions. You can have the case play sounds if you’ve misplaced it.

The Ultrahuman ring lasts slightly longer on a charge: eight to 10 days, according to the company, versus six to nine for the Oura Ring 5. The Ultrahuman ring also has several different battery modes, with “chill mode” lasting me about two weeks.

To sum up: the Ultrahuman ring lasts longer on a charge and has more capacity in its charging case. You also get the charging case for free. But the Oura Ring 5’s charging case is smaller and much easier to carry around. Once again, we’re looking at two decent options: The Oura case is more expensive for what you get, but it’s also nicer to use.

Oura is the most expensive smart ring out there, and it requires a subscription. That makes it the priciest option, giving Ultrahuman an opening to beat it simply by virtue of being cheaper. But this one is closer to a wash, depending on the choices you make. If you’re looking for the cheapest possible smart ring, well, you’d probably end up with something else entirely, like a RingConn Air. But between the Oura Ring 5 and the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, the latter is cheaper than the Oura Ring 5...but only if you’re saying no to all the extras. Let me break it down.

The Oura Ring 5 costs $399 for the shiny black and silver models, and $499 for gold, rose, and the matte versions of the black and silver. The subscription costs $5.99/month (or $69.99/year, which is only a $2 savings), and the Oura is basically useless without the subscription.

Here's how the cost works out on an annual basis:

Oura Ring 5 in black or silver: $399 + $5.99/month subscription = $470.88 for one year, $542.76 for two years

Oura Ring 5 in other colors: $499 + $5.99/month subscription = $570.88 for one year, $642.76 for two years.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is $479 for all colors, and there is no subscription for basic use of the ring. But you can't necessarily stop there, because the Ultrahuman app includes “PowerPlugs” that will give you extra features or analysis screens. Some are totally free, including the caffeine window,  smart alarms, a new parent mode, and a limited version of the cycle and ovulation tracker, but others carry a monthly fee. And if you consider all the optional subscription fees for different PowerPlugs, they can quickly add up:

HealthEx, to connect medical records: $4.99/month

Most people probably wouldn't choose all of them, but even if you just wanted, say, respiratory health and cycle & ovulation pro, you’d quickly outstrip the price of an Oura Ring’s subscription. On the other hand, Ultrahuman also offers an Ultrahuman Max plan for $9.99/month or $99.99/year that includes all the PowerPlugs mentioned above, plus the Les Mills workouts that normally run $11.99/month. That's cheaper than subscribing to all of the options individually, but it will also make the Ultrahuman Ring Pro more expensive than the Oura Ring 5: $578.99 total for one year, or $678.98 for two years. In short, if you want everything that each ring has to offer, the Ultrahuman will cost you more.

Here's the big caveat: I wouldn't recommend bothering with most of the PowerPlugs. For example, "UltraSync for Tesla" recommends settings for your car based on how rested you are, which will be useless if you don't have a Tesla, and probably even if you do. "Cardio adaptability" measures a metric that Ultrahuman says is subtly different from HRV; Oura doesn't measure this adaptability metric, but it's not clear to me whether it's even worth measuring at all (I'd argue probably not).

Ultrahuman's respiratory health PowerPlug ($3.99/month) records sounds while you sleep, which Oura doesn't do; but Oura reports breathing disturbances based on the ring's data, which Ultrahuman doesn't do. Ultrahuman's feature is more expensive.

Ultrahuman offers a premium version of its cycle tracker for $3.99/month, while Oura has a partnership with Natural Cycles that cost $149.99/year. Either will provide more detailed (and, each company says, more accurate) cycle tracking than the basic tracking each app provides without the extras. Oura's option is more expensive.

Ultrahuman's HealthEx Powerplug ($4.99/month) displays information from your medical records throughout the app; Oura lets you import your medical records for free, but uses them mainly in the Advisor (chatbot) and dedicated areas of the app. Ultrahuman's option is more expensive.

Oura's app gives you scores for your readiness, sleep, and recent activity, and it tracks how stressed you seem to be throughout the day. A message at the top of the main screen gives you advice for what to do that day—for example, scaling back your workouts if you seem to be tired or stressed. Ultrahuman does pretty much the same thing, giving you a "next best action" that changes throughout the day, but tends to stick to predictable themes: get more activity if you've been sitting, and that sort of thing.

Both give detailed breakdowns of the factors that contribute to your scores, and both likely overstate how useful their scores are (you don't actually need to change your workout plans just because you had a less-than-perfect night of sleep). But the apps handle the basics pretty similarly: Both have partners and integrations, and you can book blood tests through either app, if you want to do that for some reason.

Ultrahuman gives you a bit more guidance on circadian rhythms, urging you to get in extra steps during certain times of day, and offering to micromanage your caffeine intake. It has a "longevity" tab that puts your long-term habits in terms of how many years they are supposedly subtracting from (or adding to) your lifespan, including measurable metrics like VO2max and a few things that are more inscrutable, like arterial stiffness.

Oura has a whole tab of "vitals" that it calculates from your day-to-day data, which I find more useful than Ultrahuman's data views. The items here include "resilience," which compares your stress to your recovery; a "symptom radar" that can sometimes flag when you're sick; and metrics of sleep regularity and how you're breathing. And, of course, you can check your "cardiovascular age" to see how much younger (or older) you should feel.

Overall, I prefer Oura's approach because the metrics make more sense, are easier to find, and are less likely to feel like they're going way out on a limb relative to the underlying science. Ultrahuman wants you to feel like a cutting-edge biohacker; Oura does a bit more to keep things down to earth. It is a bit funny to remember that both apps, and their wealth of data, are basically just pulling from heart rate readings throughout the day and night. Neither app gives you any truly important information the other doesn't, but Oura's makes more sense to me.

#3357. Apple says memory costs and Siri AI will weigh on holiday quarter profit margins

Following today’s earnings report, Apple held its quarterly earnings call, during which the company discussed the impact of rising memory costs on its profit margins and warned of additional pressure from Siri AI expenses during the holiday quarter. Here are the details.

Over the past few quarters, Apple has repeatedly warned that rising component costs would put pressure on its profit margins. Last quarter, gross margin was 50.1%, up from 49.3% in Q2. However, that included a roughly two-percentage-point benefit from tariff refunds.

Today, Apple reported that its gross margin fell to 47.9% in Q4 2026, with product gross margin dropping to 37.2%, down from 40.1% in the previous quarter. That represented a 2.2-percentage-point decline in company-wide gross margin and a 2.9-percentage-point drop in product gross margin.

Against the backdrop of record September quarter revenue of $114.5 billion, Apple CFO Kevan Parekh explained that tariff refunds once again provided some relief, though not enough to offset the impact of rising memory costs. He also noted that, excluding the impact of tariff refunds, the sequential decline in gross margins would have been roughly one percentage point, primarily due to higher memory costs:

“We saw strong performance in many services categories with all-time records in video, cloud services, payment services, and advertising, and a September quarter record in music. Company gross margin was 47.9%, and products gross margin was 37.2%. These both included a benefit from tariff refunds, which had a favorable impact of approximately 1 percentage point in the September quarter. When you remove the tariff refunds from both the June and September quarters, both company and product gross margin would be down about one point sequentially, primarily driven by higher memory costs.”

Parekh added that the pressure on Apple’s margins isn’t expected to ease anytime soon, with the company forecasting gross margins of between 45% and 46% for Q1 2027.

He attributed the expected decline primarily to higher memory costs, alongside the impact of the ongoing Siri AI rollout.

When asked to elaborate, Parekh explained that Siri AI will affect Apple’s margins in two ways. First, running the service will increase cloud costs. Second, Apple will have to spread out the recognition of some revenue from devices that include Siri AI over their lifetimes, rather than counting it all at the time of sale.

This, he added, is an accounting practice Apple already follows for other services bundled with its devices, such as Maps, Siri, and iCloud:

“Consistent with how we’ve always accounted for Maps, Siri, and iCloud, for the devices we sell that include these bundled services, we defer a portion of the revenue and recognize it over the life of the device.”

Meanwhile, CEO John Ternus described the current memory pricing situation as “unprecedented,” adding that Apple expects the cost of purchasing memory components to continue rising beyond the December quarter.

Ternus said recent price increases across the Mac, iPad, and iPhone lineups would help offset some of those costs, alongside existing inventory purchased at lower prices and savings on certain non-memory components. He also warned that the benefits of carrying lower-cost memory inventory would diminish over time. Apple did not say whether it expects to raise product prices yet again to compensate.
