#3330. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he says he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his company Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he says can yield “small data” solutions to big issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

The great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having said that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a new paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Having said that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing company with millions of users.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

“In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI

I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and said, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

Over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing new here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and said, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one company or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that showed up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand new model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very quickly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. New tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an important piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is important, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention quickly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

For example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an important tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

“In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng

Synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

To make these issues more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a company approaches Landing AI and says it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift issue. I find it really important to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and update the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

Ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent new neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s important for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor, where she helps develop and shape the magazine’s longform stories. She also oversees Spectrum's coverage of artificial intelligence and biomedical engineering. She holds a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University.

#3329. Eight 'Winter Arc' Rules That Will Actually Deliver Results

There are a lot of terrible social media trends out there aimed at self-improvement, yet even though everybody has been making fun of the "Winter Arc" craze, I actually think it’s a good one. During your Winter Arc, you promise yourself you’ll stick to your fitness and self-care routines during (and despite) the end-of-year chaos. It's a good goal, with one caveat: Make sure you choose rules that will actually improve your life and deliver results.

Think of the “arc” in the sense of a “story arc.” The Winter Arc is a self-improvement journey that unfolds over the last few months of the calendar year. The most hardcore #gymtok-ers will tell you the Winter Arc officially begins on Oct. 1, but others start in early November, or whenever they get around to it. The "when" isn't critical, though—whenever you read this is a fine time to start. The close of the Winter Arc is fixed, however: It ends Jan. 1, just as everybody who is less dedicated than you is waking from their holiday food comas and resolving to get in shape.

You get to choose your own terms for your Winter Arc. The general vibe is one of locking in, committing to your goals, and actually doing the things you’re always saying you’ll do. TikToker @carlyupgraded has said that her own mental image of someone nailing their Winter Arc is “hood up, headphones on, getting ready to go for a run in the rain at 5 a.m.”

It turns out I’ve accidentally been Winter-Arc-ing for years; I just didn’t know it had a catchy name. Why save your gym routine for New Year’s when you’ll have the place to yourself all December? We’re even gifted with an extra hour in the mornings to fill with something productive.

I really love the mindset shift involved. Commonly, people are active in the summer (great time for outdoor fun), may or may not stick with their routines in the fall, and let everything fall apart as the holidays approach. Who has time to go to the gym when you’re planning Thanksgiving, attending holiday parties, studying for final exams, or whatever else the end of the year throws in front of you?

But that’s the exact reason why this time of year is the best to start (or restart) a fitness routine, or really any kind of routine. When you start a routine during a busy time of year, you’ll be forced to make it sustainable. The gym routine you can stick with amid the chaos isn’t going to be one you drop after a few months. You’re already training yourself to work around obstacles as they come up, which is a key component of self-efficacy. And when the chaos clears on Jan. 1, your routine will be even easier to stick to.

Of course, there are ways to lean in too hard: Choosing unsustainable habits, falling for bad diet advice, mistaking not masturbating for some kind of health hack, the usual suspects. There’s also the pitfall of focusing too much on the vibes and too little on what you’re actually going to do or how you’ll benefit.

And then there’s the framing: You were working on yourself all year, but you’re in danger of letting up on the gas, but you’re committed to locking in so that you’re a step ahead of everybody who takes this time to slack off. I really don’t love this tack. Self-improvement is not a competition. There’s a difference between being consistent in your training and healthy eating (good) and seeing the pursuit of health and fitness as something where you always have to work harder because you’re at risk of getting left behind.

I also don’t love how gendered the Winter Arc TikToks tend to be. When you search for Winter Arc content, the first few suggestions include “winter arc for women” and “winter arc for men.” When I first started looking at the Winter Arc trend a few years ago, the women’s versions were more likely to include restrictive dieting or to focus on how the Winter Arc will finally (sigh) snatch your waist. These days, the focus is more on personal goal setting: Lots of the girlies filming their Winter Arc rules are doing so in a notebook and talking about journaling exercises that will help you identify what you need to work on to get to your "best self." Sometimes this is all monetized; training plans and journaling prompts can, of course, be purchased at the link in bio.

I do like that many of the women’s versions emphasize sustainability and setting your own goals rather than copying somebody else's. I don't love the enormity of the mental burden you're supposed to shoulder before even beginning. Should I really have to file an in-depth written report with myself before revamping every area of my life with a 100% commitment to multiple goals?

The men’s versions tend to go off the rails in another direction, with rules like “no girls” or “go ghost.” No distractions! Here, I've seen a shift over the years as well: at first there was overly serious content, followed quickly by satire (yelling at the viewer to get divorced and go work out in the dark). Now the men's videos tend to be more vibes-based, featuring images of pre-dawn workouts and plates full of salad with motivational quotes playing in the background. When the men give their rules, they tend to be simpler than the women's—no journaling exercises—but they often boil down to the same overly strict routines. (And then, of course, they'll offer to sell you a 90-day or 60-day plan.)

If you’re going to do a Winter Arc (or if you’re already doing one), make sure to structure it in a way that benefits you. Choosing 10 overly ambitious goals and setting yourself up for failure is not a healthy way to approach self-improvement, OK? Pick goals that are meaningful, achievable without divine intervention, and trackable with tools you already have at hand (for example, tracking your steps with a Fitbit or your running mileage with a Garmin watch).

It’s also helpful to think of developing yourself over this arc, rather than taking it as a three-month (or two-month) challenge where you have to do everything right all the time. If you currently wake up at 8 a.m. and want to wake up at 5 a.m., you don’t have to set your alarm for 5 a.m. tomorrow. It’s OK to aim for 7:30 a.m., make that a habit, then try for 7:00 a.m., and so on.

With that in mind, here are some "rules" I've seen from creators that I'm actually on board with (so long as you don't overwhelm yourself with them):

Wake up earlier. A great goal, especially if you take advantage of the time change to make things easier on your body.

Get to bed on time. Never a bad idea. Cultivating good sleep habits in general is always worthwhile.

Get your steps in. Be thoughtful about what your target is: 10,000 is not for everybody. Better to choose a number that would be a modest improvement on what you already do.

Exercise X times per week. Pick a number that works for you, and get into it. Be realistic about your goal, and for the best results, be consistent even if you’re sore at first.

Eat healthy. This is a great goal, with the major caveat that there are a lot of ways to eat healthy. You don’t need to cut out sugar or pretend that there’s something evil about seed oils. Do get more protein and veggies.

Be more thoughtful about using social media. I’m not going to tell you to delete all your apps (“except TikTok,” as the TikTokers say). But it’s fair to consider whether you might want to delete a few apps, turn off some notifications, or put your phone on Do Not Disturb for more hours of the day.

Journal or read more. Journaling can be great for working through your feelings or cultivating a creative habit. Reading can be entertainment or a great way to learn. Choose whichever you need most.

Learn a new skill. I’ve mostly seen this one in the men’s TikToks, and I love it. They’re often thinking of “skills” that will help in some kind of entrepreneurship grift they’re about to sell you, but there are tons of skills that will come in handy in life, or that are at least fun to learn. Practice a language, get better at cooking, make some art. Skills are, as I’ve noted, a multi-layered exercise for your brain. And they may come in handy someday.

This year I've slacked off on my fitness routine as I've gotten more involved in other hobbies, but I'm actually looking forward to being more consistent. My winter goals include exercising early in the day when possible and reading 20 minutes each day. (I'm even tracking the second one with a sticker chart.)

#3328. Apple explains the $400 premium for the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display

Apple argued that the touchscreen isn’t the headline feature of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, merely a bonus.

The headline should instead be the quality of the display itself – with the company effectively suggesting that the $400 premium is positively cheap for what you’re getting …

Apple published a white paper in which it argues that the latest MacBook Pro display is essentially a smaller version of its professional reference monitor, the Studio Display XDR.

$400 for the screen and new design isn’t my issue, my issue is the cost of storage and memory. $600 more to go from 24gb to 48gb or nearly a grand for 64gb. You can easily spend nearly double the cost of the machine just getting it to a semi-future proof spec.

Given that this costs anywhere from $2,899 to $3,599 just for a display (albeit a significantly larger one with a correspondingly higher resolution), this does put into perspective that $400 extra over the MacBook Pro with the standard screen. Here’s what Apple has to say about it:

PROLED XDR display, the best display in a pro laptop, finally overcomes these historic limitations. For the first time, a MacBook Pro display uses tandem OLED technology, delivering up to 1000 nits of sustained full-screen brightness, 2000 nits of peak high dynamic range (HDR) and standard dynamic range (SDR) brightness, and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio with accurate, per-pixel black levels.

It’s driven in real time by an all-new display engine in M5 Pro and M5 Max, which continuously compensates each pixel for content, usage, temperature, and ambient conditions—delivering creative precision out of the box and protecting panel lifespan over time. And a unique manufacturing process ensures panel-to-panel consistency and minimizes off-axis color shift, a first for any OLED laptop.

As Macworld spotted, that’s almost identical to the company’s description of the the Studio Display XDR.

In fact, the PROLED XDR in the MacBook Pro is the only display other than the Studio Display XDR that supports Apple CMF 2026, the next generation of CIE 1931. Apple says CMF 2026 “more precisely aligns the appearance of the display with an ideal D65 illuminant—the standard reference for white—and significantly improves appearance matching across display technologies, which is important for workflows that use multiple displays side by side.”

Resolution aside, the other specs are identical with just one exception: the contrast ratio. As for that exception, the MacBook display comes out on top with a 10 million to 1 contrast ratio, in contrast with the Studio Display XDR’s one million.

Does this change your own perspective of the price premium of the OLED model? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

Don't assume AI will be unbiased when it comes to data centers

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Ask ChatGPT about a major AI data center project, and you might get a fairly straightforward description of what it is, where it's being built and how much companies plan to invest. Ask Google AI about the same project's challenges, and you could walk away with a much more negative impression.

That's one of the findings from new research published by Five Blocks, a digital reputation management company that examined how eight AI engines describe 25 of America's largest AI data center projects.

The researchers found that none of the 1,200 general project descriptions they rated were negative. But when the question changed to what challenges each project faced, 55% of answers were classified as negative.

The differences between AI platforms were even more surprising. Google AI Mode produced negative answers to the challenges question 88% of the time, compared with just 6% for ChatGPT.

As AI data centers expand across the country, and Americans question what these projects could mean for their electricity bills, water supplies and neighborhoods, the research raises an important issue. The AI tool someone chooses, along with the words they type, can dramatically change the information they receive.

For the first study, published Tuesday, Five Blocks asked eight AI engines two questions about 25 major U.S. data center projects every day throughout September 2026.

The prompts were deliberately simple: "Tell me about [project]" and "What challenges does [project] face?"

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

That small change produced dramatically different results. General descriptions tended to emphasize a project's size, investment and technological ambitions. When asked about challenges, however, AI engines were much more likely to focus on problems or opposition surrounding the developments.

Some projects attracted considerably more negative responses than others.

More than 80% of challenge-related answers about Fermi America's Project Matador, Meta's Hyperion, Stargate and Vantage's Lighthouse were rated negative.

By comparison, Amazon's Project Rainier and Microsoft's Fairwater project in Atlanta received negative responses roughly 20% of the time or less.

Even projects belonging to the same company received different treatment. Microsoft's Atlanta development had a negative-response rate of about one in five, while its Wisconsin project approached seven in ten.

One particularly striking finding involved Microsoft's own AI assistant. According to the study, Copilot's general description of the Fairwater Wisconsin project incorrectly claimed the project didn't exist until September 24.

The results suggest that AI-generated descriptions aren't necessarily reliable snapshots of a project's current status, and different platforms may emphasize completely different aspects of the same development.

1. The neutral question: Tell me about Microsoft's Fairwater AI data center project in Wisconsin.Both agents immediately described the benefits of the AI data centers. Gemini called it a "purpose-built" campus while ChatGPT highlighted the amount of jobs the center would bring to the community. 2. The challenges question: What challenges does Microsoft's Fairwater AI data center project in Wisconsin face?While both agents shared the negative impact of data centers, both highlighted the "ambitions" of Microsoft. 3. The homeowner question: I live near Microsoft's Fairwater data center project in Wisconsin. Should I be worried about my electricity bills, water supply or property value? I found it annoying that ChatGPT created an image of the data center each time. It sort of glossed over any concerns and then created a survey about how close to the data center I live. Gemini told me that many fears were "over stated."

A second Five Blocks study, published November 2, examined how AI engines discuss data centers more broadly.

Researchers asked eight AI engines six questions about data centers every day throughout September, then compared their answers with responses about other energy and infrastructure developments, including pipelines, fracking sites, nuclear power plants, wind farms and solar farms.

They found that 83% of answers discussing data centers and their neighbors offered what the researchers classified as one-sided criticism. That was the same percentage recorded for oil and gas pipelines, but considerably higher than the 35% reported for solar farms.

Even questions specifically about economic benefits frequently produced qualified responses. Seven in ten answers about data center economic benefits included a counterpoint, compared with fewer than two in ten for solar farms.

Tax incentives were another recurring theme. Approximately two-thirds of answers concerning data centers and neighboring communities mentioned tax breaks, while nearly one-quarter brought up nondisclosure agreements.

ChatGPT was also an outlier in this study. According to Five Blocks, it was the only AI engine that consistently provided balanced responses about community concerns, while the other seven were rated as one-sided in nearly every evaluated answer.

There's an important difference between an AI chatbot giving a negative answer and giving an inaccurate one.

If someone asks about the challenges facing a proposed data center, it's reasonable for an AI assistant to discuss potential electricity demand, water consumption, local opposition and infrastructure costs.

Those are legitimate issues that communities and policymakers are already debating. And that's why the research illustrates a problem for anyone using AI to understand a complicated issue. Two systems can provide very different impressions without necessarily inventing any facts.

If you're researching a data center proposed near your home, relying on one AI-generated summary probably isn't enough.

A more useful approach is to ask questions that encourage the chatbot to consider different sides of the issue. For example, rather than simply asking what a data center project is, try this prompt:

Explain the potential benefits and drawbacks of the proposed data center in my community. Include its possible effects on electricity rates, water use, jobs, tax revenue and nearby residents. Separate confirmed facts from estimates and provide links to original sources.

You can also ask the chatbot to identify information it couldn't verify, explain which claims come from the developer and which come from independent sources, and distinguish between proposed plans and approved construction.

For a second opinion, run the same prompt through another AI platform. If ChatGPT and Google AI produce noticeably different answers, that's a reason to investigate the underlying sources rather than assume one chatbot must be correct.

The Five Blocks research shows why turning to AI for answers is an approach deserves caution, particularly on the topic of data centers. As more data centers are proposed around the world and in our own neighborhoods, it's best to get information from your town's own local planning board documents, utility filings and public hearing records. AI can help you do this research, but be sure to fact-check it on your own rather than relying on AI summaries.

#3324. Meet the Anthropic Engineer Keeping Its AI Agent Trustworthy

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

His data systems make sure Claude’s answers are accurate

IEEE Senior Member Gurmeet Saran is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind Claude’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs.

If you’ve ever wondered how Claude and similar AI agents can answer complex questions in seconds and where they get the information, you’re not alone.

Gurmeet Saran works to find that answer every day as an engineer at Anthropic in San Francisco, the AI research company behind Claude. The IEEE senior member is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind the chatbot’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs.

Gurmeet Saran Employer Anthropic in San FranciscoTitle Member of technical staffMember grade IEEE senior memberAlma maters University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India

University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India

Safety is a priority for Anthropic, he says. According to Claude’s mission statement, the company wants the AI agent to be “genuinely helpful to the people it works with or on behalf of, as well as to society, while avoiding actions that are unsafe, unethical, or deceptive.” Crucial to the mission is ensuring that researchers can observe and understand how AI models behave, a challenge that is especially acute for large language models, Saran says.

“We have decent tools to monitor databases and web services,” he says, “but for LLMs, we’re still figuring it out.”

Saran’s interest in computing systems dates back to his childhood in Kolkata, where he logged as much time as he could in the school computer lab.

“I remember the first time I used one of the computers,” he says. “What struck me was that you could write instructions, and the machine would follow them exactly. No ambiguity.

After graduating from high school in 1999, he stayed in India to pursue advanced degrees. He earned a bachelor’s degree in electronics and telecommunication engineering in 2004 at the University of Kalyani. In 2010, he earned a master’s degree in software engineering from the Birla Institute of Technology and Science in Pilani.

While a graduate student, he began his career in 2007 at Yahoo as a technical lead of the data team in Bengaluru, India. While there, he encountered the project that shaped his career trajectory: working on web analytics and business intelligence reporting solutions.

“We kept running into a frustrating problem,” he recalls. “Different teams would calculate the same website metric—something like daily active site users—using slightly different logic, and end up with conflicting answers. It sounds like a small issue, but when leadership is making decisions about resource allocation and product development using that data, not knowing which number is correct becomes a problem.”

The team built a central data repository with defined metrics, essentially serving as a single source of truth. Saran created a model that defined what “daily active site users” means, breaking down which events counted, how to handle edge cases (or when standard code fails), and more.

With the new model, data teams across the company could rely on a standard method to determine the number of daily active users for the projects and sites they were responsible for and obtain comparable results using the same logic.

From there, Saran and his team built Yahoo! Digits, an internal web analytics tool used for all the company’s products.

Saran left Yahoo in 2010 to join Intuit as a staff engineer in Mountain View, Calif. He helped build the analytics infrastructure that unified data across the company’s products, including TurboTax and QuickBooks accounting software. During his tenure, Intuit developed a feature that detected fraudulent tax filings in real time. It required Saran and other engineers to build a system to protect taxpayer data while adhering to strict U.S. Internal Revenue Service policies.

“IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations.”

Saran joined Meta (known as Facebook at the time) in 2016 as a lead software engineer in Menlo Park, Calif. The company was facing controversy over its video metrics: Meta publicly acknowledged an error that caused it to overstate the number of views for posted videos.

“This wasn’t a coding bug; it was an architectural problem,” Saran says. He built a system that worked similarly to what he had developed at Intuit, whereby one single truth was defined to govern all video view metrics across the site.

That system, Metric360, eventually became part of the site’s architecture. By the time he left Meta in 2021, he says, Metric360 was being used across the company to calculate video metrics.

He left the company to become a principal software engineer at Wealthfront, a financial services company in Palo Alto, Calif. He helped build the company’s data infrastructure.

Saran joined Anthropic in 2025 as a member of the technical staff.

To describe the implications of his work, he uses a medical analogy: “Imagine a doctor is monitoring a patient’s vital signs and making treatment decisions based on those numbers. What if one or a few of the medical devices used were slightly miscalibrated? Even if most readings are fine, it’s a serious problem because the difficult decisions happen in the margins.

“It’s the same with AI systems. My job is essentially to make sure the instruments are giving accurate readings—that the data means what it says it means.”

His job comes with high stakes and complex problems to solve.

“AI agents are especially tricky to observe,” he says. “When a system is taking sequences of actions [generating conversational responses with different users], you need a way to capture what it did, what information it was working from, and whether outcomes matched what the end user expected. And you have to do all of that without exposing anyone’s private information—the systems are designed to recognize sensitive data and keep it protected as it flows through. It’s a much more demanding observability problem than anything I’ve worked on before.”

Solving for system reliability while AI is still in its early days of adoption is both Saran’s passion and the problem that keeps him up at night, he says.

“I think making AI systems genuinely auditable and transparent is one of the more important engineering problems of the next decade,” he says, “and it doesn’t get talked about as much as model capabilities do.”

“After more than 20 years of building data infrastructure across organizations like Yahoo, Intuit, Meta, and Wealthfront,” he says, “I wanted to contribute back to the technical community through peer review, publishing, and engaging with the broader engineering research ecosystem.”

He says he believes IEEE can play an essential role in shaping the future of AI through its standards work.

“We have standards for everything, from building codes to software testing,” he says. “AI infrastructure needs something similar, and IEEE has the credibility and the reach to do that.”

Another problem that IEEE can solve for, he says, is access: “IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters, especially as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations in a few cities.”

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

Nobody wants their smart home turning stupid overnight. Here's how to future-proof yours

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, smart homes are hot right now – apps and AI are weaving their way into every facet of home life, from turning on the lights and checking security footage to adjusting the thermostat and managing your family's hectic schedule.

"Smart" doesn't always mean... smart, though, and embedding technology into everyday household appliances can sometimes backfire.

Take Neato Robotics' robot vacuum, for example, which ceased operating in May 2023 before its parent company, Vorwerk, phased out cloud services from October 2025 – leaving owners without app controls.

Some might laugh and point to perfectly functional "dumb" vacuums, but Neato is hardly alone in this brave new world: smart lights, cameras, thermostats, and myriad other gadgets can depend on services that might vanish overnight.

In 2026, when almost everything comes with an app or cloud features, buying smart is becoming increasingly important – especially if you want to avoid gadgets with a hidden expiration date.

While 'the cloud' might be nice branding, the reality is that many smart gadgets rely on physical infrastructure operated by manufacturers or third-party providers to process commands, manage features, and so on.

For cloud-dependent gadgets, then, the hardware isn't always quite as independent as it might seem.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The situation is exemplified by Belkin, one of the top smart home accessory makers. Back in January, Belkin discontinued cloud services for numerous WeMo products, affecting smart plugs and other household gadgets.

As a result, the WeMo app stopped working, alongside cloud-dependent features like Google Assistant integration. For anyone who'd paid good money for these gadgets, it was subpar, to say the least.

Some devices, however, got a reprieve of sorts: those already configured with Apple's HomeKit before the shutdown could continue working locally.

Even some really popular devices from large companies haven't escaped this. As Google migrated Nest devices to its platform, it discontinued support for some of the original Nest Learning Thermostats.

Not every gadget is like this, though. Some can communicate directly over your home network, keeping smart lights and plugs responding to commands without an internet connection or their manufacturer's servers – provided the local controller and network still work.

Enter Matter, a smart home standard backed by tech giants like Apple, Google, and Amazon that allows compatible gadgets to communicate locally with a controller, without relying on proprietary cloud services for basic functions.

Sadly, Matter is not a panacea. Some manufacturer-specific features, firmware updates, and remote access may still require internet connectivity, and certain products need an app or account for their initial setup.

Local control can offer a good amount of protection from a capricious company that cuts off your gadgets, but choosing the right devices in the first place is still key.

If you're buying new smart home gadgets, there are four things worth checking before handing over your money. We'll explore each of them in turn.

Devices that offer local control and Matter compatibility are a great place to start, as they're less vulnerable to manufacturers switching off cloud services. In our guide to the best smart plugs, options like the TP-Link Tapo Smart Plug Mini support Matter out of the box.

When the internet goes down, what happens? Can you still turn on the lights or adjust your heating? These are some of the key questions that will help when things go awry. Prioritize essential functions that can work independently, especially when it comes to expensive appliances or security equipment.

Choosing a subscription-free camera with local recording, for example, could save you a lot of headaches – although it's worth checking whether you can still access your footage without the manufacturer's app.

Research a manufacturer's support policies and commitments before buying, so you won't be caught out. A heavily discounted gadget might seem like an attractive option – only for you to discover it's already several years into its support period.

It's also worth checking the company's track record of withdrawing support or shutting down services; a promise of security updates isn't necessarily a guarantee that cloud features will survive.

Check whether your device can work with another ecosystem or controller – a compatible smart home hub could be useful here. As we saw with Belkin, existing HomeKit setups survived the shutdown, but owners couldn't configure their devices again afterwards.

Being able to reset and reconnect your gadgets without the manufacturer's servers could save you a lot of stress down the line

This smart plug from TP-Link is one of the best smart plugs for its small size and affordable price. It supports Matter, so it works across all major smart home ecosystems. Plus, its feature-packed app monitors energy usage and lets you schedule when the connected devices turn on and off. A great way to make any appliance "smart."

Smart home gadgets can make everyday life a lot more convenient, offering quick ways to control all manner of household devices, and there's no reason to be put off by the occasional corporate shutdown.

No connected gadget is entirely future-proof, and even the biggest tech companies can discontinue services – especially for older products with relatively few users.

A sensible approach, then, is to pick gadgets that can retain their essential functions even if the manufacturer's cloud services disappear.

A truly smart home is one that can still switch off the lights even when someone switches off the server.

#3321. Your Android Can Get Hacked Without You Doing Anything at All

You probably know that clicking suspicious links online or opening attachments from strangers in an email or text is a recipe for hacking. It's a dangerous world out there online, so it's always important to be vigilant. However, the danger doesn't always involve something you do. There are ways to hack your devices without requiring any intervention on your part whatsoever—and one such example is likely plaguing your Android device right now.

As reported by The Hacker News, there is a critical Android security flaw that could enable remote code execution on your device. In other words, bad actors could use the flaw to run their own code on your phone, effectively taking over the device for their own gain. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-58868, isn't universal, but it is widespread: It currently affects Android 14 through Android 17, the latest version of Google's OS. If your phone runs Android 12 or Android 13, it may be unaffected, as Google doesn't identify these versions in its security bulletin, but it doesn't explicitly rule them out, either.

There are two silver linings here, however. One, Google hasn't confirmed any active exploits for this security flaw. While that isn't a guarantee that bad actors have missed this exploit so far, it at least opens that possibility. As such, there may be time for users to patch their devices before hackers truly take advantage of the flaw. Second, Google does have a patch for the flaw. The patch may not be available to you right away, however, as it's up to both the manufacturer of your phone and your carrier to issue these updates. Still, a patch is, at the very least, on its way.

This flaw is perhaps the most important to fix, but it's not the only serious issue. In all, Google's latest bulletin highlights 216 vulnerabilities, and, of those, 23 are "critical." As The Hacker News explains, two other of those critical flaws could also allow remote code execution when exploited.

To see whether the patch is installed on your end, open the Settings app on your phone, tap "About phone" or "About tablet," then choose the Android version on-screen. Look for a date of "2026-11-01" or later. All security patches from Nov. 1 and on will fix this issue. If not, you'll ned to wait for the patch.

#3318. What Stood Out In Media Coverage Of Democrats’ Rout Of Trump & Republicans In Midterm Elections

Tuesday’s election results were a shocker, by both the number of seats that Democrats flipped in the House and the Senate and the scale of their victory. James Talarico won his race for U.S. Senate in Texas by double digits, after weeks in which prognosticators warned that his campaign against Ken Paxton would come down to the wire.

In fact, the Democratic strength appeared to have been underestimated, and Vice President JD Vance affirmed that in an X post on Wednesday, when he wrote that “the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.”

For the networks, it shouldn’t have been difficult to keep viewers glued, especially when results came in fast and furious from 9-11 p.m. ET. Here’s what stood out on one of the most surprising midterms in recent memory. Watch on Deadline

RELATED: Media Stocks & Markets Surge In Post-Election Rally, But Musk’s Companies Buck Trend

The Early Signs: After a day in which social media figures tried to draw conclusions from turnout data — a lot of it off the mark — it was a relief to finally get results when they started rolling in around 6 p.m. ET, when the polls in the eastern part of Indiana closed. That was when Rep. Victoria Spartz (R-IN) looked to be in trouble in a challenge from J.D. Ford. On NewsNation, Chris Stirewalt expressed surprise, saying: “Sweet, fancy Moses. How much of the vote is in?” CNN and other networks cautioned that it was still early, noting that the early vote tended to favor Democrats. In the end, Ford won, as did another candidate, Democrat Zach Dembo, who flipped a seat in another early poll-closing state, Kentucky. About an hour later, CNN’s Jake Tapper said, “I’d rather be on Team Blue than Team Red.” The initial results were a reminder that in hindsight, the signs of a wave were right there from the start.

RELATED: Hollywood A-Listers Send A Message To Voters On Social Media

More Than a Wave: Analysts and pundits started talking of Democrats’ overperformance from the start, but it wasn’t until networks started to call the South Carolina U.S. Senate seat for Annie Andrews that it became crystal clear this was more than just a wave. “Brutal,” said Sean Hannity on Fox News, which called the race in the 10 p.m. ET hour, not too long after NBC News.

Trump’s Media Rounds: For a president facing a rebuke, Donald Trump was making the media rounds, including an interview with The New York Times and an extended appearance on Fox News, after earlier raging at the network for platforming Democrats. The president gave no indication of challenging the results and congratulated the Democrats, which was some relief to democracy watchers worried of a protracted midterm challenge. While Trump weighed in on topics like Greenland to Fox News, perhaps the most interesting interview was during Politico‘s coverage, as Dasha Burns called him directly from her cell phone, giving a glimpse of what happens when a reporter calls him directly.

Trump told her, “I wasn’t on the ballot, and we didn’t get the people out, but I wasn’t on the ballot.” The president previously had told supporters to act as if he was on the ballot, but so be it.

RELATED: Nithya Raman & Karen Bass In Dead Heat As L.A. Mayor Vote Counting Continues In Nail-Biter Election

MS NOW’s First Election Night: This was the network’s first major Election Night since the split from Comcast — and it was perhaps fitting for the leftward primetime hosts that the solo outing would be for a blue tsunami. “For capital D and small D Democrats, and to everyone who voted for them tonight, that celebration can absolutely begin,” Rachel Maddow declared when the call was made that Democrats had regained control. One of the key moments came later in the evening, when Jen Psaki, citing a source, said that Sen. Susan Collins had conceded her Maine re-election race to Troy Jackson, even though major networks had yet to declare a winner. More and more, Election Nights have been turned into events for networks, all with the intent of keeping viewers within their own universe of coverage. MS NOW featured watch parties tied to its Membership service and featured coverage in Times Square, with its coverage on a big screen.

RELATED: Xavier Becerra Elected California Governor

Political Junkies: NBC News’ Kornacki Cam — a nonstop stream of its data guru Steve Kornacki — went for 10½ half hours. He made it to about 3:26 a.m. ET before announcing he was taking a break, but did not return. “I was sure 13 hours would be fine but things caught up to me in a hurry at hour 10,” he later wrote on X, apologizing for the abrupt ending.

It didn’t matter: Kornacki’s livestream ended up drawing 6.1 million views on YouTube, per NBC News, and the network led on watch time across four platforms monitored by Stream Charts.

Networks overall offered even deeper dives for viewers, what with CBS’s The Nerd Show and CNN’s Sightline. Their offerings were even more so than even 2024, in part to capture more political junkies and to compete with the many podcasters, influencers and creators offering their own midterm coverage.

RELATED: Mike Johnson To Step Down From House Republican Leadership After Democrats’ Blowout Victories In The Midterms

NewsNation’s Calls: The network called the House for Democrats at 9:11 p.m. ET and the Senate at 11:21 p.m. ET. NewsNation is teamed up with DecisionDesk HQ, a different data provider than other networks. There was some boasting about the network’s calls ahead of other news outlets, as they also had been the first to call the presidential race for Donald Trump in 2024. Leland Vittert said at one point on Tuesday, “I actually just texted the head of communications for the Talarico race and said, ‘Hey, you guys might want to turn on NewsNation because we’ve already declared the winner. And the other networks are 45 minutes behind.'”

#3317. 'Ocarina of Time' for Switch 2 Might Already Have a Weird Glitch

Thursday is a big day for Zelda fans. That's when the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time officially launches on Switch 2, marking the first major linear (i.e., non-open-world) 3D Zelda game since the 2016 Twilight Princess remake on Wii U. I, for one, have been waiting for this day for years. I loved the N64 original and the 3DS remake, so to have the chance to play a modern take on the definitive Zelda is so exciting—that is, if it actually runs as it should.

I stumbled upon this interesting post on X from Austin John Plays, a YouTuber with a host of Zelda coverage. According to Austin John Plays, Ocarina of Time already ships with a weird glitch that won't necessarily break your experience, but which may slow it down for a while, and perhaps even confuse players into thinking something is wrong with their game or their console.

As his post explains, if you're playing the physical copy of Ocarina of Time, and it's the first game you've ever played on your Switch 2—maybe you got one of those fancy new Zelda anniversary consoles and want to break it in properly?—you may run into glaring performance issues: The game may freeze, your controller may stop working, and the FPS may drop to single digits.

Luckily, Austin John Plays says the fix is easy: just wait. Eventually, your game will boot back to the title screen. When it does, don't try to play right away. Instead, close the game, restart your Switch 2, then try relaunching Ocarina of Time. Austin John Plays advises you may need to repeat this process two or three times, but after that, you shouldn't continue to run into issues. I wouldn't be surprised if Nintendo releases a patch right away for this glitch if it turns out to be as widespread as this post implies.

However, seeing as the game doesn't come out until tomorrow, there's something you can do to prevent it. Austin John Plays thinks the bug only impacts Switch 2 consoles that haven't run other games before. If you've had your console a while, you're likely set. But if you just bought the 40th anniversary Zelda edition of the Switch 2, you might not have had a chance to run a game on it yet. As such, download a game from the e-shop—even a free demo—just to get the system running. Hopefully, that will be enough to circumvent the glitch, and prevent issues when Ocarina of Time launches tomorrow.

#3316. John Ternus talks plans to improve Siri AI

During Apple’s quarterly earnings call, CEO John Ternus was asked repeatedly about Siri AI’s future. Here’s what he said about Apple’s plans for improving and expanding Siri AI.

Sometimes when Apple launches a new feature or product, the company sees its work as finished, and whatever ships goes unchanged for far too long. Many might characterize Siri this way, arguing the assistant went years without meaningful improvement or updates.

But according to Apple CEO John Ternus, the Siri AI that just shipped is only the beginning of what’s planned.

Yesterday on Apple’s quarterly earnings call, Ternus gave a rundown of Siri AI’s capabilities. He concluded: “We’re really excited to have rolled all these innovations out, and there’s still so much more we plan to do.”

This signals that Apple doesn’t see Siri AI as a feature that can now be left alone for a while. Instead, as we already saw in iOS 27.2 last week, Apple is focused on rapidly improving it.

Now that Siri AI is out, I would like to see it iterate as follows:

Support for a wider range of file types, such as PDF.

Accessing it from Search (especially on the Mac) should be instantaneous and reliable.

Proactively suggesting and reminding the user based on what it knows.

What are those future plans? It sounds like agentic capabilities may be among them. Ternus said:

With Siri AI, we really have the kind of—the Siri we always wanted. It’s primarily request-based today, but as we talked about at WWDC, it’s built on a modern, orchestrator-driven architecture that gives us real room to expand capabilities over time.

It’s telling that Ternus says Siri is “primarily request-based today” and mentions “room to expand capabilities” before pivoting to mention agentic features. It sounds like Apple is already, behind-the-scenes, envisioning and working toward a version of Siri that won’t need to be “primarily request-based.”

Finally, later in the call when discussing opportunities for services growth, including potentially launching new services, Ternus says: “We think intelligence is going to be another opportunity as well.” This refers back to an earlier discussion of Apple’s intent to charge a fee for expanded usage limits on certain Siri AI and Apple Intelligence capabilities. The idea is that as Siri evolves and improves, Apple will have opportunities to charge for certain features.

What are your takeaways from Ternus’s comments on Siri AI? Let us know in the comments.

How to improve auto activity tracking on the Fitbit Edge and Fitbit Air

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I just reviewed the Fitbit Edge and the Fitbit Air, and they are easily two of the best fitness trackers of 2026, and devices I’ll likely be recommending for the foreseeable future.

However, one key criticism I had for both: Unreliable auto workout detection. Less of an issue for the screen-sporting Fitbit Edge than the screen-free Fitbit Air, I was hopeful Google would be quick to address this complaint with a firmware update.

And sure enough, the Mountain View Mammoth did just that, announcing improvements to Automatic Activity Detection not just for the latest Fitbits but also the Pixel Watch 5 and older Pixel Watch models.

The update expands the list of trackable activities from just a handful, like walking and bike riding, to over 100, with lots of popular and nuanced exercises covered.

However, even without the latest firmware, there's a quick and easy way to improve auto activity tracking on the Fitbit Air and Fitbit Edge that's buried within the menus of the Google Health app.

This fix addresses one of the two key conditions needed for workout tracking to kick in. You see, Google wearables, by default, require a sustained heart rate and a minimum workout duration of 15 minutes for auto-detection to work.

However, users can manually lower the minimum duration to ten minutes, a change I've found tends to make auto-detection more reliable than the default settings. Here's how to change it.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Read on to see full illustrated instructions for each step.

To improve auto activity tracking on the Fitbit Edge, Fitbit Air, or Pixel Watch 5, first, open the Google Health app on your smartphone and tap on your profile picture in the top right corner of the screen.

Next, scroll down and tap on "Google Health Settings," and then scroll down and tap on "Activity" under the "Preferences" banner.

Once on the Activity page, scroll down and tap on "Activity Detection" near the bottom of the page under the 'Feature settings' banner.

On the Activity Detection page, go ahead and tap on one of the listed activities, like "Walk" or "Bike." Next, tap on "Minimum Duration" to adjust it to a shorter threshold.

Change the minimum duration threshold from the default to 10 minutes by swiping up or down on the options shown.

Finally, with the duration changed to 10 minutes, tap on "Save" and then the back button in the upper left to adjust the minimum duration for other workout types.

I recommend changing the workout duration to ten minutes — the minimum — for all of the activities listed, including walking, biking, and “All other workouts.” Unfortunately, when it comes to “Sports” workouts, the default duration of 15 minutes is the shortest option.

It’s also worth noting that users can revisit a mislabeled activity in the Google Health app and manually correct the workout type. Moreover, the more activities you log on your Fitbit or Pixel Watch, the better your device should get at auto-detecting your favorites.

Finally, keep in mind that auto-detected activities can take up to 30 minutes before appearing in the Google Health app.

#3313. Resurgent Box Office Drives AMC Theatres’ Record Q3: CEO Says Chain Has Finally Recovered

AMC Entertainment swung to the black for the three months ended in September on higher revenue, noting market share gains in both domestic and international markets with CEO Adam Aron calling the chain’s second consecutive record quarter.

The world’s largest exhibitor swung to a profit of $109.3 million from a year-earlier loss of $298.2 million. Revenue rose 31% to $1.7 billion and surpassed a previous all-time high achieved in Q2 of 2026.

During the quarter, the company completed a $3.97 billion refinancing covering approximately 97% of its debt, extending maturities to late 2031 and 2033, simplifying its capital structure and reducing cost of capital. Aron said that allows the company to “move forward from a position of significantly increased balance sheet strength.” Related Stories News Political Ad Revenue Breaks Record For Sinclair, Lifting It To Better-Than-Expected Q3 Results News Snap Swings To Profit As SPECS Set To Roll Out; Stock Takes A Hit

On a call after the earnings report, he also said AMC would be cash-flow positive for full-year 2026. Watch on Deadline

Strengthening the balance sheet has been his key priority since after the dark days of the pandemic pummeled theaters and was particularly devastating to chains like AMC, which already carried significant debt after years of expansion. Rumors of imminent bankruptcy have dogged the company for years since. On the call, Aron insisted AMC has outrun the crisis after paying down several billion dollars in debt over time and with the help of a newly healthy box office. “On this webcast, I declare that AMC has finally emerged from the storm clouds created by Covid,” he said.

The current fourth quarter continues strong with the October domestic box office up some 35% year on year, he said, anticipating upcoming films I Play Rocky, Wild Horse Nine, Ebenezer, The Further Misadventures of Cliff Booth, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, Dune: Part Three, Avengers: Doomsday, Mr. Irrelevant and Jumanji: Open World, which Aron called “an impressive and promising film slate that is a fitting close to a wonderful year for moviegoers.

He sees the remaining film slate propelling both the domestic and global box office to their highest full-year levels in seven years, with domestic box office easily hitting $10 billion or more.

“Today, we can finally say that AMC has recovered. To our studio partners, lenders, business partners, employees and our millions of passionate shareholders, thank you for standing with us as we traveled through a long, and at times brutal, road. Mere survival was never the goal. Our goal ultimately was to thrive, and that is exactly and precisely where our focus now lies. We are highly energized by the tremendous opportunities ahead.”

#3312. Apple Wallet driver’s licenses coming to three new states soon

Apple Wallet driver’s licenses recently launched in Virginia and Oklahoma, but three more states are expected to follow soon, bringing us close to 20 US states on board.

Digital IDs are becoming far more common than they were when Apple first added support in the Wallet app back in 2021. And today, 16 US states plus Puerto Rico support the feature on iPhone.

The latest additions, Virginia and Oklahoma, debuted just in the last couple months.

And it looks like three more states will be coming soon:

This summer evidence was discovered of both Utah and Virginia being added to Apple’s backend for driver’s license support. Virginia has since gone live, so it’s expected that Utah will launch as one of the next supported states.

Kentucky previously announced it will support Apple Wallet driver’s licenses after upgrading its digital ID system this summer. All indications are that the upgrade has been completed, so based on the state’s original plans, we should see licenses in Apple Wallet soon.

North Carolina recently announced the launch of its new digital driver’s license system. As part of the announcement, it confirmed licenses will be supported in Apple Wallet by early 2027.

Additional states might always surprise us and launch in Wallet before Utah, Kentucky, or North Carolina. We’ve seen a clear acceleration of states signing on to offer Wallet driver’s licenses.

But for now at least, the three states above appear the strongest candidates to debut soon.

For more info on states that have pledged Apple Wallet support, see our coverage here.

#3311. 10 Shows Like 'Phony' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What if you knew your mom wasn't really your mom, but no one believed you? That's the improbable but entertaining premise of Hulu's Phony, which stars Sam Nivola as a teenager who wakes up from a car accident and quickly comes to believe that his mother (Friday Night Lights' Connie Britton) is an imposter. Of course, no one believes him. I'm not sure I believe him, but it'll be pretty boring if it turns out that he just had a really bad concussion the whole time.

It's a coming-of-age drama and a surreal mystery with hints of comedy, and though it borrows elements from other shows, it stands apart for the skill with which it blends everything together. While you wait to see how the story plays out, here are 10 more twisted mysteries to stream now.

A twisty-turny (and well-reviewed) bit of fake identity folderol, Apple Cider Vinegar stars Kaitlyn Dever as Belle Gibson, a real-life Australian cancer survivor (except not really!) With a cheeky sense of humor and a willingness to distort reality, the show follows the wellness influencer as she fakes multiple cancer diagnoses in order to better market her alternative, MAHA-esque app and remedies to the unwitting. As her livelihood comes under threat, her lies grow more elaborate. Stream Apple Cider Vinegar on Netflix.

Alia Shawkat stars here as Dory Sief, an aimless millennial who decides, after seeing a missing-person poster for a college acquaintance, that she's going to make it her purpose to track her down—with the extremely begrudging support of her friends. But neither Chantal nor her disappearance are anything like what Dory expects. The show shifts focus from season to season. Initially a darkly comic take on a Nancy Drew-style mystery, it later finds the gang desperate to cover up a mostly unintentional murder, and getting in deeper each season. It's a funny, smart, and weird and shares talent with Phony in the form of writer/producer Anthony King, who serves as co-showrunner on the new series. Stream Search Party on Netflix.

This one's largely about adults, so it skips the coming-of-age angle central to Phony, but it has a quirky mystery, gaslighting, and a protagonist whose sanity is questioned by just about everyone all the same. This fun and very loose adaptation of the 1989 Tom Hanks film finds Keke Palmer's Samira and Jack Whitehall's Rob moving back to his impossibly safe and tidy hometown. Their house happens to be across the street from a dilapidated Victorian eyesore that may or may not have been the location of a murder a couple of decades before—a murder of a girl who made the mistake of trying to get away. As Samira adjusts to new motherhood and life on the cul-de-sac, she learns that even the nicest of her neighbors have secrets, and comes to suspect that her husband knows more about the missing girl than he's letting on. Stream The 'Burbs on Peacock.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate, working her way into the missing girl's social circle, and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Based on a Harlan Coben novel, Fool Me Once is a bit more of a political thriller than a coming-of-age thing, but we're still in "what the hell is up with my family?" territory: Michelle Keegan plays Maya Stern, a former special ops pilot dealing with the murder of her husband, whom she then impossibly catches playing with their daughter on a nanny cam. The resulting mystery ties into the earlier death of her sister and leads to a web of conspiracy involving her husband's family and a shady pharmaceutical company. Stream Fool Me Once on Netflix.

A vibe match more than anything else, this dark and twisty mystery with a slightly surreal sense of humor also features a single mom who is definitely not what she appears to be. Kim Mo-mi (Lee Han-byeol, initially), the Mask Girl of the title, is a uniquely complicated woman; she always wanted to be a K-Pop idol, but it was always made clear to her that she's not nearly pretty enough for that kind of stardom. So, in order to fill that void, she's got a side hustle. On top of her boring office job, she puts on a blonde wig and a mask to perform as a camgirl for anonymous men. It's a means to express herself creatively and sexually with a level of control—until a mistake causes her to lose that control, a co-worker discovers her secret life, and desperation leads to murder. The show shifts perspectives continually, feeling most like Phony when it focuses on Mo-mi's daughter. Stream Mask Girl on Netflix.

Flipping things around a bit, albeit in a similar "am I just being paranoid?" vein, The Girlfriend deals with a mom who may or may not be freaking out for no reason. Starring Robin Wright as Laura Sanderson, a wealthy art gallery owner in London whose son (Laurie Davidson) brings home a new, working-class girlfriend, Cherry Laine (Olivia Cooke)—immediately strikes Laura as not-our-kind. But is there more to it? Can someone with the name "Cherry Laine" truly be trusted? There's definitely something off, and we're kept guessing as to whether or not this is the story of a dangerous con artist or an overbearing mom—or maybe a little of each. Stream The Girlfriend on Prime Video.

Coming from Irish playwright and Derry Girls creator Lisa McGee, this show eschews the relatively subtle dark comedy of Phony for something much more gloriously surreal. Three high school friends from Belfast reunite after learning that an estranged bestie has died unexpectedly—except that maybe she didn't; a mixed blessing given that they all have secrets that they were hoping would be buried with the maybe departed. Now they're off to investigate the mystery of the murder(?), which turns into a hunt for the friend that they only thought they knew, while inadvertently revealing plenty of secrets of their own. The tone is all over the place in a way that somehow works, with flashes of sincerity balancing out the comedy. Stream How to Get to Heaven From Belfast on Netflix.

Shin Hye-sun offers up a phenomenal performance as Sarah Kim (well: sort of), a wealthy businesswoman who is discovered, at the series' opening, under a sewer grate. The police detective charged to investigate quickly finds inconsistencies in the woman's identity, and after interviewing Sarah's friend and business associate, comes to feel that neither woman is exactly (or anything, like she seems. Though it takes itself more seriously than Phony, it's still an addictively twisty mystery built around a constructed identity. Stream The Art of Sarah on Netflix.

There's a lot going on in this steamy, telenovela-esque drama. Camila Román (Carolina Miranda) finally meets Fernando Castell (Rodolfo Salas), a Tinder match, in Las Vegas, and things get very hot very quickly—he's everything he seemed to be and then some. If anything, she's the sketchy one: a dancer, not a nurse as she said, and with a possessive ex following her around. Still, it's all going great until she decides to surprise Fernando after he flies back to Colombia (which: never do that), and gets a totally different dude when she asks for him at his work. And that's just the beginning! Stream Fake Profile on Netflix.
